Father_Notes: William Airy was a farmer who through self-education acquired posts in the Excise; he later lost his Excise post due to financial difficulties.
Education_Institution: Byatt Walker's School; Trinity College, Cambridge
Education_Notes: Attended Byatt Walker's school at Colchester from age ten, where he learned arithmetic, bookkeeping, and the slide rule. Entered Trinity College, Cambridge as a sizar in October 1819 and graduated as Senior Wrangler in 1823, supporting himself by taking pupils from his second term onward.
Education_Locations: Colchester, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; Cambridge, Unknown, England, 1819, 1823
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Transformed observational astronomy in Britain through systematic reform of the Royal Greenwich Observatory. Made contributions to optics, including the invention of a cylindrical lens to correct astigmatism. Undertook numerical lunar theory based on Delaunay's equations. Published extensively on practical and theoretical optics, practical astronomy, and mathematical topics including trigonometry, partial differential equations, and error theory.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Lucasian professor at Cambridge (1826–1828) at £99 per annum, supplemented by £100 per annum as ex officio member of the Board of Longitude. Plumian professor and director of Cambridge Observatory (1828–1835) at £500 per annum. Astronomer Royal at Greenwich (1835–1881), the post that defined his career.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed Astronomer Royal by the Admiralty in 1835; the Admiralty's interest in navigational aids provided the institutional framework for his reforms at Greenwich.
Instruments_Notes: Invented a cylindrical lens to correct astigmatism, a method he studied throughout his life and which remains in use.

Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of mathematics at University of the Pacific (1891–1894); assistant astronomer at Lick Observatory (1895), promoted to astronomer (1907), associate director (1923), and director (1930); retired in 1935.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Superintendent of the Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew from 1783; compiled Hortus Kewensis (1789), a three-volume catalog of approximately 5,500 cultivated plants with descriptions of new species, provenance, and introduction dates. Recognized for superior practical knowledge of living plants and their cultivation.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Engaged by Princess Augusta in 1759 to establish and manage the botanical garden at Kew House; assumed full control of the gardens in 1783 under royal patronage.
Patronage_Notes: Patronized by Princess Augusta (who engaged him in 1759), John Stuart third earl of Bute (who encouraged him and introduced many new species), and Sir Joseph Banks (who befriended him and advised on the collection after 1772).
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by George Taylor. Aiton, Hortus Kewensis; or, a Catalogue of the Plants Cultivated in the Royal Botanic Garden at Kew, 3 vols. (London, 1789). Father_Notes: William Aiton was in charge of the living collections at the Royal Botanic Garden, Kew, and styled himself "Gardens to His Majesty."
Education_Notes: Attended school at Chiswick until age thirteen, then transferred to a school at Camberwell. At age sixteen entered Kew as assistant to his father, gaining practical knowledge of horticulture and experience with living plants.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Director-general of the royal gardens at Kew, Richmond, Kensington, Buckingham Palace, Brighton, and Windsor. Maintained his father's association with Sir Joseph Banks and worked to enrich Kew's plant collections. Co-founder of the Royal Horticultural Society in 1804. Prepared enlarged edition of Hortus Kewensis and an epitome thereof.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Succeeded his father as director-general of the royal gardens at Kew in 1793 and expanded his authority under George IV to include other royal gardens. Also worked as a landscape gardener, receiving commissions from the Duke of Kent and other nobility. After 1841 his authority was restricted to the pleasure grounds at Kew until his resignation.
Patronage_Notes: Served successive monarchs as director-general of royal gardens. Received invaluable patronage from Sir Joseph Banks until Banks's death in 1820, after which royal funding for Kew was severely restricted.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Horticultural Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: One of seven gentlemen who founded the Royal Horticultural Society on 7 March 1804 at Mr. Hatchard's House, on the initiative of John Wedgwood.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by George Taylor. Original works: Delineations of Exotick Plants Cultivated in the Royal Gardens at Kew (London, 1796); Hortus Kewensis; or a Catalogue of the Plants Cultivated in the Royal Botanic Garden at Kew, 2nd ed., 5 vols. Education_Notes: Studied mathematics under Masatada Irie of the Nakanishi school in youth; later studied mathematics and astronomy under Nushizumi Yamaji, who initiated him into the secret mathematical principles of the Seki school. He was over thirty when he began with Yamaji.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Refined the mathematics of the Seki school tradition, developing innovative work in geometry within an algebraic and numerical framework. Developed yenri, a method for determining areas of circles, spheres, and curved figures using techniques analogous to definite integration. Worked on logarithms, yo jutsu (circle inscription problems), and the volume of intersecting cylinders using double integration.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as a retainer of the Shinjo family, stationed in Edo throughout his life.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Shin'ichirō Oya. Works: Fukyu sampo; Kohai jutsu kai; Enchu kokuen jutsu.
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Shin'ichirō Oya.

Alt_Name: Alanus de Insulis; Alain of Lille
Education_Institution: University of Paris; University of Montpellier
Education_Notes: Taught theology at Paris and Montpellier; no formal degree is recorded.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; Montpellier, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Member of the Cistercian order; wrote against the Albigensians.
Scientific_Disciplines: Philosophy; Theology; Natural Philosophy; Astronomy; Arithmetic; Geometry
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Attempted to construct a deductive theology derived from axioms in the manner of mathematics. Influenced by Neoplatonic philosophy and Boethius. In the Anticlaudianus, alluded to astronomical concepts including the eccentric and possibly the equant, and mentioned Ptolemy and Abū Maʿshar. Treated arithmetic and geometry as components of the liberal arts within his allegorical framework.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught theology at Paris and Montpellier; became a member of the Cistercian order.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Claudia Kren. Original works: Thomas Wright, The Anglo-Latin Poets and Epigrammatists of the Twelfth Century (London, 1875); R. Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Claudia Kren.

Alt_Name: Honoré Charles Grimaldi; Albert of Monaco
Father_Notes: Charles III of Monaco (Honoré Grimaldi); Albert succeeded him as sovereign prince in 1889.
Education_Notes: No formal education is recorded. Trained as a naval officer; served as lieutenant-commander in the French navy during the Franco-Prussian War (1870).
Scientific_Disciplines: Oceanography; Natural History; Zoology; Physiology; Anthropology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer oceanographer who conducted nearly forty years of systematic North Atlantic voyages (1873–1915), studying currents, water temperature, bathymetry, and deep-sea fauna. Investigated the venom of Physalia and contributed to the discovery of anaphylaxis. Conducted plankton research to depths exceeding 6,000 meters. Also founded institutions devoted to anthropology and human paleontology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Financed his oceanographic expeditions from personal wealth as a sovereign prince. Founded and directed the Musée Océanographique de Monaco (1910) and Institut Océanographique, Paris (1911), establishing publications to disseminate findings.
Patronage_Notes: As Prince of Monaco from 1889, he held sovereign authority and used his position and resources to advance oceanographic science.
Instruments: Hirondelle; Hirondelle II; Princesse Alice I; Princesse Alice II; Richard bottle; Polyhedral nets
Instruments_Notes: Commissioned and captained four research vessels over four decades, progressively upgrading equipment. Used the Richard bottle to sample water at depth and measure temperature gradients. Designed large baited polyhedral nets for deep-sea fauna collection, achieving record dredging depths of 6,035 meters.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences, Paris; Académie de Médecine; Académie d'Agriculture
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Corresponding member of the Académie des Sciences; elected foreign associate member in 1909, succeeding Lord Kelvin. Foreign associate of the Académie de Médecine. Member of the Académie d'Agriculture for model farming practices at his estate.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Georges Petit. Original works include Sur le Gulf-Stream (Paris, 1886); numerous articles in Comptes rendus de l'Académie des sciences, Bulletin du Musée Océanographique, and Bulletin de l'Institut Océanographique (1885–1921); La carrière d'un navigateur (Monaco, 1901; 1966 ed. with introduction by J.-Y. Cousteau). Secondary literature: C. Carpine, Les navires océanographiques (1966); R. Damien, Albert Ier Prince Souverain de Monaco (1964); M. Fontaine, La découverte de l'anaphylaxie (1951); L. Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Georges Petit.

Alt_Name: Albert de Ricmestrop; Albertus de Saxonia
Father_Notes: Bernard de Ricmestorp was a well-to-do burgher of Helmstedt.
Education_Notes: Studied at the University of Paris, obtaining the master of arts degree in 1351. Studied theology but never received a theological degree. Influenced by Jean Buridan and Nicole Oresme at Paris.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1351
Religion_Notes: Held benefices and ecclesiastical positions including parochial priest at Laa and canon of Hildesheim. Accused of heresy by some clergy who claimed he taught astrological determinism denying human free will, but survived the accusation.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Wrote extensive questions on Aristotle's Physics, De caelo et mundo, and other natural philosophical treatises, closely modeled on Buridan's work. Composed the Tractatus proportionum on mathematical analysis of motion, synthesizing Oxford mathematical traditions with Buridan's dynamics. Authored a comprehensive logic textbook integrating Ockham and Buridan. Contributed intelligent discussions of projectile motion and gravitational acceleration, though lacked originality as primarily a transmitter of earlier scholastic ideas.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught on the faculty of arts at the University of Paris and served as rector in 1353. First rector of the University of Vienna in 1365. Held ecclesiastical benefices and served as bishop of Halberstadt from 1366 until his death, though his bishopric was marked by political and financial difficulties.
Patronage_Notes: Pope Urban V commissioned various works and obtained a benefice at Mainz for him. Albert played a major role in obtaining papal authorization for the establishment of the University of Vienna.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Ernest A. Moody. Original works: Expositio aurea et admodum utilis super artem veterem (Bologna, 1496); Quaestiones subtilissimae super libros Posteriorum (Venice, 1497); Logica Albertutii (Venice, 1522); Sophismata (Paris, 1490, 1495); Subtilissimae quaestiones super octo libros Physicorum (Venice, 1504, 1516); Quaestiones in libros de caelo et mundo (Pavia, 1481; Venice, 1492, 1497, 1520); Tractatus proportionum (Bologna, 1502, 1506; Padua, 1482, 1484, 1487; Venice, 1477, 1494, 1496; Paris, s.a.). Zoubov, Quelques Observations sur l'Auteur du Traité Anonyme (Isis, 1959).
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Ernest A. Moody.

Father_Notes: Colonel in Württemberg and teacher at the Karlsschule in Stuttgart; ennobled in 1807. Mother came from middle-class family with court connections.
Education_Notes: Entered the Bergkadettenkorps in Stuttgart in 1809, where he received instruction in general scientific subjects and specialized training in mineralogy, geology, and mining.
Education_Locations: Stuttgart, Unknown, Germany, 1809, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering investigator of Triassic formations in southwest Germany; coined the term Triassic for the oldest Mesozoic formations and characterized its three divisions by petrographic and paleontologic features. Also investigated crystalline slate and eruptive rocks in the Black Forest.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held positions at Württemberg saltworks from 1815 onward, including inspector at Friedrichshall (1820), manager at Wilhelmshall (1828–1852), mining counselor (1836), and manager again at Friedrichshall (1852–1870). Recognized as one of the foremost saltmining engineers.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed mining counselor in 1836 by the Württemberg government.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Hans Baumgärtel. Father_Notes: Lorenzo Alberti was a member of the wealthy Florentine bourgeoisie engaged in commercial and banking enterprises with branches across Europe; he died suddenly while in Venice, leaving Leone Battista and his siblings orphaned.
Education_Institution: University of Padua; University of Bologna
Education_Notes: Advanced education began at Padua; continued at Bologna after 1421 where he studied law and received a doctorate in canon law. Pursued mathematics, natural sciences, and physics at an advanced level as relaxation from legal studies.
Education_Locations: Padua, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown; Bologna, Unknown, Italy, 1421, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Served as a functionary at the papal court from 1432 onward and was part of Pope Eugene IV's entourage.
Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; Physics; Natural History; Engineering; Optics; Geometry
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Wrote Ludi matematici on mathematical problems including lunules and the squaring of the circle; composed lost treatises on motion and weight (De motibus Ponderis) and mathematical commentaries. Contributed to optics through theory of vision and the camera obscura. Applied mathematics and physics to engineering, town planning, and architecture. Speculated on natural phenomena including earthquakes, water circulation, plant decomposition, and fossils.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as functionary at the papal court from 1432; was in the service of a cardinal between 1430 and 1432 who took him to France, Belgium, and Germany. Worked for humanistic families ruling principalities, including the Malatesta court at Rimini. Practiced as painter, sculptor, and architect.
Patronage_Notes: Served Pope Eugene IV and the papal court; was in the entourage of a cardinal (1430–1432); worked at the court of the Malatesta family at Rimini where he designed the Malatesta Temple.
Instruments: Camera Obscura; Topographical Instruments; Odometer; Sulcometer
Instruments_Notes: Developed or described various instruments including the camera obscura (possibly borrowed from Brunelleschi), topographical instruments for surveying, an odometer for measuring land distances, and a sulcometer for measuring distances traveled by ships. Also discussed balances, clocks, sundials, pulleys, water mills, windmills, and canal locks.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Bertrand Gille. Original works: De re aedificatoria (Florence, 1485); Opere volgari dei L.B. Education_Notes: Received elementary education in Nuremberg after the family moved there in 1541. Studied medicine at Wittenberg, earning M.D. in 1574, and taught in the medical faculty there for many years.
Education_Locations: Wittenberg, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1574
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Chiefly interested in anatomy. Conducted early public demonstrations of venous valves beginning in 1579 and provided the first illustrations of them in his Tres orations (1585). Also studied the lacrimal apparatus, ileocecal valve, cochlea, renal papillae, and problems of deafness and muteness. Investigated scurvy and recommended citrus fruit as preventive.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught in the medical faculty at Wittenberg for many years. In 1592 became physician to Duke Friedrich Wilhelm of Saxony.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed physician to Duke Friedrich Wilhelm of Saxony in 1592.

Alt_Name: Albert the Great; Universal Doctor; Albert of Lauingen; Albert of Bollstädt
Father_Notes: Born into a wealthy and powerful family of the military nobility; childhood spent at family manor in Bollstädt.
Education_Institution: University of Padua; University of Paris; University of Cologne
Education_Notes: Studied liberal arts at Padua; recruited into Dominican Order by Jordan of Saxony; likely studied theology and was ordained a priest in Germany; taught in various priories before being sent to University of Paris ca. 1241; became first German Dominican master of theology and lectured in the chair for foreigners (1245–1248); established studium generale at Cologne in 1248.
Education_Locations: Padua, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, 1241, 1248; Cologne, Unknown, Prussia, 1248, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Dominican friar; took part in Council of Lyons (1274); attempted to block the condemnation of 1277 affecting Aquinas' teachings; canonized by Pope Pius XI on 16 December 1931; declared patron of all who cultivate the natural sciences by Pope Pius XII on 16 December 1941.
Scientific_Disciplines: Natural Philosophy; Physics; Optics; Mechanics; Astronomy; Botany; Zoology; Anatomy; Embryology; Medicine; Alchemy; Mineralogy; Natural History; Mathematics; Logic; Metaphysics; Philosophy
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Principal importance derives from rediscovering Aristotle and introducing Greek and Arab science into medieval universities. Composed monumental paraphrase of all known works of Aristotle and Pseudo-Aristotle (17 of 40 volumes in Cologne edition). Practiced empiricist methodology with detailed observations of natural phenomena. Made advances in optics (refraction, burning lens), acoustics, heat, and rainbow theory. Speculated on composition of Milky Way and lunar surface features. Compiled list of ~100 minerals with properties. Excelled in biological sciences with masterwork De vegetabilibus et plantis; pioneered systematic plant classification and morphology. De animalibus includes detailed studies of reproduction, embryology, and insect behavior; described northern animal types unknown to Aristotle. Contributed to veterinary and medical science.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught theology and natural philosophy at University of Paris (1245–1248) and established and taught at studium generale at Cologne (from 1248). Served as provincial of German Dominicans (1253–1256) and bishop of Regensburg (1260–1262). Spent latter part of life in preaching and teaching, mainly at Cologne.
Patronage_Notes: Recruited into Dominican Order by its master general Jordan of Saxony; supported by Dominican leadership in his scholarly work.

Father_Notes: Father Friedrich Wilhelm Albrecht was a soap boiler; both grandfathers were also soap boilers, and maternal grandfather Christian Friedrich Pohle was a senior official of the soap boilers' guild of Dresden.
Education_Institution: Polytechnicum in Dresden; University of Leipzig
Education_Notes: Studied mathematics and natural sciences at the Polytechnicum in Dresden (an engineering school), passing examinations around 1865. Subsequently studied astronomy at the University of Leipzig to develop theoretical knowledge; graduated in 1869.
Education_Locations: Dresden, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1865; Leipzig, Unknown, Germany, 1865, 1869
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Specialized in precise astronomical and geodetic measurements, particularly longitude and latitude determination using electrical telegraph methods. Directed the Geodetic Institute's astronomy department and the International Latitude Service, establishing precise geographic coordinates across Europe and internationally.
Means_of_Support_Notes: From 1866 assistant in the central European degree measurement project. Appointed to the newly founded Geodetic Institute in Potsdam in 1869; appointed director of its astronomy department in 1873, a post held until his death. Became professor in 1875.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed director of the astronomy department at the Geodetic Institute in Potsdam, a state research institution.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: International Latitude Service
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Directed the International Latitude Service from 1895 onward, a cooperative network of research institutes across multiple countries coordinating precise latitude determination.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Hans Baumgärtel. Original works include dissertation "Über die Bestimmung von Längendifferenzen mit Hilfe des elektrischen Telegraphen" (Leipzig, 1869); "Genauigkeit der telegraphischen Ortsbestimmung," Astronomische Nachrichten 89 (1877); "Ausgleichungen des deutschen Längenbestimmungsnetzes," ibid. 95 (1879); "Provisorische Resultate der Beobachtungsreihen Berlin, Potsdam und Prag betr. der Veränderlichkeit der Polhöhe," Internationale Erdmessung, Publikationen (Berlin, 1890); "Stand der Erforschung der Breitenvariation," Internationale Erdmessung, Verhandlungen (Berlin, 1894–1896); multiple longitude determinations (Potsdam–Pulkovo 1901, Potsdam–Greenwich 1903, Potsdam–Jena–Gotha–Göttingen 1909); "Bestimmung der Polhöhe und des Azimutes in Memel im Jahre 1907," ibid. Education_Notes: Pupil of Pythagoras; studied in Crotona in close contact with Pythagoreans and physicians.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Wrote on medical affairs, meteorological and astrological problems, and philosophical questions including the immortality of the soul. Formulated a general pathophysiology of internal diseases based on the balance of opposite bodily qualities and classified disease causes into environmental, nutritional, and lifestyle factors. Engaged in ocular dissection to investigate vision.

Father_Notes: Born of a noble Northumbrian family.
Education_Notes: Educated at the cathedral school of York under archbishops Egbert and Aelbert, where he was exposed to the finest pedagogical traditions of early English learning and the legacy of the Venerable Bede. Became head of the school and library in 778.
Education_Locations: York, Unknown, England, Unknown, 778
Religion_Notes: Cleric; sent to Rome in 780 to receive the pallium as part of his ecclesiastical duties.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Promoted the study of the seven liberal arts (trivium and quadrivium) in the Frankish realm. Expressed interest in astronomy motivated by calendrical calculations and the computus. Authored mathematical puzzles requiring geometrical and algebraic solutions. Wrote elementary textbooks and dialogues on natural philosophy and the physical world, though with limited scientific depth.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Head of the cathedral school of York from 778; appointed minister of education to Charlemagne in 782 and leading spirit of the palace school. Granted the abbeys of Ferrières, Troyes, and St. Martin at Tours.
Patronage_Notes: Served as educational advisor and minister of education to Charlemagne, who rewarded him with abbeys and supported his educational reforms.

Duemmler, eds., Monumenta Alcuiana, Vol. VI of Bibliotheca Rerum Germanicarum, P. Jaffe, ed. (Berlin, 1873). Secondary: E.S. Duckett, Alcuin, Friend of Charlemagne (New York, 1951); C.J.B. Father_Notes: Father was a schoolteacher in the industrialized Kattowitz region of Upper Silesia.
Education_Institution: University of Berlin; University of Kiel
Education_Notes: Completed Oberrealschule in Berlin; studied chemistry at University of Berlin and University of Kiel, where he earned his doctorate in 1926 under Otto Diels with a dissertation on the azoester reaction.
Education_Locations: Berlin, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Kiel, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1926
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Developed the diene synthesis (Diels-Alder reaction), a major synthetic method in organic chemistry involving the addition of dienes to dienophiles. Demonstrated the reaction's broad scope, stereochemical properties, and applications in structural analysis, terpene chemistry, and biosynthesis. Shared the 1950 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Otto Diels.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Reader in organic chemistry at University of Kiel (1930); extraordinary professor at Kiel (1934); research director at Bayer Werke in Leverkusen (1936–1940); ordinary professor and director of the chemical institute at University of Cologne (1940–1958); dean of the Faculty of Philosophy at Cologne (1949–1950).
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Aaron J. Ihde. Father_Notes: Born and brought up in extreme poverty.
Education_Notes: Began formal education as an adult at Bologna; within a few years (ca. 1260) was teaching at the university. No degree is named in the source.
Education_Locations: Bologna, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, 1260
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: One of the founders of medical study at Bologna. Established the dialectical method of teaching in the medical school, which persisted until the sixteenth century. Developed the Consilia, a new form of medical literature comprising clinical cases with treatment advice. Commentaries on Hippocrates, Galen, Hunayn Isḥāq, Avicenna, and other classical and Islamic writers. Advocated for better translations of classical and Arabic medical texts and encouraged readers to consult originals alongside commentaries.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught medicine at the University of Bologna from ca. 1260. Also a well-known and successful medical practitioner with a reputation for charging very high fees; Pope Honorius IV was among his patients.
Patronage_Notes: Pope Honorius IV was one of his patients.

Education_Notes: No formal education is mentioned in the entry.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted extensive experiments on galvanism and animal electricity, including work on muscular contraction in dissected animal parts and living tissue. Investigated the velocity of electric current and applied galvanic principles to practical problems including lighthouses and quarrying.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of physics at the University of Bologna from 1794.
Patronage_Notes: Knighted by the emperor of Austria and made councillor of state in Milan.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Academia della Scienze di Bologna; Société Galvanique of Paris
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Presented experimental results to the Academia della Scienze di Bologna; lectured before the Société Galvanique of Paris in 1802. Helped organize a society at Bologna to promote galvanism.

Father_Notes: Teseo Aldrovandi was a notary and secretary of the Senate of Bologna; the family was of noble status.
Education_Notes: Studied mathematics under Annibale della Nave in Bologna; Latin under Giovanni Gandolfo; law for seven years; philosophy under Bologna masters; attended University of Padua around 1545 to study medicine and mathematics under Pietro Catena. Received M.D. on 23 November 1553.
Education_Locations: Padua, Unknown, Italy, 1545, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Charged with heresy upon return to Bologna from Padua, probably due to the university's reputation for teaching Averroës' doctrines; exonerated himself in Rome. His mother was a first cousin of Pope Gregory XIII.
Scientific_Disciplines: Natural History; Botany; Zoology; Ornithology; Ichthyology; Embryology; Teratology; Mineralogy; Pharmacology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in systematic natural history, extending the study of medicinal plants to encompass animals and minerals. Conducted embryological studies examining chick development day by day, demonstrating that the heart forms in the yolk sac and precedes liver formation. Collected specimens across Italy and established a comprehensive museum. Published major illustrated folios on birds, insects, animals, fish, serpents, and minerals.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Admitted to the Collegio dei Dottori in 1553, entitling him to practice medicine and teach. Appointed teacher of logic at University of Bologna with support from a senator uncle. Later appointed professor of the history of simples (1561) and curator of the botanical garden. Received financial support from Pope Gregory XIII for publication of his works.
Patronage_Notes: Pope Gregory XIII, his mother's first cousin, granted him a large sum of money to aid publication of his works and provided benevolence and esteem.

Father_Notes: Chevalier Destouches-Canon, a cavalry officer, located the abandoned infant and arranged his upbringing and education.
Education_Notes: Attended Collège de Quatre-Nations (Mazarin), a Jansenist school offering classics, rhetoric, and mathematics. Initially studied law and medicine before turning to mathematics. Self-taught in advanced mathematics through study of Varignon, Newton, L'Hospital, and the Bernoullis.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Raised in a Catholic environment; attended a Jansenist school. Rejected a religious career despite family expectations.
Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; Physics; Mechanics; Fluid Mechanics; Celestial Mechanics; Calculus
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in mathematical physics and rational mechanics. Formulated d'Alembert's principle and the wave equation. Developed partial differential equations and techniques for solving them. Contributed to fluid mechanics, celestial mechanics (precession of equinoxes), and the calculus of limits. Also wrote on music theory.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Adjoint in astronomy at the Académie des Sciences from 1741; associé géomètre from 1746. Supported by patrons including Frederick the Great (visited court in 1764). Lived with adoptive family until age 47.
Patronage_Notes: Visited and was repeatedly invited by Frederick the Great to the Prussian court; declined permanent appointment as president of the Prussian Academy. Supported by salon society, particularly Mme. du Deffand and Mlle. de Lespinasse.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences; Académie Française; Prussian Academy; other European scientific academies
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to Académie des Sciences in 1741. Elected to Académie Française in 1754, largely due to his Discours préliminaire to the Encyclopédie. Elected perpetual secretary of the Académie Française in 1772.

Education_Notes: Studied under the Peripatetic philosophers Herminus, Sosigenes, and Aristocles. No formal degree is recorded.
Scientific_Disciplines: Philosophy; Logic; Metaphysics; Natural Philosophy; Mathematics; Optics
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Peripatetic philosopher renowned as an interpreter of Aristotle's doctrines. Major contributions to noetics (theory of intellect), psychology, metaphysics, logic, natural philosophy, and ethics. Developed theories of intelligibles, human and divine intellect, free will, fate, providence, and vision. Commented extensively on Aristotelian texts and engaged with Stoic and mathematical problems.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught philosophy as a Peripatetic master; his reputation rests on his scholarly interpretation and commentary on Aristotle.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Compiler of zoological and natural history works emphasizing animal behavior and lore. Authored On Animals, a principal source on birds later cited by Athenaeus; wrote on theriac and its curative properties; compiled dream interpretations based on plant and bird properties. Followed Aristotle in zoological reporting.

Alt_Name: Alexander of Tralles; Alexandros of Tralles
Father_Notes: Stephanus was a physician; Alexander had four brothers, including Anthemius (a mechanician involved in rebuilding Hagia Sophia) and Dioscorus (also a physician), indicating a family of educated professionals.
Education_Notes: No formal education is recorded. Alexander was the protégé of the father of Cosmas and wrote his medical work at an advanced age when he could no longer practice.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Practiced internal medicine with extensive clinical experience and original observations. Wrote a twelve-book handbook on internal medicine, including works on fever and intestinal worms. Known for empiricism, self-reliance, and willingness to criticize Galen. His work was influential in Byzantine medicine and widely translated into Latin and Arabic.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced medicine extensively in Rome, Gaul, and Spain. Wrote his medical handbook at an advanced age when he could no longer practice actively.

Alt_Name: Alfonso el Sabio; Alfonso the Learned; Alfonso X of Castile
Father_Notes: Son of Ferdinand III of Castile and León; mother was Beatrice of Swabia, granddaughter of Frederick Barbarossa. Descended from the Hohenstaufens.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Sponsored the Tablas alfonsinas, a new edition of al-Zargālī's astronomical tables with observations made 1262–1272, employing Ptolemaic celestial mechanics, mean orbits, equations, declination, and trigonometric theory of sines and chords. Supported the Libros del saber de astronomia, a fifteen-treatise collection on astronomical instruments including astrolabes, quadrants, and clocks. Encouraged translation of Arabic astronomical and astrological works. Also sponsored a vernacular translation of the Liber picatrix, an Arabic work on magic.
Means_of_Support_Notes: King of Castile and León from 1252; ruled until deposed by the Cortes in 1282, though Seville remained loyal.
Patronage_Notes: As king, Alfonso directly patronized astronomical and scientific translation projects at his court, including the Tablas alfonsinas and the Libros del saber de astronomia.
Instruments_Notes: The Libros del saber de astronomia includes studies of the spherical astrolabe, quadrants, clocks, and other astronomical instruments. Alfonso may have encouraged Rabi Zag of Toledo to prepare a treatise on the quadrant.

Education_Notes: Attended Brown University, earning Ph.B. (1915), M.A. in biology (1916), and Ph.D. in biology (1921). Studies interrupted briefly during World War I by military service.
Education_Locations: Providence, Unknown, United States, Unknown, 1915; Providence, Unknown, United States, 1915, 1921
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Discovered estrogen and elucidated the hormonal control of the female reproductive cycle. Investigated the role of the ovarian follicle in estrus, the induction of puberty by estrogen, hormonal mechanisms in primates, and the relationship between estrogenic stimulation and malignancy.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Instructor in anatomy at Washington University (1919–1923); professor of anatomy at University of Missouri (1923–1933), serving also as dean of the medical school and director of university hospitals; professor of anatomy and chairman of the department at Yale School of Medicine (1933–1943).
Scientific_Societies_Membership: American Association of Anatomists; Association for the Study of Internal Secretions
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Member and president of both societies. Received honorary degrees from Brown, Yale, and Washington universities. Made a member of the French Legion of Honor (1937) and awarded the Baly Medal by the Royal College of Physicians (1941). Advisory trustee and member of the Scientific Advisory Committee of the International Cancer Research Foundation (1939–1943).

Father_Notes: Francesco Alpini was a physician; Prospero was the oldest of four children.
Education_Notes: Studied medicine at the University of Padua under Melchiore Guilandino, the second director of the botanical garden; received his degree on 28 August 1578.
Education_Locations: Padua, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, 1578
Scientific_Disciplines: Botany; Natural History; Medicine; Zoology; Mineralogy
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer study of Egyptian flora and Mediterranean plants, particularly Cretan flora. Described fifty-seven Egyptian plants in De plantis Aegypti, including coffee, banana, and baobab. Observed sexual fertilization of date palms and phototropic movements in tamarind leaves. Studied Egyptian and Turkish medicine, introducing moxa technique to Europe. Contributed to early Egyptology through natural history observations.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced medicine briefly in Camposampiero near Padua; served as physician to the Venetian consul to Cairo (1580–1583); elected lettore dei semplici (reader in simples) at University of Padua in 1594; became prefetto ed ostensore dei semplici (prefect and demonstrator of simples) and director of the botanical garden at Padua in 1603.
Patronage_Notes: Employed as physician to Giorgio Emo, Venetian consul to Cairo, from 1580.

Father_Notes: Jacob Alsted was a Reformed Church minister who died in 1622.
Education_Notes: Elementary education at Ballersbach; entered the lower school of Herborn Academy in 1602 and completed studies there. Undertook the customary academic peregrination visiting Frankfurt am Main, Heidelberg, Strasbourg, and Basel, where he met Amandus Polanus von Polandsdorf. Attended the Synod of Dordrecht in 1618.
Education_Locations: Herborn, Unknown, Germany, 1602, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Reformed Church background through both parents; worked within Calvinist institutions throughout his career.
Scientific_Disciplines: Natural Philosophy; Philosophy; Mathematics; Astronomy; Logic
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Wrote systematically on natural philosophy, physics, mathematics, and astronomy. Authored commentaries on the cabala and the Ars magna of Lull, treatises on Ramist and traditional logic, mnemonics, and physics. The Systema physicae harmonicae analyzed physical principles from four systems: Mosaic, rabbinical-cabalistic, Peripatetic, and chemical. Discussed improved surveying techniques and the Copernican hypothesis, which he rejected on scriptural grounds. His major contribution was the conception of the encyclopedia as a universal system of knowledge.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Teacher and examiner at Herborn Academy high school from 1608; professor of philosophy from 1610; rector and professor of theology from 1619. In 1629 became first rector of the new high school at Stuhlweissenburg, established by Prince Gabriel Bethlen.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by Protestant prince Gabriel Bethlen von Siebenbürgen, who established the high school at Stuhlweissenburg where Alsted became rector in 1629.

Father_Notes: Born into a wealthy country family.

Education_Notes: Attended San Ildefonso College, graduating in 1753 with a bachelor of arts degree. Received a bachelor of divinity degree from the University of Mexico in 1756 and was subsequently ordained as a Roman Catholic priest.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Enthusiastic naturalist devoted to all branches of natural science. Defended the advanced botanical knowledge of ancient Mexicans and engaged in botanical controversies. Founded several scientific periodicals to promote scientific advancement and technology in New Spain.

Determined isotherms for numerous gases and liquids; studied elasticity of solids and mercury; investigated specific heats, Van der Waals' law, and related phenomena in fluid mechanics.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Agrégé and professor of physics at the Faculté Libre des Sciences of Lyons; examiner at the École Polytechnique.
Instruments: Manometer with free-moving pistons in viscous liquids; Mercury column manometer
Instruments_Notes: Invented a manometer with free-moving pistons in viscous liquids (molasses or castor oil) to measure pressures above 3,000 atmospheres, overcoming the limitations of glass tubes. Used a 327-meter-high mercury column at Verpilleux mine shaft to determine nitrogen compressibility. His manometer was adopted in military and firearms laboratories; the reversed apparatus enabled creation and measurement of high pressures.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected corresponding member of the Académie des Sciences on 5 May 1890; became full member on 9 June 1902. Received the Prix Lacaze pour la Physique from the Institut in 1893.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Jacques Payen. Papers presented to Académie des Sciences, listed in Comptes rendus indexes for Vols. 62–91 (12 papers), 92–121 (48 papers), 122–151 (18 papers), 152–181 (4 papers). Key publications: Annales de chimie et de physique (1873–1893); Journal de physique (1880–1896). Notice sur les travaux scientifiques de M. E. H. Amagat (Paris, 1896).
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Jacques Payen.

Father_Notes: Antonio Ameghino was a mason and warehouse keeper who emigrated from Italy to Argentina.
Education_Institution: Escuela Normal de Preceptores; Museum of Natural Sciences; School of Anthropology
Education_Notes: Received scanty formal education; attended Escuela Normal de Preceptores in Buenos Aires from 1868, enabling him to teach school in Mercedes in the early 1870s. Took courses at the Museum of Natural Sciences and School of Anthropology in Paris during his three-year residence in Europe (1878–1881). Self-educated in geology, paleontology, and anthropology through field work and museum study.
Education_Locations: Buenos Aires, Unknown, Argentina, 1868, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, 1878, 1881; Paris, Unknown, France, 1878, 1881
Scientific_Disciplines: Paleontology; Geology; Anthropology; Natural History; Prehistory
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in Argentine paleontology and prehistory; discovered over 6,000 fossil species and classified thirty-five suborders of fossil mammals. Established a paleontological geochronology of Argentine formations from Cretaceous through Holocene. His anthropological work on Pampean man and protohumanoid theories (Tetraprothomo, Triprothomo, Diprothomo) proved controversial and largely discredited. Advocated Darwinian transformism and uniformitarianism.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught school in Mercedes in early 1870s; held chair of zoology at University of Córdoba (1884); professor of geology and mineralogy at University of La Plata (1887, 1906); secretary of La Plata Museum (1886–1890); director of Museum of Natural Sciences in Buenos Aires (1902–1911). Also supported himself by selling fossils in Europe, operating a secondhand bookshop in Buenos Aires (1882 onward), and founding Revista argentina de historia natural.
Patronage_Notes: Obtained chair at University of Córdoba with help of Juárez Celman (1884); appointed secretary of La Plata Museum through nomination by Francisco Moreno (1886); made director of Museum of Natural Sciences in Buenos Aires by minister of education Joaquín González (1902).
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Scientific Society of Argentina
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Presented works to the Scientific Society of Argentina in the 1870s; maintained correspondence with European naturalists including Paul Gervais and Henri Gervais.

(La Plata, 1913–1936). Key publications: Contribución al conocimiento de los mamíferos fósiles de la República Argentina, 2 vols. (Buenos Aires, 1880); Filogenia (Buenos Aires, 1884); La antigüedad del hombre en el río de La Plata (La Plata, 1915). Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Justo Garate.

Father_Notes: Father George L. Ames was a physician who died in 1869 when Joseph was five years old.
Education_Institution: Shattuck School; Johns Hopkins University; University of Berlin; Johns Hopkins University
Education_Notes: Attended Shattuck School in Faribault, Minnesota; graduated from Johns Hopkins University in 1886; spent two years in Helmholtz's laboratory in Berlin; earned Ph.D. from Johns Hopkins in 1890 under Henry A. Rowland.
Education_Locations: Faribault, Minnesota, United States, Unknown, Unknown; Baltimore, Maryland, United States, Unknown, 1886; Berlin, Unknown, Germany, 1886, 1888; Baltimore, Maryland, United States, 1888, 1890
Religion_Notes: Raised an Episcopalian.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Research focused on spectroscopy, particularly finding relationships among spectral lines. Working with Rowland in the 1890s, he measured spectra of complex atoms and sought empirical relationships among wave numbers. Concluded that theoretical considerations were necessary to advance the field. Abandoned research by 1913 to focus on administration.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Joined Johns Hopkins faculty after earning his Ph.D. in 1890; served as director of the physical laboratory from 1901 to 1926, provost from 1926 to 1929, and president from 1929 to 1935. Served on the National Research Council and the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics during World War I and after.
Patronage_Notes: Served on the National Academy of Sciences' National Research Council and the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics, becoming chairman of the NACA's Executive Committee in 1919 and chairman of the entire NACA from 1927 to 1939.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: National Academy of Sciences; American Physical Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Member of the National Academy of Sciences; elected president of the American Physical Society in 1919.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Daniel J. Kevles. Archives of Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, Maryland (scattered papers). National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics records, National Archives, Washington, D.C. (principal correspondence). NACA Annual Reports during Ames's administration. Henry Crew, 'Joseph Sweetman Ames,' National Academy of Sciences Biographical Memoirs, 23 (1945), 181–201.
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Daniel J. Kevles.

Father_Notes: Prosperous Ipswich merchant; both parents died during Ames's childhood.
Education_Notes: Matriculated at Christ's College, Cambridge as a pensioner in 1593/1594; obtained B.A. in 1597/1598 and M.A. in 1601. Became fellow of Christ's College from 1601 to 1610, where he studied under the Puritan theologian William Perkins.
Education_Locations: Cambridge, Unknown, England, 1593, 1610
Religion_Notes: Prominent Puritan theologian; took up the controversial theological position of William Perkins; suspended from degrees and expelled from Cambridge in 1609 due to Puritan agitation; advised the Calvinist faction at the Synod of Dordrecht in 1618.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Systematized Calvinist theology and developed Ramist philosophy; stressed practical divinity and the unity of theology and ethics; adopted empirical approach to natural philosophy akin to Bacon's inductive method; integrated theology, ethics, and natural philosophy into an encyclopedic system (Technometria); influenced scientific outlook of figures such as John Winthrop Jr., Samuel Hartlib, and Robert Boyle toward problems of social usefulness.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Fellow of Christ's College, Cambridge (1601–1610); held minor clerical positions at Leiden and The Hague; chaplain to Sir Horace Vere at Brill; appointed to chair of divinity at University of Franeker (1622–1633), where he served as rector (1626–1632); minister and lecturer to English congregation at Rotterdam (1633).
Patronage_Notes: Served as chaplain to Sir Horace Vere, English governor at Brill. Appointed to chair of divinity at University of Franeker following his prominence at the Synod of Dordrecht.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Charles Webster. (Amsterdam, 1658); Medulla theologiae (Franeker, 1623; Amsterdam, 1627, 1659); De Conscientia et eius iure vel casibus libri quinque (Amsterdam, 1631, 1670); Demonstratio logicae verae (Leiden, 1632; Cambridge, 1646); Disputatio theologica adversus metaphysicam (Leiden, 1632; Hanau, 1640; Cambridge, 1646); Technometria (Amsterdam–Leiden, 1632, 1633); Theses logicae (Cambridge, 1646). Father_Notes: Giuseppe Amici was a ministerial official; mother Maria Dalloca came from a well-to-do family.
Education_Notes: Graduated as an engineer-architect in 1807 and immediately became a mathematics teacher at the Modena lyceum.
Education_Locations: Bologna, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, 1807
Scientific_Disciplines: Optics; Microscopy; Natural History; Botany; Anatomy; Physiology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in optical instrument design and compound microscopy; achieved decisive improvements in resolving power through the hemispheric frontal lens and immersion microscopy techniques. Made major biological discoveries including the pollen tube's passage through the pistil (1821), palisade parenchyma in leaves, and observations on plant fertilization, protoplasm circulation, histology, and plant pathology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Mathematics teacher at Modena lyceum from 1807; from 1831 headed the astronomical observatory and Royal Museum of Physics and Natural History in Florence until 1859; then director of microscopic research at the museum until retirement.
Patronage_Notes: Invited to Florence in 1831 by the grand duke of Tuscany to direct the observatory and museum.
Instruments: Microscope; Prism; Micrometer; Telescope; Concave Mirror; Astronomical Lens
Instruments_Notes: Designed and built improved compound microscopes with hemispheric frontal lenses and pioneered immersion microscopy using water, olive oil, and sassafras oil. Invented the Amici prism and reconsidered the direct-vision prism. Constructed a masterpiece astronomical lens of 285 mm diameter presented at the 1841 Third Congress of Italian Scientists. Invented new micrometers and distance-measuring telescopes for astronomical observations.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Società Italiana delle Scienze; Accademia dei Georgofili
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Published extensively in the memoirs of the Italian Society of Sciences and the Academy of Georgofili; maintained correspondence with leading scientists including Ottaviano Mossotti.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Vasco Ronchi. Religion_Notes: Possibly became Christian in name only; the school included both pagan and Christian faculty and students.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Head of the Platonic school in Alexandria from 485; harmonized Platonic and Aristotelian thought; accomplished mathematician and astronomer; made astronomical observations leading to the deduction of the primum mobile; divided theoretical philosophy into theology, mathematics, and physics.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Head of the Platonic school in Alexandria.

Father_Notes: Father was a lawyer from Normandy who settled in Paris.
Education_Notes: Became deaf during adolescence. Studied drawing, surveying, and architecture; gained practical knowledge of applied mechanics through employment on public works projects. Later studied celestial mechanics. No formal degree is recorded.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered improvements to hygrometers, barometers, and thermometers. Developed an optical telegraph for signal transmission. Proposed a thermic motor using hot air and external combustion. Established laws of friction in machines and proportionality between friction and pressure. Made fundamental observations on gas expansion with temperature and proposed the boiling point of water as a fixed thermometric reference. Investigated the behavior of liquids under expansion and tested Boyle's law at low pressures.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Employed on various public works projects. Member of the Académie des Sciences, where he published his papers.
Patronage_Notes: Demonstrated his optical telegraph to the royal family between 1688 and 1695.
Instruments: Hygrometer; Barometer; Thermometer; Optical Telegraph; Thermic Motor; Air Thermometer
Instruments_Notes: Invented a hygrometer using a ball of beechwood, horn, or leather filled with mercury (1687). Developed a shortened barometer with parallel tubes connected alternately (1688). Created an optical telegraph consisting of stations equipped with spyglasses for rapid signal transmission. Designed a cisternless barometer with a tube that narrowed to suspend the mercury column, later broadened into an inverted funnel shape. Constructed an air thermometer independent of atmospheric pressure using a U-shaped tube. Proposed a thermic motor using hot air and external combustion (1699). Designed a U-tube barometer without an open mercury surface for shipboard use.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Published numerous papers in the Mémoires de l'Académie des Sciences from 1688 to 1705.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Jacques Payen. Original works: excerpts in Journal des savants (8 March 1688, 10 May 1688); Remarques et expériences physiques sur la construction d'une nouvelle clepsydre (Paris, 1695); papers in Mémoires de l'Académie des Sciences including "De la résistance causée dans les machines" (1699), "Moyen de substituer commodément l'action du feu" (1702), "Discours sur quelques propriétés de l'air" (1702), "Le thermométre réduit à une mesure fixe et certaine" (1703), "Discours sur les barométres" (1704), and "Barométres sans mercure à l'usage de la mer" (1705). Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Jacques Payen.

Father_Notes: Jean-Jacques Ampère was a merchant of independent means, influenced by Rousseau's educational theories, and maintained an extensive library that profoundly shaped his son's early intellectual development.
Education_Notes: Largely self-educated through his father's library, reading Buffon, the Encyclopédie, and works by Euler and Bernoulli. Taught himself mathematics, number theory, and Latin. No formal institutional education is recorded.
Religion_Notes: Raised in a devout Catholic household by his mother. Throughout his life he struggled with doubts sown by Enlightenment philosophy but repeatedly renewed his faith, which shaped his philosophical and scientific approach.
Scientific_Disciplines: Physics; Electrodynamics; Mathematics; Chemistry; Philosophy; Natural History
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of electrodynamics, founding the science between 1820 and 1827 following Oersted's discovery. Contributed to mathematics (partial differential equations, probability theory), chemistry (molecular theory, classification of elements, early recognition of chlorine and iodine as elements), and developed a comprehensive philosophical classification of the sciences.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Mathematics teacher in Lyons (1799–1802); professor of physics and chemistry at École Centrale of Bourg-en-Bresse (1802–1804); répétiteur in mathematics at École Polytechnique in Paris (1804–1808); inspector general of the newly formed university system (1808–1836, with interruption in the 1820s); assistant professor of astronomy at University of Paris (1820); chair of experimental physics at Collège de France (1824).
Patronage_Notes: Appointed inspector general of the university system by the French government, a position that provided security and enabled his scientific work.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences; Institut Impérial
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected member of the class of mathematics in the Institut Impérial on 28 November 1814. Active participant in the Académie des Sciences, where he presented his electrodynamic discoveries in September and October 1820.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by L. Pearce Williams. Original works: Correspondance du Grand Ampère, ed. Louis de Launay, 3 vols. (Paris, 1936–1943); Mémoires sur l'électrodynamique, 2 vols. (Paris, 1885–1887); Mémoire sur la théorie mathématique des phénomènes électrodynamiques uniquement déduite de l'expérience (Paris, 1827). Education_Institution: University of Jena; University of Königsberg; Geneva Observatory; University of Zurich
Education_Notes: Studied theology at Jena and Königsberg; earned doctorate in 1848 under the influence of Franz Neumann. Spent a year at Geneva observatory with Plantamour before completing Habilitation at Zurich and beginning teaching career.
Education_Locations: Jena, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Königsberg, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1848; Geneva, Unknown, Switzerland, 1848, 1849; Zurich, Unknown, Switzerland, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Early work in mathematical physics including magnetic distribution, heat conduction, and attraction theory; generalized Ivory's theorem on ellipsoid attraction. Major contribution was the polar planimeter (1854), a precision instrument for measuring areas of plane curves using polar coordinates. Later research focused on precision and engineering instruments.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Lectured on mathematics and mathematical physics at Zurich for four semesters; held post at Gymnasium in Schaffhausen from 1851. Established precision tools workshop in 1854, devoted full time from 1857 onward; workshop produced 50,000 polar planimeters and 700 momentum planimeters by his death.
Instruments: Polar Planimeter; Momentum Planimeter; Hydrometric Rotor
Instruments_Notes: Invented the polar planimeter (1856), which measured areas enclosed by plane curves using a polar coordinate system; eliminated bulkiness and cost of earlier Cartesian-based instruments. Also developed the momentum planimeter for calculating static and inertial moments and Fourier coefficients. Designed a hydrometric rotor with electrical signal apparatus.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Naturforschende Gesellschaft in Zurich; Paris Academy
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Active member of Naturforschende Gesellschaft in Zurich from 1848 until death. Corresponding member of Paris Academy from 1892.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by M.S. Mahoney. Education_Notes: Learned in arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, rhetoric, and philosophy; headed the Aristotelian school in Alexandria.
Religion_Notes: Consecrated bishop of Caesarea by Bishop Theotecnus; later became bishop of Laodicea around A.D. 280 and remained in that office until his death. Known for Christian and humanitarian character.
Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; Arithmetic; Astronomy; Philosophy; Natural Philosophy
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Composed Introduction to Arithmetic in ten books, treating the first ten natural numbers with both arithmetical properties and Neoplatonic mysticism. Wrote The Canons of Anatolius on the Paschal, applying astronomical knowledge to the calculation of Easter. Demonstrated competence in geometry and astronomy alongside philosophical learning.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Headed the Aristotelian school in Alexandria; served as bishop of Caesarea and later bishop of Laodicea.
Patronage_Notes: Consecrated and appointed as successor by Bishop Theotecnus of Caesarea.

Father_Notes: Born of wealthy parents; Anaxagoras renounced his inheritance to pursue natural philosophy.
Education_Notes: At age twenty traveled to Athens, where he spent thirty years engaged in natural philosophy and intellectual discourse.
Religion_Notes: Prosecuted for impiety, allegedly for holding the sun to be a mass of red-hot stone; the charge was likely politically motivated to attack his friend Pericles.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Developed a pluralist natural philosophy reconciling Parmenidean logic with multiplicity and change. Proposed that matter is infinitely divisible and that all substances preexist in food. Introduced Mind (Nous) as an immaterial moving cause governing a cosmic vortex. Offered a rational but unfruitful astronomy explaining celestial bodies as fragments torn from earth and ignited by friction.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Renounced his inheritance but supported himself through intellectual work and friendship with Pericles in Athens.
Patronage_Notes: Friend and intellectual companion of Pericles, the leading Athenian statesman.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Wrote on the magical or peculiar effects of minerals, herbs, and animal substances and their medicinal preparations. Known for magical tricks and illusions. Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Developed a cosmogony explaining the origin and structure of the world through natural law. Drew a map of the inhabited world and wrote a geographical treatise. Proposed theories of celestial bodies, eclipses, and the origin of animals and humans from inanimate matter. Formulated an impersonal law of nature governing all phenomena.

Education_Notes: May have been a student of Anaximander; certainly knew Anaximander's work.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Developed a cosmological and astronomical system based on air as the fundamental infinite substance, explaining transformation through condensation and rarefaction. Proposed that the earth is a flat disk supported by air, that heavenly bodies are annular in form and carried by air, and that the cosmos breathes by inhaling surrounding air.

Education_Notes: Intern in Nancy hospitals from 1898; received M.D. in 1899 and docteur ès sciences from University of Nancy in 1903.

Scientific_Disciplines: Biology; Anatomy; Embryology; Physiology; Cytology; Endocrinology; Teratogenesis
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Early work in anatomy and cytology, including studies on hermaphroditic genital glands. Collaborated with Pol Bouin for twenty-five years on reproductive physiology in mammals, establishing that the interstitial gland of the testis produces hormones for secondary sexual characteristics and that the corpus luteum prepares the uterine mucosa for implantation and mammary development. Later pioneered experimental embryology and teratogenesis, elucidating bilateral symmetry determination in amphibian embryos and developing new methods using physical and chemical means to produce controlled developmental abnormalities.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professeur agrégé of anatomy at Faculté de Médecine in Lyons (1904); professeur titulaire of anatomy at Nancy (1908) and of embryology at Strasbourg (1919), holding the first chair of embryology in France. Continued research at Institut de Physico-Chimie Biologique in Paris after retirement from teaching.

Father_Notes: Reverend John Anderson; mother was Annie Masson, daughter of a minister.

Religion_Notes: Described as a Christian free-thinker.
Scientific_Disciplines: Geology; Geophysics; Structural Geology; Mineralogy; Optics
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Structural geologist and tectonist specializing in the dynamics of faulting, igneous intrusion, lineation in schists, crustal heat and structure, and volcanism. Made important contributions to mineral optics, particularly the Becke line effect. Applied mathematical analysis to geophysical problems.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Joined the Geological Survey of Great Britain in 1903 as a geologist, retiring as senior geologist in 1928 due to ill health. Served in the army 1916–1917, wounded in France. Main scientific work done in leisure time while employed by the Survey.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society of Edinburgh; Geological Society of London; Geological Society of Edinburgh
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Awarded medals by the Royal Society of Edinburgh, the Geological Society of London, and the Geological Society of Edinburgh.

Education_Notes: Studied one term at the mathematical faculty of Kazan University; entered the economics faculty of the Petersburg Polytechnical Institute in 1907 and graduated in 1912 as a candidate in economics. Pupil and assistant of A. A. Tschuprow.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Developed the variance-difference method for analyzing time series; pioneered sampling methods in agricultural studies; conducted research in quantity theory of money and index-number theory from the statistical viewpoint; advocated application of mathematical statistics to economics and developed nonparametric methods.

Education_Notes: Studied medicine at Edinburgh University, graduating in 1841 with a doctoral thesis on chemical changes in nutrition and physiological processes. Studied under Berzelius in Stockholm in 1842 and worked in Liebig's laboratory in Giessen in 1843; visited other European centers of chemical and medical research before returning to Edinburgh.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering work on organic bases derived from coal tar and bone oil distillation; discovered picoline (1846), pyridine, lutidine, and collidine, establishing them as a homologous series; investigated codeine and alkaloids; elucidated the composition of anthracene. Also conducted extensive analyses of soils, manures, and cattle foods, and published on agricultural chemistry.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Lecturer in extramural medical school in Edinburgh from 1846; professor of chemistry at Glasgow from 1852 until illness in 1869. Served as chemist to the Highland and Agricultural Society of Scotland, examining crop composition over twenty-five years.

Father_Notes: Chief clerk at the Banque de France; his work may have influenced Andoyer's early interest in numerical computation.
Education_Notes: Graduated at the top of his class in mathematical science from the École Normale Supérieure in 1884; wrote his doctoral thesis on the theory of intermediate orbits applied to the moon in 1887.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1884
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Research focused on celestial mechanics, including perturbation theory, special cases of the three-body and n-body problems, and lunar motion. Developed specialized computational methods for ephemerides, particularly for lunar theory. Worked on Lagrangian libration points, asteroid perturbations, and stability of the solar system.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught astronomy at the Sorbonne for thirty-seven years, beginning as maître de conférences in 1892 and becoming full professor in 1903. Also worked at the telescope in Toulouse preparing photographic sky maps. Member of the Bureau des Longitudes from 1910, where he edited Connaissance des temps and prepared ephemerides, especially during World War I.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected member of the Académie des Sciences in 1919.

Education_Institution: École Normale Supérieure; University of Paris (Sorbonne)
Education_Notes: Graduated from École Normale Supérieure in Paris in 1864 with a degree in physics. Taught for one year in Nevers before returning to Paris as assistant astronomer under Urbain Leverrier at the Paris Observatory. Awarded a doctorate by the Sorbonne in 1876 for his thesis on diffraction in optical instruments.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1864; Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1876
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted observational research on solar parallax through transit of Venus observations and asteroid measurements. Investigated instrumental sources of error, particularly diffraction effects in optical instruments and the black drop effect in telescopic observations. Later compiled meteorological and climatological statistics for the Lyons region.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant astronomer at the Paris Observatory under Urbain Leverrier; later became professor at the University of Lyons and director of the Lyons Observatory, positions he held for the final thirty-four years of his life.
Patronage_Notes: Corresponding member of the Académie Française and the Bureau des Longitudes.
Instruments_Notes: Investigated diffraction effects in optical instruments and the black drop effect observed in telescopic observations of Venus transits, leading to improvements in understanding instrumental sources of error.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie Française; Bureau des Longitudes
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Served as a corresponding member of both institutions.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Sally H. Dieke. Father_Notes: Lutheran minister who neglected his family and ministry to pursue alchemy; died in 1601.
Education_Notes: Early education at home under his father's influence, with wide-ranging classical and natural studies. Entered Tübingen University in 1601, received B.A. in 1603 and M.A. in 1605. Studied theology under Matthias Hafenreffer and mathematics under Michael Maestlin. Expelled in 1607 for a student violation; spent five years traveling with periods of residence and study at Tübingen and work as a private tutor. Traveled in Germany, France, Spain, Austria, Italy, and Switzerland; visited Lausanne, Geneva, Rome, and Italian Platonic academies. Returned to Tübingen in 1612 to study theology and mathematics.
Education_Locations: Tübingen, Unknown, Germany, 1601, 1607
Religion_Notes: Devoted to Lutheran theology and the service of his church. Dissatisfied with the increasing formality of Lutheran orthodoxy, he sought to create a Christian union of all believers dedicated to pious living and study of nature. His work influenced the later Pietist movement through his devotion to Johann Arndt.
Scientific_Disciplines: Philosophy; Natural Philosophy; Theology; Mathematics; Astronomy; Music
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Avid interests in astronomy, mathematics, mechanics, music, and painting from youth. Studied the book of nature and nature-mysticism. Advocated for the study of creation as revelation of God's wisdom; emphasized correct observation and experiment. Influenced by Paracelsus, Valentin Weigel, and Campanella. Promoted universal education including study of nature and crafts.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Parson at Vaihingen (1614–1620); dean at Calw (1620–1638); court preacher and councillor in Stuttgart (1639–1650); bishop and abbot at Bebenhausen (1650–1654). Also employed as a private tutor during his years of travel.
Patronage_Notes: Served as court preacher and councillor under the Duke of Württemberg. Had connections with the learned Duke August of Braunschweig-Lüneburg-Wolfenbüttel.

Education_Notes: Studied chemistry at Glasgow and briefly in Dumas's laboratory in Paris in 1830. Studied medicine for four years at Dublin and one year at Edinburgh, receiving the M.D. in 1835.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Early work on passivity of metals extending Schönbein's discoveries. Conducted extensive thermochemistry research (1841–1848) on heats of neutralization, formation of water and oxides, and metallic halides. Investigated the constitution of ozone, concluding it was oxygen in an allotropic condition. Best known for studies on the continuity of gaseous and liquid states and discovery of the critical temperature of carbon dioxide in 1861.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Established a medical practice in Belfast after qualifying in 1835. Appointed first professor of chemistry at Belfast Academical Institution; became first vice-president of Queen's College, Belfast in 1845, and professor of chemistry there from 1849 until retirement in 1879.

Father_Notes: Ivan Andreevich Andrusov was a navigator for a steamship company; died in a shipwreck on the Black Sea in 1870.
Education_Institution: Kerch Gymnasium; Novorossiysk University; University of Vienna; University of Munich; Petersburg University
Education_Notes: Attended Kerch Gymnasium, graduating in 1880. Studied at Novorossiysk University in Odessa (1880–1884), initially concentrating on zoology under I. I. Mechnikov and V. O. Kovalevski, then shifting to geology and paleontology. Defended master's dissertation in 1890 at Petersburg University on fauna of Kerch limestones. Studied abroad in Vienna and Munich (1884–1886) under M. Neumayr, E. Suess, and K. Zittel. Defended doctoral dissertation in 1897 on fossils and living dreissenoids.
Education_Locations: Kerch, Unknown, Russia, Unknown, 1880; Odessa, Unknown, Russia, 1880, 1884; Vienna, Unknown, Austria, 1884, 1886; Munich, Unknown, Germany, 1884, 1886; Saint Petersburg, Unknown, Russia, 1890, 1890
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in oceanographic research on the Black Sea, Sea of Marmara, and Caspian Sea, studying depths, currents, and bottom sediments. Founder of stratigraphy of Neocene deposits in southern Russia. Established detailed subdivision of Tertiary deposits in Caucasus oil-bearing regions, defining stratigraphic units including Tarkhanski, Chokrak, Karagan, and Konka horizons. Described numerous new mollusk species as key fossils for Neocene stages. Contributed to development of paleoecology through study of paleoenvironments and biocenosis. Studied fossil reefs and named onkoids (bioherms). Conducted extensive paleontological and paleogeographical research across southern Russia, Transcaspian region, and central Asia.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant at Petersburg University laboratory (1889); assistant professor at Novorossiysk University (1890); assistant professor at Petersburg University (1893); professor extraordinaire at University of Yuriev (1896); full professor at University of Kiev (1905–1912); geologist on Geological Committee and professor at Bestuzhev Higher Women's School in Petersburg (1912); director of Peter I Geological Museum of Academy of Sciences; professor at Tavricheski University in Simferopol (1918).
Patronage_Notes: Petersburg Society of Naturalists sponsored expeditions to Transcaspian region (1887) and Black Sea research aboard Chernomorets (1890). Academy of Sciences awarded Lomonosov Prize (1897) and elected him corresponding member (1910) and academician (1914). Ukrainian Academy of Sciences elected him full member (1918).
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Petersburg Society of Naturalists; Kiev Society of Naturalists; Ukrainian Academy of Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Active member and organizer at Petersburg and Kiev societies. President of Kiev Society of Naturalists (1905–1912). Organizer of seventh session of International Geological Congress (1897). Founder and editor of journal Geologicheski vestnik (Geological Herald).

Studied mathematics under Bonaventura Cavalieri at the University of Bologna, where Cavalieri recognized his ability and encouraged his mathematical research.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Developed and extended Cavalieri's method of indivisibles to solve problems of infinitesimals, areas, volumes, and centers of gravity. Studied spirals generalizing Archimedes' spiral and solids of revolution (cochleae). Examined fluid statics based on Archimedes' principle and Torricelli's experiments, including capillary attraction. Engaged in cosmological polemic regarding Ptolemaic and Copernican systems.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed reader of literature, philosophy, and theology at Ferrara in his order's faculty. Served as prior of the Gesuati monastery in Venice around 1652. Held the professorship of mathematics at the University of Padua from 2 January 1663 until his death, a position formerly held by Galileo.
Patronage_Notes: The Republic of Venice offered him the professorship of mathematics at the University of Padua on 2 January 1663.

Education_Notes: Studied at University of Vienna from 1468 under Regiomontanus, receiving the baccalaureate in January 1471. Continued studies in Italy, where he received the master's degree in liberal arts and doctorate in medicine.

Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced medicine and astrology in Augsburg; appointed to the Faculty of Liberal Arts at University of Vienna in 1494, where he remained for the rest of his life.

Education_Institution: Technische Hochschule Darmstadt; University of Heidelberg; University of Tübingen
Education_Notes: Studied engineering briefly at Technische Hochschule Darmstadt before switching to chemistry; obtained Ph.D. from University of Heidelberg in 1874; further studies in chemistry at Tübingen under Rudolf Fittig.
Education_Locations: Darmstadt, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Heidelberg, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1874; Tübingen, Unknown, Germany, 1874, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Specialized in organic chemistry, particularly the structure of organic compounds. Major research areas included polybasic acids, isomerism of maleic and fumaric acids, oxalic acid derivatives, aromatic hydrocarbons, phenolic compounds, and coumarin synthesis. Pioneered vacuum distillation methods and combined physical methods with chemical synthesis to establish molecular structure.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as assistant to August Kekulé at University of Bonn from 1875; instructor in 1878; Unterrichtsassistent in 1882; associate professor in 1889; full professor and director of the Chemical Institute in 1898; rector of the university during World War I; remained director of research until retirement in 1922.

Religion_Notes: Carthusian monk.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Observed celestial changes and comets, concentrating on the constellations Cygnus and Cassiopeia. Discovered the nova Variable R Volpecula (1670–1672). Prepared one of the first ephemerides of a variable star, studying Mira Ceti and proposing a model of its light variation. Argued that comets obey regular celestial laws with orbits centered far from Earth, rejecting Cartesian vortex theory and proposing comets as diaphanous bodies transmitting solar rays. Compiled a star catalog.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Carthusian monk; his astronomical work was conducted within the monastic community at Dijon.

Father_Notes: Father was Stephanus, a physician. Family from Tralles in western Asia Minor was learned; brothers included a man of letters, a lawyer, and two physicians.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Designed and oversaw construction of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople (begun 532 A.D.) with Isidorus of Miletus. Worked on conic sections and reflectors. Authored On Remarkable Mechanical Devices, treating elliptical and parabolic reflectors, the construction of ellipses, and the reflection of parallel rays. Solved the problem of directing a solar ray through an aperture to a fixed spot at any hour and season.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Employed by Justinian to design and oversee the reconstruction of Hagia Sophia and repair of flood defenses at Daras.
Patronage_Notes: Patronized by the Emperor Justinian I for major architectural and engineering projects.
Instruments_Notes: Designed elliptical reflectors with foci positioned to direct solar rays through an aperture to a fixed point. Developed parabolic reflectors to focus parallel rays to a single focal point.

Alt_Name: Antiphon of Rhamnus; Antiphon the Sophist; Antiphon the Orator
Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; Philosophy; Natural Philosophy; Cosmology; Psychology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Attempted to square the circle using compass and ruler, proposing to inscribe polygons within a circle and progressively refine them until sides coincide with the circumference. Discussed the physical formation of the universe, the nature of heavenly bodies, and the doctrine of opposite qualities as primary substances. Developed a famous doctrine opposing nature and convention, arguing for a basic human nature common to all peoples.
Means_of_Support_Notes: First native Athenian classed as a professional teacher of young men (Sophist); took part in Athenian politics.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by G. B. Kerferd.
