Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Devoted primarily to telescopic observation of Mars; conducted detailed studies of the planet's surface features, canals, and rotation period. Later pursued historical studies of Greek and Egyptian astronomy.
Means_of_Support_Notes: From 1893 guest observer at Flammarion's private observatory at Juvisy; from 1909 authorized by H. Deslandres to use the large telescope at Meudon Observatory, where he conducted his most important work.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by Camille Flammarion, who provided access to his private observatory and published Antoniadi's observations in L'astronomie. Received the Cross of Chevalier of the Legion of Honor from the French government.
Instruments_Notes: Employed a forty-two-centimeter equatorial at Juvisy from 1893; made extensive use of the large telescope at Meudon Observatory from 1909 onward for detailed observations of Mars.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: British Astronomical Association; Astronomical Society of France
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Appointed director of the Mars section of the British Astronomical Association; published regularly in L'astronomie and the Bulletin de la Société astronomique de France.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Giorgio Abetti. La planète Mars (Paris, 1930). L'astronomie, 58 (1944). G. Abetti, Storia dell'astronomia (Florence, 1963). Contributions to Bulletin de la Société astronomique de France and Journal of the British Astronomical Association.

Father_Notes: His father was a soldier; his mother was the daughter of a peasant.
Education_Notes: Studied at the Physics and Mathematics Faculty of Moscow University, where he was influenced by Darwinian evolutionary concepts and the interconnection of natural phenomena. No degree is named in the source.
Education_Locations: Moscow, Unknown, Russia, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines: Geography; Physical Geography; Geomorphology; Hydrology; Limnology; Anthropology; Ethnography; Natural History
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Founder of Russian academic geography and limnology. Pioneered the study of orography and lake formation in Russia. Developed a comprehensive classification of geography as a science bridging natural and human knowledge. Conducted anthropological studies of racial types and ethnographic research on Siberian peoples and material culture. Published approximately one thousand papers across geography, anthropology, ethnography, and the history of science.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Headed the department of anthropology at Moscow University from 1876, and from 1884 headed the newly organized department of geography and ethnography. After the October Revolution, participated in the establishment of the Soviet government, particularly in Gosplan (State Planning Committee).
Patronage_Notes: Upon Lenin's recommendation, enlisted to compile and edit the first Soviet world atlas, Atlas mira.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Society for the Acclimatization of Animals and Plants; Society of Lovers of Natural Science, Anthropology, and Ethnography; Academy of Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Secretary of the Society for the Acclimatization of Animals and Plants after graduating from university. Elected president of the Society of Lovers of Natural Science, Anthropology, and Ethnography in 1890, where he organized the geographic section and made Moscow a major center of geographic thought. Elected member of the Academy of Sciences in St. Petersburg in 1896; became honored member two years later.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered accurate cartographic methods based on triangulation nets and honest representation of unknown territories. Produced 211 maps and plans, including notably accurate maps of China, France, Africa, and ancient regions. Made significant contributions to ancient historical geography through comparative study of ancient and modern measurements.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Named royal geographer in 1717; secretary to the duke of Orléans; succeeded Buache as chief royal geographer in 1773 and as assistant geographer to the Académie Royale des Sciences.
Patronage_Notes: Served as secretary to the duke of Orléans (regent during the minority of Louis XV); appointed royal geographer by the crown; patronized by the Jesuits who commissioned maps of China.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres; Académie Royale des Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres in 1754; served as assistant geographer to the Académie Royale des Sciences from 1773.

Father_Notes: István Apáthy was a professor at the University of Budapest and an expert in international law.
Education_Institution: University of Budapest; Marine Biological Laboratory
Education_Notes: Attended high school in Budapest; studied medicine at the University of Budapest; worked at the Institute of Pathology from 1883 to 1884 as a student; obtained his doctor's degree in 1885; worked as assistant to Theodor Margó at the Institute of Zoology and Comparative Anatomy in Budapest; held a scholarship at the marine biological laboratory in Naples from 1886 to 1889 under Anton Dohrn.
Education_Locations: Budapest, Unknown, Austria-Hungary, Unknown, 1885; Naples, Unknown, Italy, 1886, 1889
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Principal contributions in zoology concerned systematic and comparative anatomy of Hirudinea and their nervous systems. Pioneered neurohistology, defending the concept of continuous networks of neurofibrils connecting neurons; developed original gold chloride impregnation technique. Made major advances in microscopic technique, including tissue fixation, embedding, sectioning, staining, and impregnation methods; authored Die Mikrotechnik der thierischen Morphologie, a standard handbook for two generations of histologists.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant at the Institute of Zoology and Comparative Anatomy in Budapest after 1885; held scholarship at marine biological laboratory in Naples 1886–1889; appointed professor of zoology at Kolozsvár in 1890 and professor of histology and embryology shortly thereafter; founded a modern histological research institute at Kolozsvár; appointed professor of zoology at Szeged University after World War I.
Patronage_Notes: After World War I, appointed by the Hungarian Republic as government commissioner of Transylvanian affairs to the Rumanian National Committee in Sibiu.
Instruments_Notes: Developed and improved microscopic techniques including original gold chloride impregnation method for studying neurofibrils; designed and used specialized microscopes in his research.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Hungarian Academy of Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected corresponding member of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences in 1895; appointed honorary foreign member of the Royal Medicinal Academy of Belgium in 1905.

Father_Notes: Apelt briefly worked in his father's business around 1839 before turning to academic life.
Education_Institution: Gymnasium; University of Jena; University of Leipzig
Education_Notes: Studied mathematics and philosophy under Jakob Fries at Jena from 1831 to 1833; continued studies at Leipzig until 1835 under A. F. Moebius, specializing in astronomy and physics. No formal degree is named.
Education_Locations: Zittau, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Jena, Unknown, Germany, 1831, 1833; Leipzig, Unknown, Germany, 1833, 1835
Scientific_Disciplines: Philosophy; Epistemology; History of Science; Mathematics; Astronomy; Physics; Metaphysics
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering methodologist of science and historian of astronomy and cosmology. His Theorie der Induction analyzed scientific method, mathematical induction, and the foundations of mathematical inference, engaging with contemporary debates among Comte, Mill, Herschel, and Whewell. Wrote extensively on the Copernican revolution, Greek astronomy, Kepler's natural philosophy, and the scientific work of F. H. Jacobi. Insisted that scientific knowledge and historical scrutiny of the sciences were essential for epistemology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Became Privatdozent at the University of Jena in 1839 and spent the rest of his life there, lecturing on mathematics, astronomy, and philosophy.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by L. L. Laudan. Original works include De viribus naturae primitivis (Jena, 1839); Die Epochen der Geschichte der Menschheit, 2 vols. Alt_Name: Petrus Apianus; Peter Bienewitz; Peter Bennewitz
Education_Institution: University of Leipzig; University of Vienna
Education_Notes: Studied mathematics and astronomy at Leipzig and Vienna; quickly established a reputation as an outstanding mathematician.
Education_Locations: Leipzig, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Vienna, Unknown, Austria, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in astronomical and geographical instrumentation and a leading popularizer of these subjects in the sixteenth century. Major works include Cosmographia (1524), defining terrestrial grids and surveying methods; Astronomicon Caesareum (1540), with observations of comets and the statement that comets point their tails away from the sun; and Instrumentum sinuum sive primi mobilis (1534), containing the first printed sine tables calculated to every minute with decimal radius division. Suggested lunar distances for measuring longitude and supported solar eclipses for that purpose.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed professor of mathematics at the University of Ingolstadt, where he remained until his death. Also active as a compiler and publisher of maps and astronomical works.
Patronage_Notes: Knighted by Charles V.
Instruments_Notes: Designed a quadrant and an armillary sphere that were popular in his day. Made imaginative use of simple mechanical devices, particularly valvelles, to provide information on the position and movement of celestial bodies.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by George Kish. F. Van Ortroy, Bibliographie de l'oeuvre de Pierre Apian, Bibliographie moderne (Mar.–Oct. 1901). S. Education_Notes: Studied in Alexandria; visited Pergamum and Ephesus. No formal degree is recorded.
Education_Locations: Alexandria, Unknown, Egypt, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Renowned for the Conics, a comprehensive treatise on conic sections that became the standard work on the subject. Developed the theory of parabola, hyperbola, and ellipse using oblique conjugation. Contributed to astronomical theory through work on epicyclic and eccentric models for planetary motion. Wrote on burning mirrors and catoptrics.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Domiciled in Alexandria for a period; corresponded with and dedicated works to Eudemus of Pergamum and Attalus (likely a Macedonian patron rather than King Attalus I). Supported by patrons who facilitated his mathematical research.
Patronage_Notes: Dedicated books of the Conics to Eudemus of Pergamum and to Attalus, a Macedonian of high status. The latter may have been a patron of his work.

Father_Notes: Master dyer who managed production at the Ritterhus with two sons from a previous marriage; died in 1867.
Education_Notes: Transferred to the lycée in 1869 at his own insistence. Went to Nancy in 1871 to prepare for university. Entered the École Normale in 1873 and graduated first in his class in 1876, earning his doctorate three months after graduation.
Education_Locations: Strasbourg, Unknown, France, 1869, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, 1873, 1876
Religion_Notes: Born into a Catholic Alsatian family but rejected Catholic piety in his youth.
Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; Algebra; Geometry; Projective Geometry; Mathematical Physics; Mechanics; Analysis; Complex Analysis
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Early work in projective geometry following Chasles; turned to algebraic functions, differential equations, and complex analysis. Generalized classical results on elliptic and hypergeometric functions to multiple variables. Noted physical significance of imaginary periods of elliptic functions in pendulum problems. Developed Appell polynomials. Later work focused increasingly on mechanics and rational mechanics, including equations of motion for holonomic and non-holonomic systems. Work consisted of brilliant solutions to particular problems rather than development of general theories.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held multiple teaching posts simultaneously, including chair of mechanics at the Sorbonne from 1885. Served as dean of the Faculty of Science of the University of Paris from 1903 to 1920 and rector from 1920 to 1925. Held various government posts including membership in the Conseil Supérieure d'Instruction Publique.
Patronage_Notes: Served in government educational posts and was instrumental in initiating large-scale projects including the Cité Universitaire.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Académie des Sciences in 1892.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Kenneth O. May. Appell's "Notice sur les travaux scientifiques," Acta mathematica, 45 (1925), 161–285. Education_Institution: University of London; St. John's College, Cambridge
Education_Notes: Matriculated at University of London at age sixteen; won scholarship to St. John's College, Cambridge at eighteen; graduated with first class honours in physics in 1913; undertook postgraduate work in crystallography under William Henry Bragg.
Education_Locations: London, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; Cambridge, Unknown, England, Unknown, 1913
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in radiophysics and atmospheric physics. Investigated vacuum tubes and radio signal fading. Discovered the Appleton (F) layer and D layer of the ionosphere; experimentally proved the existence of the Kennelly-Heaviside (E) layer; determined sky wave polarization and calculated reflection coefficients and electron densities of atmospheric layers.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Wheatstone professor of physics at King's College, University of London (1924–1936); Jacksonian professor of natural philosophy at University of Cambridge (1936–1939); secretary of the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research; principal and vice-chancellor of University of Edinburgh (1949–1965).
Patronage_Notes: Appointed secretary of the government's Department of Scientific and Industrial Research; later principal and vice-chancellor of University of Edinburgh, a government-supported institution.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; International Scientific Radio Union
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1927. President of the International Scientific Radio Union (URSI) from 1934 to 1952. Vice-president of the U.S. Institute of Radio Engineers in 1932. Instrumental in organizing the first International Geophysical Year in 1957.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Charles Süsskind. J. A. Ratcliffe, Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society, 12 (1966), 1–21. Obituaries in The Times (London), 23 April 1965; Science and Culture, 31 (1965), 348–350.

Alt_Name: Saint Thomas Aquinas; Thomas of Aquino
Father_Notes: Landolfo of Aquino, a nobleman who served the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II; the family held the castle of Roccasecca and had significant political standing, though their position was precarious due to Frederick's conflict with the papacy.
Education_Institution: Abbey of Monte Cassino; University of Naples; University of Paris; University of Cologne; University of Paris
Education_Notes: Elementary education at the abbey of Monte Cassino from 1231; studied grammar and logic under Master Martin and natural science under Peter of Ireland at the University of Naples after 1239. Entered the Dominican order at Naples in 1245 and studied at Paris and Cologne (1245–1252) under Albertus Magnus, who was translating and paraphrasing Aristotle's works. Sent to Paris in 1252 to read the Sentences at the priory of Saint-Jacques.
Education_Locations: Monte Cassino, Unknown, Italy, 1231, 1239; Naples, Unknown, Italy, 1239, 1244; Paris, Unknown, France, 1245, 1252; Cologne, Unknown, Germany, 1248, 1252; Paris, Unknown, France, 1252, 1259
Religion_Notes: Deeply committed Catholic theologian and Dominican friar; canonized on 18 July 1323 and subsequently approved by the Roman Catholic Church as its most representative teacher.
Scientific_Disciplines: Philosophy; Natural Philosophy; Theology; Physics; Astronomy; Chemistry; Biology; Metaphysics; Logic
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Synthesized Christian revelation with Aristotelian science across all areas of knowledge. Made significant contributions to medieval physics (kinematics, dynamics, gravitation, projectile motion), astronomy (evaluated Eudoxian and Ptolemaic systems), chemistry (theory of elemental presence in compounds), and biology (commentaries on Aristotle's works on the soul, sensation, and memory). His approach to metaphysical problems proceeded through physical sciences; in later life he turned to commenting on all physical works of Aristotle.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught theology and philosophy at the University of Paris (1256–1259, 1269–1272); taught at Dominican priories and studia in Italy (Anagni, Orvieto, Rome, Viterbo, Naples) from 1259–1268 and 1272–1274. Associated with papal courts of Alexander IV, Urban IV, and Clement IV.
Patronage_Notes: Served at the papal courts of Alexander IV (at Anagni and Orvieto), Urban IV (at Orvieto), and Clement IV (at Viterbo). Required papal intervention from Pope Alexander IV in 1256 to be accepted as a master at the University of Paris.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by William A. Wallace, O.P. Original works: Leonine edition, S. Thomae Aquinatis opera omnia (Rome, 1882–); Parma edition, 25 vols. Father_Notes: François Bonaventure Arago, a modest landowner of Catalonian origin, became mayor of Estagel in 1789 and was named cashier at the mint in Perpignan in 1795.
Education_Notes: Completed classical education in Perpignan; prepared for military artillery career by mastering works of Euler, Lagrange, and Laplace; entered École Polytechnique in 1803 and ranked at the head of his class for two years.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, 1803, 1805
Scientific_Disciplines: Physics; Optics; Astronomy; Magnetism; Electricity; Meteorology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in optical polarization phenomena and undulatory theory of light; made discoveries in chromatic polarization, rotary polarization, and stellar aberration; contributed to electromagnetism through work on electromagnetic induction and temporary magnetization of soft iron; studied atmospheric refraction, scintillation of stars, and solar phenomena; invented and perfected optical instruments including the polariscope and polarimeter.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Secretary of the Bureau des Longitudes from 1809; professor of descriptive geometry at École Polytechnique from 1809 to 1830; director of the Paris Observatory from 1813; taught astronomy publicly at the observatory from 1813 to 1846; perpetual secretary of the Académie des Sciences from 1830; served as deputy and minister during the Second Republic (1848).
Patronage_Notes: Supported by the Bureau des Longitudes, which placed the Paris Observatory under his direction; received government recognition through academic appointments and ministerial positions.
Instruments: Polariscope; Polarimeter; Cyanometer; Photometer; Ocular Micrometer
Instruments_Notes: Invented the polariscope in 1811 to determine degree of polarization of light rays; transformed it into a polarimeter with graduated plates to verify the cosine-squared law for double refraction; built a primitive cyanometer in 1815 to measure atmospheric blueness; proposed a photometer in 1833 to measure stellar light intensities; perfected an ocular micrometer for measuring small angles.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Société d'Arcueil; Institut de France; Royal Society; Académie des Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Institut de France as an astronomer on 18 September 1809; member of most important scientific societies; received the Royal Society's Copley Medal in 1825; elected perpetual secretary of the Académie des Sciences on 7 June 1830, replacing Fourier.

Alt_Name: Giulio Cesare Aranzio Maggio; Julius Caesar Arantius
Father_Notes: Father Ottaviano di Jacopo and mother Maria Maggi were poor; maternal uncle Bartolomeo Maggi, a surgeon and court physician, provided financial aid for his medical education.
Education_Institution: University of Padua; University of Bologna
Education_Notes: Studied at the University of Padua, where he made his first anatomical discovery in 1548 at age nineteen. Received his medical degree from the University of Bologna on 20 May 1556.
Education_Locations: Padua, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, 1548; Bologna, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, 1556
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Discovered the elevator muscle of the upper eyelid, the pedes hippocampi, the cerebellum cistern, the fourth ventricle, and the arterial duct between the aorta and pulmonary artery. Published De humano foetu opusculum (1564) and Observationes anatomicae (1579), advancing anatomy through experimental investigation of organ function. Performed rhinoplastic surgery and published De tumoribus secundum locus affectum (1571) on surgical subjects. First lecturer at Bologna to hold a separate professorship of anatomy.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Became lecturer in medicine and surgery at the University of Bologna shortly after receiving his degree in 1556, at age twenty-seven. In 1570 he secured separation of anatomy from surgery, holding both professorships for the remainder of his life.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Eugenio Dall'Osso. Education_Notes: Went to Athens as a young man and became acquainted with Stoicism.
Education_Locations: Athens, Unknown, Greece, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Author of the Phaenomena, a didactic poem describing constellations, celestial circles, calendar systems including the Metonic cycle, and weather signs derived from celestial and terrestrial phenomena. The work drew on Eudoxus of Cnidos and possibly Theophrastus; it contained astronomical errors but became highly influential and was translated into Latin by Cicero, Germanicus, and Avienus.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Spent time at the court of Antigonus Gonatas in Macedon and with Antiochus I in Syria.
Patronage_Notes: Patronized by Antigonus Gonatas (276–239 B.C.) in Macedon and by Antiochus I in Syria.

Education_Institution: University College London; Botany School, Cambridge
Education_Notes: Studied at school in northern London; attended University College, London; studied at the Botany School, Cambridge. No formal degree is named in the source.
Education_Locations: London, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; Cambridge, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering work in comparative plant anatomy, especially of monocotyledons. Published influential studies on aquatic angiosperms, the phyllode theory of monocotyledonous leaf origin, and grasses. Later work addressed the philosophy and metaphysics of scientific thought.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked largely independently throughout her life with few formal institutional contacts. Supported by personal means while conducting research and publishing.
Patronage_Notes: Influenced and encouraged by Ethel Sargant, her friend and teacher; A. C. Seward suggested her study of early printed herbals.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; Linnean Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: First woman botanist elected Fellow of the Royal Society. Received the Gold Medal of the Linnean Society in 1948.

Education_Notes: No formal education is documented. Registered as a nonpleading lawyer to the Sovereign Council of Alsace around 1780.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in operational calculus and the calculus of derivatives. Won the 1787 Academy of St. Petersburg prize for work on arbitrary functions in differential equations. Developed methods for series expansions and anticipated modern concepts including discontinuous functions, holomorphic functions, and operational symbols.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught mathematics at Collège de Colmar around 1787; taught mathematics at École d'Artillerie in Strasbourg from 1789; professor of physics at Collège Royal; director of Collège Royal April–October 1791; rector of University of Strasbourg; instituteur d'analyse at École Centrale de Paris (1794); taught at École Préparatoire; held chair of mathematics at École Centrale du Bas-Rhin (1796–1802). Served as deputy to Assemblée Législative (1791) and Convention Nationale (1792).
Patronage_Notes: Served in Revolutionary government bodies; appointed to direct École Centrale du Bas-Rhin in 1795.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences; Institut National
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected corresponding member of the Académie des Sciences in 1792; elected associate nonresident member of the Institut National (mathematics section, first class) in 1796. Member of the Amis de la Constitution (1790).
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Jean Itard. Father_Notes: Son of schoolteachers.
Education_Notes: Secondary schooling at Perpignan; admitted to École Normale Supérieure in 1904 and studied under Vidal de la Blache; passed agrégation in both history and geography in 1907.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, 1904, 1907
Scientific_Disciplines: Geography; Human Geography; Regional Geography; Urban Geography
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered the study of pastoral life in the French Alps through fieldwork and systematic investigation; established urban geography as a distinct focus through his study of Clermont-Ferrand; specialized in the geography of the Massif Central and regional geography of the Auvergne.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor at Grenoble lycée from 1907; lecturer at University of Clermont-Ferrand from 1919 and professor from 1922 to 1952.

Father_Notes: Scottish Episcopal clergyman.
Education_Institution: University of Aberdeen; University of St. Andrews
Education_Notes: Studied at Aberdeen; received doctor's degree in medicine from St. Andrews in 1696.
Education_Locations: Aberdeen, Unknown, Scotland, Unknown, Unknown; St. Andrews, Unknown, Scotland, Unknown, 1696
Religion_Notes: Son of a Scottish Episcopal clergyman; served as physician to Queen Anne.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of mathematical statistics through his paper on sex ratios at birth, which demonstrated the first known example of mathematical statistical inference and established the foundation of modern statistical reasoning. Also well acquainted with probability theory and published an English translation of Huygens' work on probability.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Settled in London in 1697 as a physician. Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1704; appointed physician extraordinary to Queen Anne in 1705 (ordinary physician from 1709); elected fellow of the Royal College of Physicians in 1710.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed physician extraordinary to Queen Anne in 1705, becoming ordinary physician in 1709.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1704.

Alt_Name: Adolphe d'Archiac; Étienne-Jules-Adolphe Desmier de Saint-Simon, Vicomte d'Archiac; Dexmier
Father_Notes: Étienne-Louis-Marie Dexmier d'Archiac de Saint-Simon, a former cavalry captain and impoverished descendant of an ancient noble family from Angoumois.
Education_Notes: Attended the school for pages at Versailles and prepared for the military academy at Saint-Cyr, admitted November 1819. No university degree recorded. Self-taught in geology; came to the study of sedimentary formations through independent research.
Education_Locations: Saint-Cyr, Unknown, France, 1819, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Specialized in sedimentary formations and stratigraphy, establishing detailed geological sections and fossil correlations across northern France, Belgium, and England. Pioneered the study of Nummulites and Foraminifera; published comprehensive history of geological progress 1834–1845. Later held chair of paleontology at the Muséum d'Histoire Naturelle, emphasizing stratigraphic paleontology and the succession of life forms through geological time.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Placed on half-pay leave from the cavalry in 1830 following his political pamphlet, which provided subsistence without active employment. Commissioned by the Ministry of Public Works to produce geological maps. Appointed professor of paleontology at the Muséum d'Histoire Naturelle in 1861.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by the assembly of professors of the Muséum d'Histoire Naturelle and the Académie des Sciences in his candidacy for the paleontology chair. Commissioned by the Ministry of Public Works for geological surveys.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Geological Society of France; Académie des Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Deputy secretary of the Geological Society in 1836, secretary in 1838, and president in 1844, 1849, and 1854. Elected member of the Académie des Sciences, Section for Mineralogy, on 27 April 1857.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Arthur Birembaut. Original works: Histoire des progrés de la géologie de 1834 á 1845, 9 vols. Education_Notes: Pupil of Agathinos; no formal institutional education is recorded.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Eclectic physician influenced by pneumatic school doctrines. Principal contributions in pathology, surgery, and therapeutics. Wrote on localized disease manifestations, the pulse, acute and chronic diseases, fever signs, surgical amputation and repair, cancer diagnosis, and materia medica.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced medicine in Rome during the reign of Trajan (98–117); achieved sufficient popularity to be mentioned by the poet Juvenal.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering work in geometry, the method of exhaustion, mechanics, hydrostatics, and the theory of the lever. Designed and built mechanical devices including the screw of Archimedes. Contributions to understanding of floating bodies and centers of gravity.
Instruments_Notes: Designed the screw mechanism for raising water, known as the Archimedean screw.

Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; Geometry; Number Theory; Music Theory; Physics; Astronomy
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Made fundamental contributions to the theory of numbers, geometry, and music. Developed the theory of means and proportions (arithmetic, geometric, and harmonic means). Solved the Delian problem of cube duplication through an ingenious three-dimensional geometric construction. Established mathematical foundations for music theory, deriving musical intervals from arithmetic and harmonic means. Elaborated a physical theory of sound based on the relationship between motion speed and pitch.
Patronage_Notes: Played a leading political role in Tarentum and concluded an alliance with Dionysius the Younger through Plato's agency.

Father_Notes: Born of poor parents.
Education_Notes: Completed a good literary and mathematical education at Verona under the patronage of Marchese Andrea Carlotti, but took no degree.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Founder of modern geology through application of Galilean methodology to earth structure and composition. Established stratigraphic chronology by identifying four successive geological orders (Primary, Secondary, Tertiary, Quaternary) in the Alps and surrounding regions. Studied fossil species variation with geological age, identified magmatic rock origins, and recognized transformations of sedimentary rocks by magmatic activity. Precursor of actualism in geology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked as independent mining expert in Upper Adige valley mines; employed by English copper and lead mining company in Montieri and Boccheggiano (1773) and mercury mining operation at Monte Amiata (1775). In 1769 appointed by Venetian Senate to office overseeing development of agriculture and industry throughout the republic, conducting research in chemistry, metallurgy, and agricultural technology.
Patronage_Notes: Early patronage by Marchese Andrea Carlotti enabled his education. Later appointed to important office by Venetian Senate in 1769 for agricultural and industrial development.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Author of a comprehensive text on the causes, symptoms, and treatment of acute and chronic diseases. Member of the Pneumatic school of physicians; his work preserves Stoic-Posidonian medical philosophy and demonstrates the school's revival of Hippocratic doctrine.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced as a physician; probably resided in Rome at some point, possibly in connection with the imperial court.

Father_Notes: Father was a clerk in government service. Mother was from Morzine, Savoy, and was described as a remarkable woman who encouraged his education and intellectual development.

Education_Notes: Initially apprenticed to an architect by his father, but redirected toward medicine by his mother. Began studies in medicine at Geneva but transferred to Lausanne, where he studied under Maurice Lugeon and became interested in Alpine geology. No formal degree is named in the source.

Scientific_Disciplines: Geology; Structural Geology; Tectonics; Stratigraphy; Metamorphism
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of Alpine structural geology and nappe theory. Developed geometric methods for analyzing complex three-dimensional rock deformations and nappe structures in the Pennine Alps. Introduced the concept of the 'Pennic' type of deformation and basement folds. Synthesized regional Alpine geology with global tectonics, incorporating Wegener's continental drift hypothesis into a comprehensive model of Eurasian structural development. Created embryotectonics, the kinematic analysis of mountain-chain evolution through time.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Succeeded Hans Schardt as professor of geology at the University of Neuchâtel in 1911, where he remained until his death.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Swiss Geological Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Lectured to the Swiss Geological Society in 1915 announcing his new research program in embryotectonics. Presided over the first congress for the study of the Precambrian and ancient mountain chains in 1931.

Father_Notes: Johann Gottlieb Argelander, a wealthy merchant from Finland.
Education_Notes: Attended secondary school in Elbing and Collegium Fridericianum in Königsberg. Entered University of Königsberg in 1817 to study political economy and political science; attended lectures by Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel and participated in observatory calculating work. Earned doctorate in 1822 with dissertation on Greenwich observations; earned lectureship the same year with study of the Great Comet of 1811.
Education_Locations: Königsberg, Unknown, Prussia, Unknown, Unknown; Königsberg, Unknown, Prussia, 1817, 1822
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in systematic observation and cataloging of stellar positions and proper motions. Developed the method of magnitude estimation by steps for observing variable stars. Created the Bonner Durchmusterung, a comprehensive catalog of 324,198 stars with positions and magnitudes. Demonstrated the spatial motion of the sun through analysis of proper motions of 390 stars, verifying Herschel's earlier work.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant at Königsberg Observatory from age twenty-one; observer at Åbo Observatory from 1823; full professor at University of Helsinki from 1828; professor of astronomy at University of Bonn from 1836 until his death.
Patronage_Notes: Formed lasting friendship with Crown Prince Friedrich Wilhelm (later Friedrich Wilhelm IV) during the Napoleonic Wars when the royal family sheltered in the Argelander home. The crown prince, after ascending the throne, supported the construction of the new observatory at Bonn.
Instruments: Transit circle; Meridian circle; Comet seeker
Instruments_Notes: Used transit circle at Königsberg to measure positions of thousands of stars. Employed a small comet seeker (7.8-centimeter aperture, 63-centimeter focal length) for the Bonner Durchmusterung observations. Developed the method of magnitude estimation by steps, which allowed reliable stellar magnitude determination without a photometer.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Academy of St. Petersburg; Royal Society of London; Academy of Berlin; Academy of Stockholm; Academy of Paris; Academy of Vienna; Academy of Boston; Academy of Brussels; Societas Fennica; Royal Astronomical Society of London; National Academy of Sciences of the United States; Astronomische Gesellschaft
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Charter member of the Astronomische Gesellschaft; member of its governing body from 1863 to 1871 and chairman from 1864 to 1867.

Father_Notes: Father Antoine Dezallier owned the d'Argenville estate near Bezons and Versailles.
Education_Notes: Studied at the Collège du Plessis; trained in the fine arts under the engraver Bernard Picart, the painter Roger de Piles, and the architect Alexandre Le Blond.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines: Natural History; Conchyliology; Mineralogy; Art History; Engraving
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Published influential works on natural history, particularly conchyliology and mineralogy. Authored a history of famous painters and contributed to the eighteenth-century vogue for natural sciences through descriptions of notable natural history collections.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Purchased the post of secretary to the king in 1716; named maître des comptes in 1733 and counsellor to the king in 1748. Supported by personal wealth and collecting activities.
Patronage_Notes: Held court and government positions under the French crown, serving as secretary to the king, maître des comptes, and royal counsellor.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Société Royale des Sciences de Montpellier; Royal Society of London; Académie de La Rochelle
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Société Royale des Sciences de Montpellier in 1740, the Royal Society of London in 1750, and the Académie de La Rochelle in 1758.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Yves Laissus. Father_Notes: Octavio Argoli was a lawyer.
Education_Notes: Evidence suggests study with Giovanni Antonio Magini around 1600, though details are uncertain. No formal degree is recorded.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Produced extensive astronomical ephemerides based on the Prutenic Tables and later on Tycho Brahe's observations. Proposed a geocentric system in which Mercury and Venus orbit the sun while Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn orbit the earth, with the earth rotating on its axis. Wrote on astrological medicine and general astrology. Planned a defense of Galileo's Dialogi.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held the chair of mathematics at the Sapienza in Rome from 1622 to 1627, losing the post apparently due to his enthusiasm for astrology. From 1632 onward served as professor of mathematics at Padua.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in the theory of conic sections, treating them as loci. Introduced terminology for sections of acute-angled, right-angled, and obtuse-angled cones. Developed the locus problem for three or four lines and likely the focus-directrix property of conic sections. His work influenced Euclid and was later superseded by Apollonius.

Education_Notes: Studied under Strato of Lampsacos, third head of the Lyceum; likely studied at Alexandria rather than Athens after Strato assumed the headship in 287 B.C.
Education_Locations: Alexandria, Unknown, Egypt, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Propounded the heliocentric theory, placing the earth in circular orbit about the sun with the fixed stars at vast distance. Developed geometric procedures for approximating sines of small angles, anticipating trigonometric methods. Calculated astronomical distances and dimensions mathematically in his treatise On the Sizes and Distances of the Sun and Moon. Known to contemporaries as 'the mathematician.'
Instruments_Notes: Invented the scaphē, a hemispherical sundial with a vertical needle to cast shadows, widely used in antiquity.

Father_Notes: Served as personal physician to Amyntas II of Macedon, grandfather of Alexander the Great. Both parents died while Aristotle was a boy.
Education_Institution: Plato's Academy; Not Specified; Court of Hermeias; Not Specified
Education_Notes: Joined Plato's Academy in Athens around 367 B.C. at age seventeen and remained for twenty years. Later served as tutor to the young prince Alexander in Macedon from 342 B.C. Organized research programs and collected a natural history museum and library of maps and manuscripts.
Education_Locations: Athens, Unknown, Greece, -367, -347; Lesbos, Unknown, Greece, -344, -342; Unknown, Unknown, Greece, Unknown, -344; Macedon, Unknown, Greece, -342, -335
Religion_Notes: Faced a charge of impiety late in life and went into voluntary exile, but the entry does not state his religious affiliation.
Scientific_Disciplines: Natural Philosophy; Physics; Astronomy; Meteorology; Biology; Zoology; Anatomy; Physiology; Mathematics; Medicine; Philosophy; Logic; Metaphysics
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Most influential ancient exponent of scientific methodology and division of sciences. Contributed foundational work in physics, cosmology, natural history, zoology, anatomy, and physiology. Developed systematic approaches to logic, metaphysics, and the analysis of causation and explanation. Pioneered the study of motion, change, the continuum, and the structure of the universe.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught at Plato's Academy for twenty years; later taught at the Lyceum in Athens for twelve years after 335 B.C. Served as tutor to Alexander the Great in Macedon, supported by the Macedonian court.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by Hermeias, ruler of a court on the far side of the Aegean, who became his father-in-law. Employed as tutor to the young prince Alexander by the Macedonian court.

Education_Notes: Joined Plato's Academy in Athens in youth; studied there for approximately twenty years. Lived on Lesbos with Theophrastus during 344–342 B.C., conducting zoological research. Founded the Lyceum in Athens after returning from Macedonia.
Education_Locations: Athens, Unknown, Greece, -367, -347
Scientific_Disciplines: Natural Philosophy; Zoology; Biology; Natural History; Physics; Metaphysics; Logic; Philosophy
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering systematic study of animal anatomy, reproduction, classification, and behavior. Developed teleological explanations of natural phenomena grounded in formal and material causation. Integrated biological observation with philosophical theory of form, matter, actuality, and potentiality. Major works include Historia animalium (descriptive zoology of ~500 animal kinds), De partibus animalium (animal structure and function), De generatione animalium (reproduction and inheritance), and Parva naturalia (physiology and sensation).
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught at Plato's Academy; founded and directed the Lyceum in Athens.
Patronage_Notes: Served as tutor to Alexander the Great; received patronage from Philip II of Macedon.

Father_Notes: Father was Nicomachus, physician to the Macedonian court.
Education_Notes: Studied at Plato's Academy in Athens from age 17 to 37; later founded his own school, the Lyceum, in Athens.
Education_Locations: Athens, Unknown, Greece, -367, -347
Scientific_Disciplines: Natural Philosophy; Anatomy; Physiology; Zoology; Natural History; Medicine
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted systematic dissections and observations of animal anatomy, particularly the cardiovascular system. Provided detailed descriptions of blood vessels, the heart, and the pulmonary system. Distinguished animals by the presence or absence of blood. Developed theories of respiration and the role of innate heat in the body.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught at Plato's Academy and later founded and directed the Lyceum in Athens. Received patronage from the Macedonian court through his father's position and later from Philip II and Alexander the Great.
Patronage_Notes: Patronized by the Macedonian court; tutored Alexander the Great.

Father_Notes: Father was Spintharus (or possibly Mnaseas), a musician whose acquaintance included Socrates, Epaminondas, and Archytas.
Education_Notes: Studied at Mantinea, an Arcadian city with a strong conservative musical tradition. Later became a pupil of Aristotle in Athens and held a position in the Lyceum, hoping to become head of the school upon Aristotle's death in 322 B.C.
Education_Locations: Mantinea, Unknown, Greece, Unknown, Unknown; Athens, Unknown, Greece, Unknown, 322
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Most famous and influential musical theorist of antiquity. Developed a radically empirical approach to harmonic theory based on the ear rather than mathematical ratios, dividing the octave into six tones and the tone into two semitones. Drew a clear distinction between rhythm as an abstract system of time units and the words, melodies, and movements in which it was incorporated. Also wrote on educational and political theory and Pythagorean doctrine.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held a position in Aristotle's Lyceum in Athens.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Made observations of fixed stars, including declinations and differences of longitude, circa 270 B.C. His measurements, though not highly accurate, were used by Hipparchus a century later to discover the precession of the equinoxes. Also wrote commentaries on Aratus and treatises on the polar stars.

Alt_Name: Vladimir Konstantinovich Arkadiev; V. K. Arkadiev
Father_Notes: Died when Vladimir was young; mother worked in a library.
Education_Notes: Attended Gymnasium, graduating in 1904. Entered Physics and Mathematics Faculty of Moscow University in 1904 and studied under N. A. Umov and P. N. Lebedev. No formal degree is named in the source.
Education_Locations: Moscow, Unknown, Russia, 1904, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in ferromagnetism and high-frequency magnetic phenomena. Discovered ferromagnetic resonance (1913) and introduced the concept of complex magnetic permeability. Developed magnetodynamics and the theory of magnetic viscosity. Demonstrated diffraction of light on large objects, constructed a high-tension impulse (lightning) generator, and perfected the levitation of a permanent magnet above a superconductor.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Studied and conducted research at Moscow University from 1904. Left in 1911 to protest administrative arbitrariness, transferring to Shanyavsky Municipal University. Returned to Moscow University after the October Revolution, where he organized and headed a large laboratory for electromagnetic research until his death.
Instruments: Lightning Generator; Electromagnetic Spectrograph; Photographic Plate for Centimeter Waves
Instruments_Notes: Developed an original generator (1922) that enabled his wife A. A. Glagoleva-Arkadieva to obtain the first electromagnetic spectra in the wavelength range of a few centimeters to 0.080 millimeters. Created a photographic plate sensitive to centimeter-length waves (1934). Constructed a high-tension impulse generator, later called a lightning generator (1925). Perfected a demonstration of permanent magnet levitation above a superconducting dish (1947).
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Academy of Sciences of the U.S.S.R.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Chosen an associate member of the Academy of Sciences of the U.S.S.R. in 1927.

Father_Notes: James Arkell was a partner in the family brewery at Kingsdown, Wiltshire.
Education_Notes: Attended boarding school; entered New College, Oxford in 1922 and graduated in geology in 1925. Awarded the Burdett-Coutts research scholarship.
Education_Locations: Oxford, Unknown, England, 1922, 1925
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Specialized in Jurassic stratigraphy and ammonite paleontology. Made major contributions to biostratigraphical classification, establishing zonal assemblages and standardizing stratigraphic nomenclature for the Jurassic system. Published comprehensive synthesis of world Jurassic geology and contributed to the Treatise on Invertebrate Paleontology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Lecturer at New College, Oxford from 1929; senior research fellow at New College 1933–1940. Principal in the Ministry of War Transport 1941–1943. Senior research fellow at Trinity College, Cambridge from 1947 until his death.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society of London; Linnean Society of Normandy; Geological Society of London; Geological Societies of France, Germany, and Egypt; Paleontological Society of America
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society of London in 1947. Honorary member or correspondent of the Linnean Society of Normandy and the Geological Societies of France, Germany, and Egypt, and the Paleontological Society of America.

Father_Notes: Father was Henry Edward Armstrong, a Fellow of the Royal Society.
Education_Notes: Trained in inorganic chemistry under Claisen and in physical chemistry under van't Hoff at Berlin; received Ph.D. in 1901. Conducted research with Emil Fischer. Received the first D.Sc. by research of the University of London for work on disaccharides, glucosides, and enzymes at Central Technical College.
Education_Locations: Berlin, Unknown, Germany, 1898, 1901
Scientific_Disciplines: Chemistry; Organic Chemistry; Physical Chemistry; Biochemistry
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering research on carbohydrates, disaccharides, glucosides, and enzymes; published one of the first monographs on carbohydrates (1910). Extensive work on heterogeneous catalysis, particularly the large-scale catalytic production of acetic acid and acetone from ethyl alcohol during World War I. Active in chemical research throughout his career.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Conducted research at Central Technical College in London; entered the chemical industry in 1905 and was intimately involved in the formation of Imperial Chemical Industries, Ltd. From 1928 served as a consultant to the chemical industry.
Patronage_Notes: During World War II served as scientific adviser to several important governmental agencies and was principal adviser to the British delegates and a delegate to the founding conference of UNESCO.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society of London
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected a Fellow of the Royal Society of London and was active in its affairs.

Father_Notes: John Armstrong was a publisher who became vice-president in charge of the American branch of Oxford University Press.
Education_Notes: Attended high school in Yonkers, New York; entered Columbia University at nineteen and studied electrical engineering under Michael Idvorsky Pupin, graduating in 1913.
Education_Locations: New York, Unknown, United States, Unknown, 1913
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered radio engineering through four major inventions: the triode feedback (regenerative) circuit, the super-heterodyne circuit, superregeneration, and frequency modulation (FM). His work fundamentally advanced electronic communication and radio receiver design.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as assistant at Columbia University; sold feedback and superheterodyne patents to Westinghouse Electric & Manufacturing Company with retained royalty rights; became a millionaire through RCA licensing agreements; engaged in patent litigation and licensing throughout his career.
Patronage_Notes: Served as U.S. Army Signal Corps officer during World War I, developing the super-heterodyne circuit while in France. Received U.S. Medal for Merit in 1945 for war work.
Instruments: Triode Feedback Circuit; Super-Heterodyne Circuit; Superregeneration Circuit; Frequency Modulation System
Instruments_Notes: Invented the triode feedback (regenerative) circuit while an undergraduate, greatly improving triode utilization. Developed the super-heterodyne circuit during World War I, which improved sensitivity and stability of radio receivers by extending heterodyne techniques to higher frequencies. Created superregeneration to overcome regenerative receiver oscillation limitations. Patented frequency modulation (FM), his greatest invention, which revolutionized radio and mobile communications despite initial industry resistance.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: American Institute of Electrical Engineers; Institute of Radio Engineers
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Received Edison Medal from the American Institute of Electrical Engineers in 1942; received Medal of Honor from the Institute of Radio Engineers in 1918, reaffirmed in 1934. Honored in the Pantheon of the International Telecommunications Union in Geneva.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Charles Süsskind. Armstrong received forty-two patents and wrote twenty-six papers listed in Lawrence Lessing, Man of High Fidelity (Philadelphia, 1956). Obituaries in New York Times (2 Feb. 1954), p. 27; and Proceedings of the Institute of Radio Engineers, 42 (1954), 635.
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Charles Süsskind.

Education_Institution: Royal College of Chemistry; University of Leipzig
Education_Notes: Studied at the Royal College of Chemistry under A.W. Hofmann and John Tyndall; conducted research under Edward Frankland; studied under Hermann Kolbe at Leipzig and received Ph.D. in 1870.
Education_Locations: London, Unknown, England, 1865, Unknown; Leipzig, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1870
Scientific_Disciplines: Chemistry; Organic Chemistry; Chemistry Education; Crystallography; Chemical Engineering
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer work on benzene structure and the centric formula; research on naphthalene structure and reactions with W.P. Wynne that advanced the dye industry; quinonoid theory for color of organic compounds; reactions of camphor and terpenes; enzyme reaction mechanisms; significant crystallography research predating X-ray diffraction; early advocate of Mendeleev's periodic table and molecular spatial configuration; devised curricula relating chemistry and engineering, regarded as father of chemical engineering.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Teaching combined with research from 1870; professor of chemistry at the Central Institution, South Kensington from 1884 until retirement in 1911; also served on the Committee on Management for Rothamsted Experiment Station.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society of London; Chemical Society of London
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society at age twenty-eight; served the Chemical Society of London as secretary, president, and vice-president; helped organize the Education Section of the British Association for the Advancement of Science and served as its president in 1902.

Alt_Name: Arnau de Vilanova; Arnaldus de Villanova
Father_Notes: Parents may have been converted Jews; no other information provided.
Education_Notes: Student at Montpellier ca. 1260. Studied for six months with the Montpellier Dominicans. Attribution of training under John Casamicciola at the University of Naples (1267–1276) rests on doubtful authenticity of the Breviarium practice. No formal degree is recorded.
Education_Locations: Montpellier, Unknown, France, 1260, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Influenced by Joachimite Peter John Olivi and the spiritual-Franciscans. Wrote prophetic and mystical works on Church reform and the Antichrist. His theological views were controversial; the De adventu antichristi was condemned in 1299, and he was spared imprisonment only through William of Nogaret's intervention. Tolerated by popes Boniface VIII and Benedict XI as a physician but not for his theology; gained papal and royal patronage under Clement V (1305).
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Principal figure in fusing Western empirical tradition with systematic medical philosophy of Greeks and Arabs at Montpellier. Translated Avicenna's De viribus cordis and Galen's De rigore from Arabic into Latin; also translated works on drugs and regimen. Lectured extensively on Hippocratic and Galenic texts. Developed coherent, systematic science of medicine on Galenic foundations, particularly through the Aphorismi de gradibus, which established mathematical pharmacy based on qualitative intensity. Wrote on astrology and oneiromancy; his epistemology blended rationalism with mysticism and divine illumination. Many alchemical texts were spuriously attributed to him.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Physician to Peter III of Aragon by 1281, and subsequently to Alfonso III. By 1291 became medical master at Montpellier's studium generale while maintaining court consultations. Practiced medicine with considerable success; attended royal patients and high-ranking ecclesiastics. Received support from the Aragonese royal family for his theological work.
Patronage_Notes: Served as physician to Peter III and Alfonso III of Aragon. Supported by James II of Aragon, who sent him on diplomatic missions and consulted him on medical matters. Patronized by Pope Clement V from 1305 onward. Later attached himself to Frederick I of Trinacria. Popes Boniface VIII and Benedict XI tolerated him as a physician.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Michael McVaugh. Father_Notes: Father was a lawyer who defended the University of Paris against the Jesuits in 1594; Antoine was the youngest of twenty children.
Education_Notes: Ordained a priest and received the doctorate in theology in 1641; entered the Sorbonne in 1643 after the death of Richelieu.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, 1643, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Ordained priest; held Jansenist views and was expelled from the Sorbonne in 1656 for these beliefs; spent much of his later life in theological dispute.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Contributed to mathematical pedagogy through the Éléments, a reworking of Euclidean theorems emphasizing clarity and fresh exposition. Engaged in philosophical correspondence with Descartes and Leibniz; wrote objections to Descartes' Méditations and disputed with Malebranche. Co-authored the Port-Royal Logic with Pierre Nicole, which elaborated the theory of clear and distinct ideas and influenced logic teaching for centuries. Co-authored the Port-Royal Grammar, which pioneered universal grammar and treated language as reflecting mental processes.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Ordained priest; entered the Sorbonne in 1643 as a member of that theological faculty until his expulsion in 1656 for Jansenist views.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Henry Nathan. Original works: Grammaire générale et raisonnée (Port-Royal Grammar; Paris, 1660); La logique ou l'art de penser (Port-Royal Logic; Paris, 1662), critical edition by P. Clair and F. Girbal (Paris, 1965); Nouveaux élémens de géométrie (Paris, 1667). Collections: Oeuvres, 45 vols. (Lausanne, 1775–1783); Oeuvres philosophiques, J. Simon and C. Jourdain, eds. (Paris, 1893). Education_Notes: Studied physics under Robert Andrews Millikan at the University of Chicago, where he earned his doctorate in 1911.
Education_Locations: Middletown, Connecticut, United States, Unknown, Unknown; Chicago, Illinois, United States, Unknown, 1911
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered the development of reliable triode designs for long-distance telephony by recognizing the importance of high vacuum; contributed to the development of magnetic alloys for sound reproduction and electroacoustics.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held positions at Bell Telephone Laboratories from its founding in 1925 as first director of research; served as captain in the U.S. Army Signal Corps during World War I.
Instruments_Notes: Developed designs utilizing reliable triodes with high vacuum, making long-distance telephony possible; earlier developed a mercury-arc repeater for transcontinental telephone lines.

Education_Institution: University of Perugia; University of Montpellier; University of Padua
Education_Notes: Studied philosophy and medicine at Perugia, Montpellier, and Padua, where he attended lectures by Fabricius. Graduated M.D. in 1605.
Education_Locations: Perugia, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown; Montpellier, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; Padua, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, 1605
Religion_Notes: Buried in the Church of Saint Luke in Venice.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered the hypothesis of preformation of the germ in plant and animal generation. Published the influential Epistola de generatione plantarum ex seminibus (1625), which posited that seeds contain a miniature preformed plant. Investigated the permeability of the interventricular septum of the heart, though no writings on this survive. His work on preformation became foundational to seventeenth-century embryology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced medicine in Venice from 1610. Attended and likely taught at Padua before settling in Venice. Declined offers to serve as personal physician to King James I of England and Pope Urban VIII.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Pietro Franceschini. Original works: Disputatio de rabie contagiosa, cui praeposita est epistola de generatione plantarum ex seminibus (Venice, 1625); Autori del bel parlare (Venice, 1643). Father_Notes: Died during Aronhold's youth; family moved to Königsberg after his death.
Education_Notes: Attended elementary school in Angerburg and Gymnasium in Rastenburg, then Gymnasium in Königsberg after his mother's relocation. Studied mathematics and natural sciences at University of Königsberg under Bessel, Jacobi, Richelot, Hesse, and Franz Neumann. Followed Jacobi to Berlin and studied under Dirichlet, Steiner, Gustav Magnus, and Dove. Did not take state examinations but received Doctor honoris causa in 1851 for his treatise on algebraic principles.
Education_Locations: Rastenburg, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Königsberg, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Königsberg, Unknown, Germany, 1841, 1845
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in the theory of invariants, developing a systematic method for studying functions unchanged under linear substitutions. Established foundational principles and derived Aronhold's differential equations, which characterize invariant theory. Also worked on plane curves, completing Plücker's problem of inflection points and formulating theorems on fourth-order curves.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught at the Artillery and Engineers' School in Berlin (1852–1854); professor at the Royal Academy of Architecture in Berlin (from 1851, appointed professor 1863); professor at the Royal Academy for Arts and Crafts (from 1860, appointed professor 1864), where he assumed Weierstrass's teaching duties in 1862.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Academy of Sciences in Göttingen
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Corresponding member from 1869.

Father_Notes: Father was an accountant of Huguenot descent.
Education_Institution: Collège Français; University of Berlin; University of Leipzig
Education_Notes: Attended Collège Français in Berlin before entering the University of Berlin in 1839 as a promising graduate student. Received Ph.D. from University of Leipzig in 1850.
Education_Locations: Berlin, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Berlin, Unknown, Germany, 1839, Unknown; Leipzig, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1850
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Diligent investigator of comets, asteroids, and nebulae. Discovered comet 1845 I, comet d'Arrest (1851 II), comet 1857 I, and asteroid (76) Freia. Made accurate measurements of nebulous objects and extended observations to 1,942 nebulae. First to note in 1873 that gaseous nebulae were preferentially located near the plane of the Milky Way, suggesting they were relatively nearby objects in our own galaxy. Began spectroscopic observations following William Huggins.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked at the Berlin Observatory under Johann Franz Encke. Appointed to a new post at the Leipzig Observatory in 1848, where he worked under August Ferdinand Möbius. Became professor at the University of Copenhagen in 1858 and director of its new observatory.
Patronage_Notes: Received a medal from the King of Denmark for discovering comet 1845 I. Elected foreign associate of the Royal Astronomical Society of London in 1848. Received the Gold Medal of the Royal Astronomical Society in 1875.
Instruments_Notes: Used an eleven-inch telescope for nebular observations at Copenhagen Observatory.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Astronomical Society of London
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected foreign associate in 1848; received Gold Medal in 1875.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Sally H. Dieke. Father_Notes: Svante Gustav Arrhenius was a surveyor and later supervisor of the University of Uppsala, and overseer of the estate of Vik.
Education_Institution: Cathedral School; University of Uppsala; University of Riga; University of Würzburg; University of Graz; University of Amsterdam
Education_Notes: Attended Cathedral School in Uppsala; entered University of Uppsala at age seventeen, studying mathematics, chemistry, and physics; passed candidate examination in 1878; pursued doctoral study in physics under Tobias Robert Thalén but was dissatisfied; worked under Erik Edlund in Stockholm from 1881; defended dissertation on electrolytic dissociation in May 1884. Traveled extensively 1886–1890 working in laboratories of Ostwald, Kohlrausch, Boltzmann, and van't Hoff.
Education_Locations: Uppsala, Unknown, Sweden, Unknown, Unknown; Uppsala, Unknown, Sweden, 1876, 1884; Riga, Unknown, Latvia, 1884, 1886; Würzburg, Unknown, Germany, 1886, 1887; Graz, Unknown, Austria, 1887, 1888; Amsterdam, Unknown, Netherlands, 1888, 1890
Scientific_Disciplines: Chemistry; Physical Chemistry; Physics; Meteorology; Cosmology; Immunochemistry
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Founder of modern physical chemistry; developed the theory of electrolytic dissociation, explaining the conductivity of electrolytic solutions and the behavior of ions in solution. Made important contributions to reaction kinetics and activation energy. Later applied physical-chemical principles to cosmic phenomena, meteorology, glacial periods, volcanic processes, and immunology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed lecturer in physical chemistry at University of Uppsala in 1884; professor of physics at Technical High School of Stockholm from 1895; rector of Technical High School 1896–1905; director of the physical chemistry department of the Nobel Institute in Stockholm from 1905 until his death.
Patronage_Notes: Received travel grant from Swedish Academy of Sciences enabling work in laboratories of prominent scientists (Ostwald, Kohlrausch, Boltzmann, van't Hoff) during 1886–1890. Wilhelm Ostwald's visit and offer of a docentship in Riga in 1884 was instrumental in securing his position at Uppsala.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Swedish Academy of Sciences; Deutsche Elektrochemische Gesellschaft; Deutsche Chemische Gesellschaft; Royal Society of London
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected honorary member of Deutsche Elektrochemische Gesellschaft in 1895; appointed to Swedish Academy of Sciences in 1901 over strong opposition; elected honorary member of Deutsche Chemische Gesellschaft in 1905; became foreign member of Royal Society of London in 1911.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by H. A. M. Snelders. Father_Notes: Member of ancient French nobility holding land and wealth in Limoges for centuries; fourth generation of physicians in the family.
Education_Institution: Lycée Impérial de Limoges; Collège Ste.-Barbe; Université de Poitiers
Education_Notes: Studied classics at Lycée Impérial de Limoges and Collège Ste.-Barbe; received baccalaureate from Université de Poitiers in 1869. Medical studies began at Limoges and continued in Paris after 1870. Became preparateur to Claude Bernard from 1873 to 1878, which constituted his principal scientific training.
Education_Locations: Limoges, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; Poitiers, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1869
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in biophysics and electrophysiology; major contributions to understanding electrical properties of muscle contraction and nerve excitation. Developed calorimetric methods for measuring animal heat and body temperature. Founded physiotherapy as a paramedical discipline through application of high-frequency electrical currents to therapeutic purposes. Extensive work on industrial applications of electricity and cryogenic studies.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Directed the laboratory for biophysics at rue St.-Jacques from 1882 to 1910, then the laboratory at Nogent-sur-Marne from 1910 to 1931. Served as government science consultant during World War I. Instrumental in founding national and international societies for electrical science and cryogenic studies.
Patronage_Notes: Benefited from Paul Bert's assistance as Minister of Public Education in establishing the laboratory at rue St.-Jacques in 1882. Worked closely with Claude Bernard as his preparateur and later with C. Brown-Séquard. Collaborated extensively with E. Marey and other leading scientists.
Instruments: Calorimeter; Thermoelectric Needles; Galvanometer; Electrodes; Myographic Equipment; Incubator; High Frequency Oscillator; Electrocoagulation Apparatus
Instruments_Notes: Designed a double-chambered calorimeter with constant interior temperature maintained by circulating ice water, achieving remarkable accuracy for measuring heat production. Invented thermoelectric needles for simultaneous temperature measurement in tissue and blood. Developed nonpolarizable silver chloride electrodes for biological research. With Deprez, invented the mobile circuit galvanometer in 1882. With Marey, invented myographic equipment. Designed the first electrically controlled constant temperature incubator for embryological and bacterial research. Pioneered use of high-frequency oscillators for therapeutic heating and electrocoagulation apparatus for surgical applications.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Academy of Sciences; Academy of Medicine; Society of Biologists; Institute for Actinology; International Society for Electrical Science; International Society for Cryogenic Studies
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to Academy of Sciences in 1894 and Academy of Medicine in 1888. Elected president of the Institute for Actinology in 1918. Active member of societies for electrotherapy, physics, electronics, civil engineering, electroceramics, and soldering. Instrumental in founding the national society for electrical science in 1881 and the international society in 1897.

Alt_Name: Petrus Arctaedius Angermannus; Petrus Arctelius Angerm.
Father_Notes: Olaus Arctaedius, a curate appointed to the living of Nordmaling in 1716; died before March 1729.
Education_Notes: Attended school at Hernösand from autumn 1716, excelling in studies and spending out-of-school hours dissecting fishes and collecting plants. Matriculated at Uppsala University on 30 October 1724. Studied chemistry and natural history in the medical faculty under Lars Roberg and Olof Rudbeck. Collaborated closely with Linnaeus from March 1729, dividing natural history interests; Artedi focused on fishes, amphibians, mammals, minerals, and alchemy.
Education_Locations: Hernösand, Unknown, Sweden, 1716, Unknown; Uppsala, Unknown, Sweden, 1724, 1729
Scientific_Disciplines: Natural History; Ichthyology; Zoology; Botany; Mineralogy; Alchemy; Anatomy
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of ichthyology and systematic zoology. Established the notion of genus in zoology, distinguished species from variety, and developed classification into classes, orders, and families. Studied fishes, amphibians, and mammals with comparative anatomical methods. Specialized in Umbelliferae in botany. Examined and dissected seventy-two fish species. His ichthyological work provided the foundation for modern fish taxonomy.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Studied at Uppsala University. In England (September 1734–1735) received financial aid from his brothers-in-law and studied collections. In Amsterdam, supported by chemist Albert Seba, who employed him to study fishes for the third volume of his Thesaurus.
Patronage_Notes: Sir Hans Sloane, president of the Royal Society, provided kind assistance during Artedi's stay in England. Albert Seba, a wealthy Amsterdam collector and chemist, employed Artedi to work on his natural history collection and provided lodging.

Father_Notes: Art dealer; family background suggests comfortable circumstances.

Education_Notes: One semester at University of Vienna before military service in 1916–1918. Resumed studies at Leipzig in January 1919 under Gustav Herglotz; awarded Ph.D. in June 1921. Spent one year at University of Göttingen after his doctorate.
Education_Locations: Vienna, Unknown, Austria, Unknown, 1916; Leipzig, Unknown, Germany, 1919, 1921; Göttingen, Unknown, Germany, 1921, 1922
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Major contributions to class field theory, L-series, and the general law of reciprocity. Developed theory of formal-real fields and solved Hilbert's problem on definite functions. Advanced abstract algebra, the theory of algebras and associative rings, and braid theory in topology. Influenced the development of algebraic topology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Lecturer at University of Hamburg (1923), extraordinary professor (1925), ordinary professor (1926). Taught at University of Notre Dame (one year), Indiana University Bloomington (1938–1946), Princeton University (1946–1958), and returned to University of Hamburg (1958–1962).

Education_Notes: Associated with Kusumapura (Pāṭaliputra, modern Patna in Bihar), the former Gupta imperial capital. No formal education or degree is recorded.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Author of the Āryabhaṭīya (499 A.D.), a comprehensive mathematical and astronomical treatise comprising four parts: introduction with parameters, mathematics, planetary models and time reckoning, and spherical astronomy including eclipses. Also wrote a lost treatise on the ardharātrika system. Developed an alphabetical system for expressing numbers and contributed to epicyclic astronomy and indeterminate equations.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Author of the Mahāsiddhānta, a comprehensive astronomical and mathematical treatise comprising eighteen chapters on planetary motion, eclipses, heliacal risings, conjunctions, arithmetic, geometry, and algebra. Father_Notes: Ayabe Yasumasa was a Confucian scholar-administrator of the Kizuki fief government.
Education_Notes: Self-taught in medicine and astronomy. Read Chinese calendrical works based on the Shou-shih system and possibly had access to seventeenth- and eighteenth-century Jesuit missionary writings. No formal institutional education is recorded.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in introducing Western observational methods and modern instruments to Japanese astronomy. Initiated precise observational techniques, ground lenses, and constructed a telescope to observe Jupiter's satellites. Developed methods for determining solar and lunar positions and calculating eclipses. Studied cyclic variation of astronomical parameters and investigated Kepler's third law.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed physician of the Kizuki fief government in 1767. After deserting his fief in 1772, practiced medicine in Osaka to support himself while pursuing astronomical research. Taught astronomy to pupils including Takahashi Yoshitoki and Hazama Shigetomi.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by wealthy Osaka merchant Hazama Shigetomi (1756–1816), one of his most able pupils, who sponsored instrument-making, astronomical observation, and the training of instrument-makers.
Instruments_Notes: Ground lenses and constructed a telescope used to observe the movements of Jupiter's satellites. His school introduced modern instruments and observational methods into Japan, replacing traditional Chinese-type instruments such as the gnomon.

Education_Notes: Trained originally as a philosopher and orator before becoming a physician.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Developed a mechanistic medical system based on solidism and atomism, rejecting humoralism. Rejected teleology and based knowledge on sensory appearances. Therapy emphasized diet, exercise, massage, and baths while avoiding powerful drugs and surgery. Opposed anatomical study. His doctrines influenced the methodist school of medicine.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Maintained a large medical practice in Rome with wealthy patients. Befriended by Cicero, Crassus, and other influential Romans. Declined an invitation to become personal physician to Mithridates Eupator, King of Pontus.

Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced surgery in Milan and was appointed first surgeon of the Spanish army in Italy from 1612 to 1620. Delivered lectures on the chylous vessels at Pavia in 1625.

Father_Notes: Simon Ashmole was a saddler in Lichfield; the family held a humble social position.
Education_Notes: Educated at Lichfield Grammar School with expectation of entering a craft. Obtained legal training in London and established a law practice in 1638, though he practiced only sporadically.
Education_Locations: Lichfield, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown
Religion_Notes: In religious and political matters he was excessively conservative and orthodox, consistent with the Anglican establishment of Restoration England.
Scientific_Disciplines: Natural Philosophy; Alchemy; Astrology; Astronomy; Botany; Medicine; Chemistry
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Deeply influenced by mathematicians and astrologers during the Civil War; formed lasting friendship with astrologer William Lilly. Extended interests from astrology to botany, medicine, and stenography. Became pupil of alchemist William Backhouse; published translations and collections of alchemical works. Saw alchemy and occult sciences as complementary to experimental natural philosophy. Founding fellow of the Royal Society in 1660, though his own outlook remained rooted in magical and astrological traditions.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Established law practice in 1638 but practiced sporadically. Appointed comptroller of the excise and Windsor herald by Charles II in 1660; the former provided large income. A fortunate marriage provided independent means. Supervised the Ashmolean Museum at Oxford from 1683 and appointed Robert Plot as keeper and first professor of chemistry.
Patronage_Notes: Charles II rewarded his Royalist loyalty in 1660 by granting him the offices of comptroller of the excise and Windsor herald. Became well known in court circles.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Became a founding fellow of the Royal Society in 1660 and made significant bequests to the society's museum.

Education_Institution: University of Cambridge; University College London; Royal Institution
Education_Notes: Read chemistry at Cambridge; began research under Sir William Bragg at University College, London, in 1921, moving with Bragg to the Royal Institution in 1923. No degree is named in the source.
