Scientific_Disciplines: Physics; X-ray Crystallography; Chemistry; Molecular Biology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in X-ray crystallography and molecular structure determination. Studied tartaric acid structures and space groups in London; at Leeds focused on natural and synthetic fiber structure, particularly wool and keratin. Discovered reversible transformation of keratin under tension and produced early X-ray models of DNA structure, proposing bases stacked 3.4 Å apart. Though his protein models were superseded by Pauling's alpha helix, his work represented the first molecular models with specific cross-linkages and contributed foundational insights to molecular biology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed lecturer in textile physics at University of Leeds in 1928, then reader, and finally professor of biomolecular structure.
Instruments_Notes: Developed X-ray diffraction techniques for studying fiber and molecular structure; took first good X-ray pictures of sodium thymonucleate in 1937 with Florence Bell.

Father_Notes: William Aston was a metal merchant and farmer.
Education_Notes: Primary education at Harbonne vicarage school; four years at Malvern College; studied at Mason's College, Birmingham (1893–1898) for the London intermediate science examination under chemists W. A. Tilden and P. F. Frankland and physicist J. H. Poynting; obtained a Forster Scholarship in 1898 to work with Frankland on stereochemistry; took a course in fermentation chemistry. No formal degree is recorded.
Education_Locations: Malvern, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; Birmingham, Unknown, England, 1893, 1898
Religion_Notes: Entry states he was of no decided religious views.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Early work on organic chemistry and stereochemistry; principal contributions to cathode rays and gaseous conduction phenomena; discovered the Aston dark space (1908); developed the mass spectrograph (1919) and demonstrated isotopy of neon; analyzed nonradioactive elements and formulated the whole-number rule for atomic masses; work on packing fraction and nuclear stability.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Brewery chemist at Wolverhampton (1900–1903); physics research student and assistant lecturer at Birmingham University (1903–1910); personal assistant and Clerk Maxwell Scholar at Cavendish Laboratory and Royal Institution (1910–1919, interrupted by war); technical assistant at Royal Aircraft Establishment, Farnborough (during World War I); fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge (1919–1945).
Patronage_Notes: Worked under J. J. Thomson at the Cavendish Laboratory and Royal Institution; Thomson assigned him the task of improving positive ray apparatus.
Instruments: Mass Spectrograph; Quartz Microbalance; Geissler Discharge Tube; Positive Ray Spectrograph
Instruments_Notes: Designed and built improved spherical discharge tubes with movable aluminum cathodes; invented a quartz microbalance sensitive to 10⁻⁹ gram (1913); developed the positive ray spectrograph (1919) with resolving power of 1 in 100 and accuracy of 1 in 10³; built two larger mass spectrographs (1927, 1935) with progressively higher resolving power and accuracy; developed photographic plates highly sensitive to positive ions for photometric analysis.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; International Union of Chemistry
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge (1919); held several honorary degrees; received medals from many scientific institutions; chairman of the Committee on Atoms of the International Union of Chemistry (1936–1945); awarded the Nobel Prize for Chemistry (1922).

Father_Notes: Protestant clergyman with probable Jewish ancestry; family chose to renounce Judaism rather than leave France.
Education_Notes: Received doctorate in medicine from Montpellier in 1703.
Education_Locations: Montpellier, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1703
Religion_Notes: Born into Protestant family with Jewish ancestry. His biblical exegesis work was criticized by both Catholic and Protestant theologians.
Scientific_Disciplines: Medicine; Anatomy; Physiology; Pathology; Surgery; Gynecology; Pediatrics; Venereology; Iatrochemistry; Natural Philosophy; Theology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Comprehensive medical educator covering anatomy, physiology, psychology, gerontology, pathology, therapy, venereology, gynecology, neurology, and pediatrics. Pioneered description of puerperal fever and septicemia from uterine infection; advised Caesarean sections only in emergencies. Anticipated reflex action in 1743, later formally described by Marshall Hall in 1833. Treatise on venereal diseases included first Occidental reproduction of Chinese medical terminology in printed Chinese characters. Biblical scholar and exegete; Conjectures sur la Genèse applied philological analysis to Old Testament authorship.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Occupied chairs of medicine at Montpellier (1716–1728) and Paris (1751); general physician to the duke of Orleans from 1728; chief physician to Augustus II of Poland from 1729; king's counsellor and physician from 1730; inspector general of mineral waters of Languedoc from 1721. Practiced medicine throughout his career.
Patronage_Notes: Served as general physician to the duke of Orleans; chief physician to Augustus II of Poland; king's counsellor and physician. Patronized by Mme. de Tencin, a patient whose salon he frequented from ca. 1730; she arranged his daughter's marriage and remembered him in her will.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie de Chirurgie
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Associated with the Académie de Chirurgie through Georges de la Faye, a member who treated his bladder tumor. Frequented the salon of Mme. de Tencin alongside Fontenelle, Marivaux, de Mairan, Mirabeau, de Boze, and Duclos.

Father_Notes: William Warren Atwater was a Methodist clergyman.
Education_Institution: University of Vermont; Wesleyan College; Yale University; University of Leipzig; University of Berlin
Education_Notes: Studied two years at University of Vermont before receiving bachelor's degree from Wesleyan College in 1865. Pursued postgraduate work at Yale University's Sheffield Scientific School under Samuel W. Johnson, earning his doctorate in 1869 with a thesis on maize composition analysis. Spent two years in postdoctoral study at Leipzig and Berlin.
Education_Locations: Burlington, Unknown, United States, Unknown, Unknown; Middletown, Connecticut, United States, Unknown, 1865; New Haven, Connecticut, United States, 1865, 1869; Leipzig, Unknown, Germany, 1869, 1871; Berlin, Unknown, Germany, 1871, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines: Chemistry; Agricultural Chemistry; Physiology; Nutrition; Metabolism
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in agricultural chemistry and the application of chemistry to agriculture, particularly fertilizer investigation and nitrogen fixation by legumes. Developed calorimetric techniques for studying human metabolism and nutrition, establishing dietary standards for the working class. His work on caloric values and nutritional science became influential in public health policy.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of chemistry at Wesleyan College from 1873 until his death. Director of Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station (1875–1877). Chief of the Office of Experiment Stations within the U.S. Department of Agriculture (1887–1889), continuing academic duties at Wesleyan. Directed the House Committee on Agriculture's nutrition research program from 1894 until his death.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed chief of the Office of Experiment Stations by the federal government following the Hatch Act of 1887. Secured support from the House Committee on Agriculture for nutrition research beginning in 1894.
Instruments_Notes: Designed and constructed the Atwater-Rosa calorimeter in collaboration with physicist E. B. Rosa at Wesleyan, beginning in 1892 and operational by 1897. The instrument was used to measure human metabolism and establish nutritional standards; its techniques were adopted by other American metabolic researchers including Graham Lusk, Francis Benedict, and H. P. Armsby.

Means_of_Support_Notes: Fellow and tutor at Trinity College, Cambridge; appointed to the Treasury in 1784 by William Pitt at £500 per annum to conduct financial calculations and revenue analysis.

Father_Notes: Father was a squire (Jean-François d'Aubuisson de Voisins); mother was Jeanne-Francoise Dassié.

Education_Notes: Entered Benedictine College of Soréze in 1779, winning prizes in infinitesimal calculus, physics, and natural history by 1786. Admitted to Artillery School in Metz in 1786. Attended Werner's courses in mineralogy, geology, and mining at the Bergakademie in Freiberg, 1800–1801, with field trips to Saxon mines.

Means_of_Support_Notes: Hired as secretary by mineralogist Alexandre Brongniart in 1816; assistant to Lamarck and Latreille at the Museum of Natural History (1825); replaced Latreille as assistant naturalist (1830); professor of zoology at the Natural History Museum from 1833.
Patronage_Notes: Patronized by Alexandre Brongniart, who hired him as secretary and influenced his scientific career; later collaborated with Jean-Baptiste Dumas and Adolphe Brongniart, both brothers-in-law.

Education_Notes: Received minimal elementary education at Nantes and Coūeron in France. In 1803 sent to a farm in eastern Pennsylvania. Means_of_Support_Notes: Failed as merchant and miller in Kentucky (1808–1819). Supported himself as itinerant artist and tutor while developing his bird portfolio. Father_Notes: Wealthy innkeeper.
Education_Notes: Studied medicine at the University of Vienna under the influence of Gerard van Swieten, who had reformed the Faculty of Medicine into Europe's leading medical school. Graduated 18 November 1752.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Founder of chest percussion as a diagnostic technique. Developed the method through seven years of systematic observation of tone changes in diseased chests at the Spanish Hospital, verified by corpse dissections and experiments. His Inventum novum (1761) presented the technique of tapping the chest wall to detect lung and heart diseases through changes in percussion tone. The method remained diagnostically valuable even after the development of X-rays.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant physician at the Spanish Hospital from 1751 to 1758 (salaried from 1755); chief physician there from 1758 to 1762. Subsequently a prominent medical practitioner in Vienna.
Patronage_Notes: Empress Maria Theresa ordered the Faculty of Medicine to admit him as a member without fees in 1757. Ennobled by Emperor Joseph II in 1784 for his medical achievements.

Father_Notes: Patricius was a minor official in the Roman province of Numidia.
Education_Notes: Thorough education in the classics of Roman rhetoric and philosophy. Taught rhetoric in Carthage from age twenty-one; later appointed professor of rhetoric in Milan. No formal degree is named.
Education_Locations: Carthage, Unknown, North Africa, Unknown, Unknown; Milan, Unknown, Italy, 383, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Raised Christian by his mother Monica. Initially attracted to Manichaeism but rejected it after realizing its claims were illusory. Underwent dramatic conversion experience centered on the letters of St. Paul and was baptized in 387. Consecrated bishop of Hippo in 395.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Developed a Neoplatonic philosophy grounded in Christian doctrine, emphasizing divine illumination as the basis of human knowledge. Critiqued astrology and addressed cosmological origins in De Genesi ad litteram. His theory of knowledge and metaphysics profoundly shaped medieval and early modern approaches to natural science.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Teacher of rhetoric in Carthage and Milan before his conversion. After baptism and return to Africa, became bishop of Hippo in 395, combining pastoral duties with an enormous writing career of nearly one hundred books and countless treatises.
Patronage_Notes: Influenced by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, whose teaching led Augustine to reconsider Christian Scripture and reject Manichaeism.

Education_Notes: Graduated from Middlebury College in 1889; received doctorate from University of Strasbourg in 1893.
Education_Locations: Middlebury, Vermont, United States, Unknown, 1889; Strasbourg, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1893
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted extensive research on radio transmission, atmospheric disturbances, and signal propagation. Developed the Austin-Cohen formula for predicting radio signal strength at remote locations. Contributed to understanding of radio static and sources of atmospheric disturbances.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Physics faculty at University of Wisconsin from 1893 to 1901; entered U.S. Bureau of Standards in 1904 and remained there until his death, serving as head of the laboratory for special radio transmission research from 1923 onward.
Patronage_Notes: Supported and employed by the U.S. Bureau of Standards and the Naval Research Laboratory; directed radio research programs for the U.S. Navy.
Instruments_Notes: Conducted long-range radio transmission experiments; contributed to design and manufacture of improved radio apparatus; the U.S. Navy began designing and manufacturing its own radio receivers partly in response to difficulties with commercial suppliers, work in which Austin was involved.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Institute of Radio Engineers; International Radio Scientific Union

Served as president of the U.S. national committee of the International Radio Scientific Union (URSI) and was unanimously nominated for URSI presidency shortly before his death.

Father_Notes: Gottfried Daniel Auwers was riding master of Göttingen University.
Education_Notes: Attended gymnasia in Göttingen and Schulpforta from 1847 to 1857. Studied at Göttingen University from 1857, where he began astronomical observations and calculations. No degree is named in the source.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Specialized in precise observation and calculation of stellar positions, proper motions, and parallaxes. Made heliometric observations of double stars and derived orbits for Sirius and Procyon. Conducted meridian observations and established fundamental star catalogs. Participated in Venus transit expeditions and determined the sun's parallax. Contributed to the development of astrophysics.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed astronomer of the Berlin Academy in 1866, where he remained for five decades. Served as permanent secretary of the Academy from 1878 until his death. Elected secretary of the Astronomical Society at its first meeting and served as its president from 1881 to 1889.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed astronomer of the Berlin Academy by the Prussian state. Awarded the Ordre pour le Mérite, grade of chancellor, and elevated to hereditary nobility in 1912.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Astronomical Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected secretary of the Astronomical Society at its founding in 1865 and served as president from 1881 to 1889. Took charge of the secretaryship of the zone commission for the Zonenunternehmen der Astronomischen Gesellschaft.

Means_of_Support_Notes: Director of the chemical institute at the University of Marburg.

Religion_Notes: Withdrew from the Académie des Sciences in 1668 and spent his final years in Rome, suggesting a turn toward religious life, though the entry does not explicitly state his faith.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Designed vacuum experiments to demonstrate air pressure on barometers; made significant contributions to the development of the micrometer and telescopic sights for astronomical observation; criticized mathematical treatises on circle quadrature; worked systematically on precision astronomical instruments from 1660 onward.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Member of the Académie des Sciences until his withdrawal in 1668; supported through institutional affiliation and patronage networks in seventeenth-century French scientific circles.
Instruments_Notes: Perfected the micrometer by replacing Malvasia's lattice of fine wires with two parallel hairs separated by a variable distance, one fixed to a mobile chassis displaced by hand or precision screw; by summer 1666 he and Picard were making systematic observations with fully developed micrometers. Contributed to the systematic development and use of telescopic sights in place of open sights during 1667–1671.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered the chemical analysis of immunological specificity and demonstrated that DNA is the transforming principle in bacterial inheritance. His 1944 work on pneumococcal transformation established DNA as the agent of hereditary change.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked briefly in clinical medicine; joined Hoagland Laboratory as researcher and lecturer in bacteriology and immunology; member of Rockefeller Institute Hospital staff from 1913 to 1948, where he conducted his major research.

Alt_Name: Amedeo Avogadro, Count; Amedeo Carlo Avogadro
Father_Notes: Count Filippo Avogadro was a distinguished lawyer and higher civil servant who became a senator of Piedmont in 1768 and advocate general to the senate of Vittorio Amedeo III in 1777. He reorganized the senate under French rule and served as its president.
Education_Notes: Received early education at home, then attended grammar school in Turin. In 1792 became bachelor of jurisprudence; in 1796 gained doctorate in ecclesiastical law. From 1800 studied mathematics and physics privately.
Education_Locations: Turin, Unknown, Italy, 1792, 1796
Religion_Notes: Described after his death as religious but not a bigot.
Scientific_Disciplines: Physics; Chemistry; Mathematics; Physical Chemistry; Electricity; Thermodynamics
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Principal contributions include Avogadro's hypothesis (1811) distinguishing atoms and molecules and relating gas volumes to molecular numbers; determination of molecular and atomic weights; studies on specific heats of gases and their relation to chemical composition; work on dielectrics and electrical phenomena; investigations of atomic volumes and their relation to electronegativity.
Means_of_Support_Notes: In 1801 appointed secretary to the prefecture of the department of Eridano. In 1806 became demonstrator at the college attached to the Academy of Turin. From 1809 professor of natural philosophy at the College of Vercelli. In 1820 appointed to the first chair of mathematical physics in Italy at Turin with salary of 600 lire; lost this position in 1822 due to political changes but was reappointed in 1834 and held it until retirement in 1850.
Patronage_Notes: Served on government commission on statistics and as president of a commission on weights and measures, where he was largely responsible for introducing the metric system in Piedmont. After 1848 served on a commission on public instruction.
Instruments_Notes: Designed a highly sensitive multiplier voltimeter (1822) that was one of the most sensitive instruments of its time. Used it to discover that certain pairs of metals plunged into concentrated nitric acid momentarily reverse the direction of electric current.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Academy of Sciences of Turin
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected corresponding member of the Academy of Sciences of Turin on 5 July 1804; became full member on 21 November 1819. Notably absent from foreign membership of the Paris Academy of Sciences and the Royal Society of London.

Father_Notes: Konrad Baade was a schoolteacher; his wife Charlotte Wulfhorst was Protestant; they initially planned a theological career for their son.

Education_Notes: Attended Friedrichs-Gymnasium in Herford from 1903 to 1912. Studied at University of Münster briefly, then transferred to Göttingen in Easter term 1913, where he remained throughout World War I. Gained competence in the observatory under Leopold Ambronn and served three years as assistant to mathematician Felix Klein. Passed doctoral examination July 1919 under Johannes Hartmann.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering observational astronomer whose work on stellar populations fundamentally altered understanding of galactic structure and cosmic distance scales. Resolved stars in the Andromeda galaxy nucleus, discovering two distinct stellar populations (Type I and Type II). Identified radio sources with optical counterparts and contributed to early quasar research. Studied globular clusters, variable stars, supernovae, and extragalactic objects.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Scientific assistant at University of Hamburg's Bergedorf Observatory from 1919; promoted to observer in 1927; became Privatdozent at Hamburg in 1928. Joined Mt. Wilson Observatory staff in 1931 and remained there until retirement in 1958. Held Gauss professorship at Göttingen upon return in 1958.
Patronage_Notes: Rockefeller fellowship in 1926 enabled visit to California observatories. Collaborated extensively with leading astronomers including Harlow Shapley, Edwin Hubble, Fritz Zwicky, Rudolf Minkowski, Lyman Spitzer Jr., and others.
Instruments: Schmidt wide-angle telescope; 100-inch telescope; 200-inch Palomar telescope; 74-inch Mt. Stromlo telescope
Instruments_Notes: Designed optical system for Schmidt wide-angle telescopes with Bernard Schmidt. Conducted major observational programs with Mt. Wilson's 100-inch reflector, achieving technically difficult resolution of Andromeda galaxy nucleus. Pioneered use of the 200-inch Palomar telescope for extragalactic research and distance measurements. Used Mt. Stromlo telescope in Australia during retirement.

Father_Notes: Parents were affluent.
Education_Notes: Privately educated as a child. Entered Cambridge University in 1810 and soon surpassed his teachers. Collaborated with George Peacock and John Herschel to reform mathematics teaching and promote Leibniz's differential notation over Newton's.
Education_Locations: Cambridge, Unknown, England, 1810, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; Computer Logic; Computer Technology; Cryptanalysis; Probability; Geophysics; Astronomy; Meteorology; Actuarial Science; Statistical Linguistics; Engineering; Optics
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in mechanized computation and the theory of functions. Devised notation for engineering drawings and wrote influential works on mass production and operational research. Diverse interests included cryptanalysis, geophysics, astronomy, altimetry, ophthalmoscopy, statistical linguistics, meteorology, actuarial science, lighthouse technology, and dendrochronology. Designed the Difference Engine to calculate and print mathematical tables using the method of finite differences, and conceived the Analytical Engine, an early programmable computing machine using Jacquard punched cards.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Elected Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at Cambridge in 1827, a position he held for twelve years but did not actively teach. Received government subsidy for his computing engine projects.
Patronage_Notes: Received government financial support for the Difference Engine project, though subsidies proved insufficient to complete the work.
Instruments_Notes: Designed the Difference Engine to mechanically calculate polynomial functions and print results using the method of finite differences; the unfinished prototype became a museum piece. Conceived the Analytical Engine, a far more sophisticated programmable machine incorporating decision-making logic and capable of performing the four arithmetic operations on numbers up to fifty decimal digits, using punched cards for coding. His son later built a small working analytical mill and printer from his designs.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; Astronomical Society; British Association; Statistical Society of London
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Fellow of the Royal Society from 1816. Helped found the Astronomical Society (1820), the British Association (1831), and the Statistical Society of London (1834). Criticized unprogressive learned societies and advocated for scientific reform.

Father_Notes: Father Pelig Babcock; Stephen managed the family farm after his father's death.
Education_Institution: Tufts College; Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute; Cornell University; University of Göttingen
Education_Notes: Received B.A. from Tufts College in 1866. Began engineering studies at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute but left to manage the family farm. Later took chemistry courses at Cornell University and became an instructor there in 1875. Pursued graduate studies in chemistry at the University of Göttingen under Hans Hübner, receiving the Ph.D. in 1879.
Education_Locations: Medford, Massachusetts, United States, Unknown, 1866; Troy, New York, United States, Unknown, Unknown; Ithaca, New York, United States, 1875, Unknown; Göttingen, Unknown, Germany, 1877, 1879
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in agricultural chemistry. Developed the Babcock test for butterfat in milk (1890), which revolutionized dairy economics. With Harry L. Russell, developed cold curing process for cheese (1900). Conducted cattle-feeding experiments (1907) that confirmed the biological non-equivalency of chemically similar feeds and contributed to the development of the vitamin concept. Also studied metabolic water in insects and investigated the structure of matter and its relation to energy.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Instructor in chemistry at Cornell University (1875–1882). Chief chemist at the New York Agricultural Experiment Station in Geneva (1882–1888). Chief chemist and professor of agricultural chemistry at the Wisconsin Agricultural Experiment Station and University of Wisconsin (1888–1913), retiring as emeritus professor.

Father_Notes: Jean Babinet was mayor of Lusignan; mother was daughter of a lieutenant-general, indicating an aristocratic family background.
Education_Notes: Received a strong literary education from his parents; entered the École Polytechnique in 1812 and graduated from it.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, 1812, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines: Physics; Optics; Meteorology; Astronomy; Geology; Mineralogy
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in wave theory of light and diffraction; formulated Babinet's principle relating diffraction phenomena to transparent and opaque systems. Invented the Babinet compensator for polarized light analysis. Conducted extensive research in meteorological optics, including rainbows, coronas, atmospheric refraction, and polarization of skylight. Also worked in mineralogy and geology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held professorships at Fontenay-le-Comte and Poitiers; became professor of physics at the Collège Louis-le-Grand in Paris in 1820; appointed librarian at the Bureau of Longitudes in 1841.
Instruments_Notes: Constructed a portable goniometer for measuring angles of refraction in minerals, improving upon Malus' design. Invented the Babinet compensator to produce or analyze arbitrarily polarized light.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected member of the physics section of the Académie des Sciences in 1840.

Father_Notes: Father was a physician and keen amateur botanist who influenced his son's devotion to natural history.
Education_Notes: Attended private schools and Charterhouse before entering St. John's College, Cambridge in 1826. Graduated B.A. in 1830 and received M.A. in 1833. Formed an enduring friendship with J.S. Henslow, professor of botany, whose enthusiasm confirmed his lifelong devotion to botany.
Education_Locations: Cambridge, Unknown, England, 1826, 1833
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Leading botanist specializing in British flora and plant taxonomy. Published Flora Bathoniensis (1834), Primitiae florae Sarnicae (1839), and his magnum opus Manual of British Botany (1843), the first complete guide to British plants arranged according to a natural system. Advocated for critical delimitation of species, demonstrated in British Rubi (1869). Made significant additions to the Cambridge Herbarium during his professorship.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Elected to the chair of botany at Cambridge in 1861 following Henslow's death, which he held until his death in 1895.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Ray Club; Ray Society; Entomological Society; Cambridge Antiquarian Society; Linnean Society; Royal Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Leading member of the Ray Club, which developed into the Ray Society (founded 1844); helped produce its publications including Memorials of John Ray and Correspondence of John Ray. Founding member of the Entomological Society in Cambridge and the Cambridge Antiquarian Society. Elected fellow of the Linnean Society in 1830 and was its senior fellow at his death. Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1851.

Education_Notes: Apprenticed to a medical practitioner in Londonderry; trained in medicine at Guy's Hospital, London; awarded M.D. by Aberdeen University in 1795; qualified as licentiate of the College of Physicians, London in 1796.
Education_Locations: London, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; Aberdeen, Unknown, Scotland, 1795, 1795
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Developed a systematic classification of minerals based on chemical composition with crystal form as secondary criterion, advancing beyond the Wernerian system. Published Systematic Arrangement of Minerals (1795) and New System of Mineralogy (1799). Active in promoting mineralogical and geological science through the Geological Society of London.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant surgeon at Haslar Naval Hospital (1777); apothecary, assistant physician, and full physician at Guy's Hospital (1781–1811), where he also lectured on chemistry; established successful private medical practice from 1796 onward and resigned from Guy's Hospital in 1811 to focus on it.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; British Mineralogical Society; Geological Society of London
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1805. Member of the British Mineralogical Society, founded 1799. Founding member of the Geological Society of London (13 November 1807); served as president 1822–1824.

Education_Notes: Studied in Rome; graduated surgeon in 1852 and physician in 1853 from the Roman School of Medicine.
Education_Locations: Rome, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, 1853
Scientific_Disciplines: Medicine; Clinical Medicine; Cardiology; Hematology; Therapeutics
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Director of the Medical Clinic of Rome from 1863 until his death. Studied heart and pleural diseases (1863–1877); illustrated Gaucher's disease (1876); studied malarial infection and its effects on erythrocytes (1866–1894). Pioneer of oxygen therapy (1870) and intravenous drug injection; first injected quinine chlorhydrate intravenously in 1890 to treat pernicious malaria; announced positive results from intravenous strophantine for heart failure (1906). Founded the medical weekly II policlinico (1893) with Francesco Durante and the Policlinico Umberto I medical center (opened 1906).
Means_of_Support_Notes: Director of the Medical Clinic of Rome from 1863 to 1916; practiced as a physician; served as Minister of Public Education (1881, 1893, 1898) and Minister of Agriculture, Commerce, and Industry (1901).
Patronage_Notes: Held ministerial posts under the Italian state; loyal to the house of Savoy.

Father_Notes: Technician in a distillery; stimulated his son's interest in science.
Education_Notes: Attended gymnasium in Kiev (1867–1875). Enrolled in the natural science section of the Department of Physics and Mathematics at Kiev University in 1875, specializing in chemistry. Expelled in 1878 for political activities; resumed studies in 1882. No formal degree is recorded.
Education_Locations: Kiev, Unknown, Russia, 1867, 1875; Kiev, Unknown, Russia, 1875, 1878; Kiev, Unknown, Russia, 1882, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of oxidation theory and biological oxidation. Developed the peroxide theory of slow oxidation (Bach-Engler theory) and extended it to biological oxidation. Conducted fundamental investigations of carbon assimilation by plants, enzymatic mechanisms, and industrial biochemistry. Contributed to enzymology and technical biochemistry.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked in Paul Schützenberger's laboratory at the Collège de France (1890–1894). Conducted independent research in Geneva (1894–1917). After 1918 directed the chemical laboratory of the chemical industry section of the Higher Soviet National Economy, which became the L.Y. Karpov Institute of Physics and Chemistry (1922). Director of the Institute of Biochemistry within the Academy of Sciences from 1935.
Patronage_Notes: Invited by Paul Schützenberger to work at the Collège de France (1890). Appointed director of the Karpov Institute on the recommendation of Lev Yakovlevich Karpov. Supported by the Soviet government after 1917; elected member of the Central Executive Committee of the U.S.S.R. (1927) and the Academy of Sciences (1929).

Elected honorary member of the Imperial Society of the Chemical Industry (London) and the American Chemical Society in 1943. Permanent president of the Dmitrii Ivanovich Mendeleev All-Union Chemical Society from 1932 until his death.

Father_Notes: Great-grandson of Benjamin Franklin; related to leading Philadelphia families.
Education_Notes: Graduated from West Point at the head of his class in 1825. Studied primary and secondary education in Europe during a two-year sojourn (1836–1838).
Education_Locations: West Point, New York, United States, Unknown, 1825
Scientific_Disciplines: Physics; Magnetism; Astronomy; Chemistry; Meteorology; Geology; Seismology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Early work in chemical analysis and heat radiation/absorption; experimented with electromagnetism and astronomy with limited success. Principal focus shifted to terrestrial magnetism and meteorology, particularly magnetic declination and inclination observations. Directed extensive tidal observations and studied earthquake-generated waves. Oversaw astronomical research including solar eclipse observations.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served in the Corps of Engineers for two years after West Point (1825–1827). Professor of natural philosophy and chemistry at University of Pennsylvania (1827–1836). Organized and directed Girard College (1836 onward). Head of the U.S. Coast Survey (1843–1867), the largest employer of physical scientists in the United States during his tenure. Also succeeded Hassler as head of the Office of Weights and Measures.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed head of the Coast Survey by the federal government in 1843. Served on the informal Commission on Conference planning the naval campaign during the Civil War (1861). Vice-president of the U.S. Sanitary Commission. Member of the Permanent Commission (1863–1864) advising the navy on technical matters.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: American Philosophical Society; Franklin Institute; American Association for the Advancement of Science; National Academy of Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Assumed leading roles in the American Philosophical Society and Franklin Institute during his Philadelphia period. First president of the National Academy of Sciences, founded in 1863.

Education_Notes: Taught physics and chemistry at the collège in Bar-sur-Aube before becoming a philosopher. No formal degree is named in the source.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered the epistemology of modern science, examining the rupture between classical and contemporary physics. Analyzed the mathematical foundations of thermodynamics, heat theory, and relativity. Developed a psychoanalytic approach to the history of scientific thought, studying mental obstacles to scientific progress. Explored the poetics of imagination and elemental symbolism in prescientific thought.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught physics and chemistry at the collège of Bar-sur-Aube; later became a philosopher and academic, publishing extensively on epistemology and the philosophy of science.

Education_Notes: Obtained the bachelor of sciences degree in 1898 and defended his doctoral dissertation on the theory of speculation two years later (1900).
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in probability theory and stochastic processes. Introduced continuity into probability problems through his theory of speculation, treating time as a variable and examining chains of probabilities. Applied probabilistic methods to market fluctuations and light propagation. First to examine stochastic methods of Markovian type, foundational to Kolmogorov's later theory. Work anticipated Einstein-Wiener theory of Brownian motion, though lacked clarity and precision that limited its immediate influence.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Named lecturer at Besançon in 1919; taught at Dijon and Rennes; professor at Besançon from 1927 to 1937, when he retired.

Father_Notes: Jean Bachet, appeals judge of Bresse and counselor to the duke of Savoy; family was ancient and noble, with grandfather Pierre Bachet a counselor to King Henry II.
Education_Notes: Early education in a Jesuit house in the duchy of Savoy. Presumably studied in Padua as a young man; may have taught in a Jesuit school in Milan or Como. Spent time in Paris and Rome.
Education_Locations: Unknown, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; Padua, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Educated by Jesuits; composed sacred Latin poetry and translations of psalms.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in mathematical recreations and number theory. Edited and translated Diophantus's Arithmetica with extensive Latin commentary, establishing the Greek text for European scholarship. Contributed to Diophantine analysis, including a generalization of ax + b = u², cx + d = w². Authored Problems plaisans et delectables, a foundational collection of arithmetical problems including magic squares, weighing problems, and river-crossing puzzles.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Member of the Académie Française from 1635. Supported by his noble family; may have taught in Jesuit schools.
Patronage_Notes: From an ancient noble family; grandfather and father held positions at court and in ducal service.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie Française
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Académie Française in 1635, though too ill with rheumatism and gout to attend the inaugural ceremony in 1634.

Means_of_Support_Notes: Extraordinary professor in Breslau after completing his habilitation in 1864; appointed to a professorship in Münster; resigned around 1890.

Doctoral dissertation on Preston's rule accepted February 1913, published 1921.

Designed innovative vacuum arc light sources with elaborate electrode mechanisms. Collaborated on hyperfine structure analysis and nuclear angular momentum determination. Work contributed to understanding of atomic structure and nuclear properties.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant to Paschen at Tübingen until 1914. Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Devoted his career to the study of Encke's comet, demonstrating that its long-term acceleration is subject to irregular changes attributable to nongravitational forces. Recalculated all planetary perturbations affecting the comet from 1819 to 1891. Investigated possible explanations including interplanetary medium, meteoroid streams, electrical forces, and mass loss.

Father_Notes: Sir Nicholas Bacon, lord keeper of the great seal; mother was Ann, daughter of Sir Anthony Cooke.
Education_Notes: Attended Trinity College, Cambridge from 1573 to 1575; entered Gray's Inn and became a barrister in 1582. No university degree is recorded.
Education_Locations: Cambridge, Unknown, England, 1573, 1575
Religion_Notes: Adhered to the middle road of the Church of England, neither authoritarian nor sectarian.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Bacon's principal contributions were in philosophy of scientific method, natural philosophy, and the organization of science. He rejected atomism and Copernican astronomy, criticized mathematical approaches to natural philosophy, and developed an inductive method for discovering the forms of simple natures. His work on heat as motion exemplifies his approach to reducing secondary qualities to primary bodies and their motions.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced as a barrister from 1582; held government positions including lord chancellor (1618–1621); devoted his later years to natural philosophy after his dismissal and retirement near St. Albans.
Patronage_Notes: Knighted on the accession of James I; made viscount St. Albans in 1621. Sought Crown support throughout his life for the organization of science, described in letters to Cecil (1592) and advertised in The Advancement of Learning (1605).
Instruments_Notes: Commended the telescope and other instruments as aids to the senses for bringing hidden and subtle processes within reach of observation.

Father_Notes: Family impoverished as a result of support for Henry III against the baronial party; unable to respond to Bacon's appeal for funds in 1266.
Education_Notes: Early instruction in Latin classics, particularly Seneca and Cicero. Acquired interest in natural philosophy and mathematics at Oxford. Took M.A. either at Oxford or Paris, probably around 1240. Lectured in the Faculty of Arts at Paris between 1241 and 1246 on Aristotelian works including Physics, Metaphysics, and pseudo-Aristotelian texts.
Education_Locations: Oxford, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, 1241, 1246
Religion_Notes: Entered the Franciscan order around 1257. Condemned and imprisoned by his order between 1277 and 1279, possibly related to heretical Averroist propositions condemned by the bishop of Paris, Stephen Tempier, in 1277.
Scientific_Disciplines: Natural Philosophy; Optics; Mathematics; Astronomy; Astrology; Alchemy; Philosophy; Calendar Reform; Geography
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Devoted his life to promotion of languages, mathematics, optics (perspectiva), and experimental science as essential sciences. Made original contributions to physiological optics through exposition of Ibn al-Haytham's account of the eye as image-forming device, providing eight rules for convex and concave spherical surfaces. Advocated for experimental science as means to certify deductive reasoning, discover new knowledge, and investigate nature's secrets. Wrote extensively on calendar reform, proposing removal of one day in 125 years. Discussed astrology as having speculative and practical parts, arguing it could illuminate celestial influences on terrestrial events without subjugating human will.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Lectured in the Faculty of Arts at Paris. Supported by papal patronage after Cardinal Guy de Foulques (later Pope Clement IV) requested his philosophical writings in 1265 and issued a papal mandate in 1266. Spent over two thousand pounds on secret books, experiments, languages, instruments, and tables.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by Cardinal Guy de Foulques, who became Pope Clement IV in February 1265. The pope requested Bacon's philosophical writings and issued a papal mandate on 22 June 1266. Bacon composed his three major works (Opus maius, Opus minus, Opus tertium) in response and sent them to the pope by his pupil John before the pope's death in November 1268.
Instruments_Notes: Discussed use of lenses for magnification to aid natural vision and for burning. Provided constructions based on Ptolemy and Ibn al-Haytham for convex refracting surfaces. Conducted experiments with lodestone held above and below a floating magnet to investigate magnetic orientation. Discussed spherical astrolabe as an instrument to be driven at constant rate, confirming efforts toward mechanical clock development.

Education_Notes: Attended cathedral school for nobility in Reval (1807–1810); studied medicine at University of Dorpat (1810–1814); continued studies in Berlin and Vienna (1814–1815, 1816–1817); studied comparative anatomy under Ignaz Döllinger at Würzburg (1815–1816).

Means_of_Support_Notes: Prosector in anatomy at Königsberg (1817); extraordinary professor of anatomy (1819); ordinary professor of zoology (1826); full member of Academy of Sciences in St. Petersburg (1834); academician for comparative anatomy and physiology (1846); ordinary professor at Medico-Chirurgical Academy in St. Petersburg (1846–1852); retired from active membership (1862) but continued as honorary member until 1867.
Patronage_Notes: Instructed the two daughters of Grand Duchess Helen Pavlovna (wife of Grand Duke Michael Pavlovitch) in natural history and enjoyed her friendship and patronage for many years beginning in 1839–1840.

Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected corresponding member of Academy of Sciences in St. Petersburg (1826); full member in zoology (1834); member of Royal Society of London and Paris Academy; founded and served as first president of Russian Entomological Society (1860).

Alt_Name: Adolf Johann Friedrich Wilhelm von Baeyer; Adolf von Baeyer
Father_Notes: Lieutenant general in the Prussian army; participated in government projects to measure degrees of latitude and longitude and in a general European measurement program on the shape of the earth.

Education_Notes: Early education at Friedrich-Wilhelms Gymnasium and University of Berlin under P.G. Dirichlet and G. Magnus, emphasizing mathematics and physics. After military service in 1856, studied experimental chemistry with R. Bunsen at Heidelberg, then entered Kekulé's private laboratory in Heidelberg in 1858. Followed Kekulé to Ghent and remained until 1860. Received doctoral degree from Berlin in 1858 for work on arsenic methyl chloride.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in structural organic chemistry and synthetic dyes. Means_of_Support_Notes: Held various teaching positions at the technical institute and military academy in Berlin after 1860. Appointed ordinary professor of chemistry at the imperial university at Strasbourg in 1872. Moved to Munich in 1875 as successor to Justus von Liebig. Instrumental in setting up a chemical laboratory at Munich in 1877.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed to imperial university positions at Strasbourg (1872) and Munich (1875) by the German state.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Berlin Academy of Sciences; German Chemical Association
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Member of multiple scientific societies; received Liebig Medal of the Berlin Chemists Congress and the Royal Society's Davy Medal; awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1905 for work on dyes and hydroaromatic compounds.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in experimental physiology and microscopic anatomy. Conducted vivisections on dogs, frogs, and other animals to study nerve function, circulation, and organ structure. Distinguished smooth from striated muscle fibers and identified two categories of muscle fibers (fibrae motrices and fibrae membranaceae). Studied the microscopic structure of muscles, brain membranes, and the physical properties of saliva, bile, and blood. Advocated for clinical observation over medical systems and theories.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced medicine in hospitals throughout Italy (Padua, Venice, Florence, Bologna, and others). Served as assistant to Marcello Malpighi in Bologna (1691–1694) and as scientific secretary in Rome (1692–1694). Appointed pope's second physician in 1695 and professor of anatomy at the Sapienza in Rome in 1696; promoted to professor of theoretical medicine at the Sapienza in 1701.
Patronage_Notes: Patronized by Marcello Malpighi, who invited him to Rome as scientific secretary and collaborator. Introduced to the papal court and became physician to Pope Innocent XII (1695) and later to Pope Clement XI (1701). Associated with influential scientists including Lancisi, Bellini, Redi, Tozzi, and Trionfetti.
Instruments_Notes: Used microscopic observation to perfect anatomical research and study the fine structure of muscles and brain membranes.

Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Royal Society in 1697, Academia Naturae Curiosorum and Arcadia in 1699, and Accademia dei Fisiocritici in 1700.

Father_Notes: Johann Wilhelm Baier was a professor of Protestant theology at the University of Jena.

Made an educational trip to mining facilities in the Hartz Mountains and northern German university towns before settling in Nuremberg.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Practiced medicine in Nuremberg and served as director of a field hospital during the War of the Spanish Succession. His lasting scientific reputation rests on his studies of minerals and fossils, particularly his systematic work Oryctographia norica (1708), which presented exact descriptions and illustrations of Jurassic fauna and laid foundations for scientific paleontology. He rejected the notion that fossils were sports of nature and believed the earth was created in one act with the Deluge as the only major subsequent change.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced as a physician in Nuremberg from 1701. Appointed professor at the medical faculty of the University of Altdorf in 1704, a position he held until his death. Elected rector of the University twice, in 1708.

Father_Notes: John Batters By Bailey was a medical practitioner.
Education_Institution: Kendal Grammar School; Clare College, Cambridge
Education_Notes: Graduated with First-class Honors in geology and physics from Clare College, Cambridge in 1902.
Education_Locations: Kendal, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; Cambridge, Unknown, England, Unknown, 1902
Religion_Notes: The entry states he was an atheist in religious matters.
Scientific_Disciplines: Geology; Tectonics; Metamorphism; Igneous Geology; Stratigraphy
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Made notable contributions to tectonics and metamorphism, igneous and general geology, and the history of geological ideas. Revolutionary tectonic reinterpretation of Dalradian schists in the Scottish Highlands using recumbent folds and fold faults. Major work on Tertiary volcanic complexes, particularly Mull. Pioneered understanding of submarine landslips and their role in sedimentation.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Geologist and district geologist with the Geological Survey of Great Britain (Scotland) from graduation until 1929; professor of geology at Glasgow University 1929–1937; director of the Geological Survey and Museum 1937–1945.
Patronage_Notes: Served as director of the Geological Survey and Museum, a government scientific post.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected Fellow of the Royal Society. Received six honorary doctorates and seven scientific medals. Knighted in 1945.

Father_Notes: Father was Liberty Hyde Bailey (senior), who had migrated from Townshend, Vermont. Mother Sarah Harrison Bailey came of a distinguished Virginia family.
Education_Institution: Michigan State Agricultural College; Harvard University
Education_Notes: Entered Michigan State Agricultural College at nineteen; trained in compound microscopy and experimental botany under William James Beal. Received B.S. in 1882 and M.S. from Michigan State. Also worked as assistant curator at Harvard herbarium under Asa Gray, 1882–1883.
Education_Locations: Lansing, Michigan, United States, Unknown, 1882; Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States, 1882, 1883
Scientific_Disciplines: Botany; Horticulture; Agriculture; Plant Taxonomy; Plant Breeding
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Recognized authority on Carex, Rubus, Cucurbita, palms, Vitis, and cultivated Brassica. Major contributions to plant nomenclature, classification, hybridization, and cross-fertilization. Authored over sixty books on horticulture, agriculture, plant breeding, and evolution, including influential encyclopedias and the Hortus. Founded and edited Baileya and Gentes herbarum journals.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of horticulture and landscape gardening at Michigan State Agricultural College from 1885; chair of practical and experimental horticulture at Cornell University from 1888; second director of Cornell's College of Agriculture from 1903; first dean of New York State College of Agriculture and director of its experiment station from 1904. Prolific author of hundreds of papers and over sixty books.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed chairman of President Theodore Roosevelt's Country Life Commission in 1908, which investigated rural improvement possibilities until 1911.

Member of multiple national academies.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Primarily a geologist specializing in the stratigraphy and chronostratigraphy of New Brunswick. With Matthew and Hartt, discovered Cambrian-age fossils in New Brunswick. Later focused on microscopic investigation of diatoms, increasing known New Brunswick species from fifty to about four hundred and producing a catalog of Canadian diatoms.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held the chair of chemistry and natural science at the University of New Brunswick from 1861 until his retirement in 1907.
Instruments_Notes: Used microscopy extensively in his diatom research, which formed the basis of his later scientific work.

Scientific_Societies_Notes: Charter member of the Royal Society of Canada; served as president of the geology section in 1888 and 1918.

Education_Notes: Graduated from Boston University with an A.M. degree in 1884; earned a second M.A. degree from Harvard in 1888. Received an honorary Sc.D. from the University of San Agustin in 1923.
Education_Locations: Boston, Massachusetts, United States, Unknown, 1884; Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States, Unknown, 1888
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered southern-hemisphere observations for Harvard Observatory. Made fundamental contributions through studies of variable stars in globular clusters and long-exposure photography that revealed the structure of the Milky Way and detected over 3,000 extragalactic objects. Established meteorological stations in Peru and published comprehensive data on Peruvian meteorology over thirty-seven years.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Forty-four-year career with Harvard Observatory beginning in 1884; served as acting director from 1919 to 1921.
Patronage_Notes: Sent to South America by E. C. Pickering, director of Harvard Observatory, to locate a suitable site for the southern observing post. Work was sponsored and directed by the Observatory.
Instruments_Notes: Used the visual photometer from the original Harvard Photometry project to extend stellar magnitude coverage to the southern sky. Worked with the 24-inch Bruce doublet telescope at the Boyden station in Arequipa, Peru, which he helped establish.

Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the National Academy of Sciences in Washington.

Father_Notes: Presbyterian minister at Shots; later professor of divinity at Glasgow University.
Education_Institution: Hamilton Grammar School; Glasgow University; Balliol College, Oxford
Education_Notes: Attended Hamilton Grammar School and Glasgow University. Studied at Balliol College, Oxford for one year. Won a scholarship to Oxford. Stayed in London with uncle William Hunter at the Windmill Street School of Anatomy before moving to Oxford. Received M.D. from Oxford in 1789.
Education_Locations: Shots Manse, Lanarkshire, Scotland, Unknown, Unknown; Glasgow, Unknown, Scotland, Unknown, Unknown; Oxford, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of systematic pathology. Published the first English text on pathology and the first systematic study in any language, Morbid Anatomy of Some of the Most Important Parts of the Human Body (1795). Serially examined organs and their morbid conditions, basing descriptions on firsthand observations and specimens from his uncles' medical museum. Work focused on thoracic and abdominal organs and the brain. By 1800 had the largest medical practice in London.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Master of the Windmill Street School of Anatomy from 1783 following his uncle's death. Elected physician to St. George's Hospital in 1787, a position held for thirteen years. Developed the largest medical practice in London by 1800.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; Royal College of Physicians
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal College of Physicians and the Royal Society soon after receiving his M.D. in 1789.

Father_Notes: Father was a mathematician and noted architect.
Education_Notes: Became a physician in 1570; no formal degree is named in the source.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Revived Hippocratic clinical observation and macrocosmic concepts of illness. Pioneered epidemiology in the West since Hippocrates, developing the concept of ephemerides during Paris epidemics (1570–1579). Provided early descriptions of plague, measles, diphtheria, adhesive pericarditis, and whooping cough. Brought rheumatism into nosology and systematized its varied presentations. Incorporated astrology into medical practice, believing solar eclipses and stellar positions influenced medical outcomes.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Became a physician in 1570 and served as dean of the Faculty of Medicine in Paris from 1580. Practiced medicine and taught at the Faculty.

Father_Notes: Jacques Bailly, keeper of the king's paintings at the Louvre, a position held by the family since Bailly's great-grandfather. The family owned a house in the fashionable suburb of Chaillot.
Education_Notes: Received schooling to prepare him for his father's office. Around age twenty, received mathematics lessons from Montcarville of the Collège Royal. Subsequently studied with Nicolas de Lacaille and Alexis Clairaut, France's greatest observational and theoretical astronomers respectively.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Undertook first astronomical research in 1759 on Halley's comet. Established his own observatory in the Louvre in 1760 and conducted extensive observational and theoretical work on Jupiter's satellites. Produced a major essay on satellite theory (1766) and an important memoir on the light and diameters of Jupiter's satellites (1771). Published a four-volume history of astronomy (1775–1782), his most lasting achievement.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Succeeded to his father's position as keeper of the king's paintings in 1768, relieved of functions in 1783 but continued to receive the pension and honorary title. Elected to the Académie des Sciences in 1763 and remained active there; elected to the Académie Française in 1783 and the Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres in 1785, becoming a triple academician.
Patronage_Notes: Held the hereditary position of keeper of the king's paintings at the Louvre, a court appointment. Supported by the Académie des Sciences through membership and recognition of his work.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences; Académie Française; Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres

Elected to the Académie Française in 1783 and to the Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres in 1785, making him only the second Frenchman (after Fontenelle) to be a triple academician.

Father_Notes: A banker; Baily was the third son.
Education_Notes: Received only elementary education. Apprenticed to a London mercantile firm at age fourteen for seven years.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in practical astronomy and standardization. Calculated mean positions of 2,881 stars (1826); worked on standard pendulum, standard yard, and earth's ellipticity; redetermined earth's density (1843). Discovered and vividly described Baily's beads phenomenon during solar eclipses. Revised and published numerous historical star catalogs.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked as a stockbroker and prospered on the stock exchange before retiring at age fifty to devote full time to astronomy. Served as president of the Astronomical Society of London for four two-year terms beginning in 1825.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; Astronomical Society of London
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Fellow of the Royal Society from 1821. One of the founders of the Astronomical Society of London (later the Royal Astronomical Society); served as president for four two-year terms, the first beginning in 1825 and the last interrupted by his death. Awarded the Gold Medal twice: 1826 for star catalog work and 1843 for earth density redetermination.

Father_Notes: George Bain was a handloom weaver; poverty forced him to remove Alexander from school at age eleven.
Education_Notes: Largely self-taught in Latin, Greek, mathematics, and mechanics during seven years of manual labor; won a bursary in 1836 to Marischal College, where he excelled and received his M.A. in 1840, adjudged the best candidate of the year.
Education_Locations: Aberdeen, Unknown, Scotland, 1836, 1840
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in philosophical psychology, emphasizing the unity and active nature of the mind; correlated mental processes with physiological processes via the nervous system; rejected faculty psychology and the mind-body dualism; followed utilitarian ethics and logic of John Stuart Mill; founded and edited the journal Mind (1876–1892).
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught mental and moral philosophy at Marischal College for five years after 1840; held various short-term lectureships for fifteen years; elected to the chair of logic at Aberdeen University in 1860 and remained until retirement in 1880; served as rector 1882–1886.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Aberdeen Philosophical Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Read papers to the Aberdeen Philosophical Society on classification of sciences, human senses, and terrestrial heat (1843–1844).

Father_Notes: Samuel Baird was a lawyer of local prominence in Reading, Pennsylvania; died in 1833.
Education_Notes: Entered Dickinson College in 1836, received B.A. in 1840 and M.A. in 1843. Briefly studied medicine in New York City in late 1841 but abandoned it after two months. Received informal instruction from established naturalists including James Dwight Dana, John James Audubon, and George N. Lawrence.

Scientific_Disciplines: Zoology; Ornithology; Mammalogy; Ichthyology; Herpetology; Natural History; Scientific Administration
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Leading vertebrate zoologist of mid-nineteenth-century America. Conducted taxonomic studies of birds, mammals, reptiles, amphibians, and fishes, often in collaboration with Charles Girard. Described seventy mammal species and 216 bird species new to science. Major works include Mammals (1857) and Birds (1858), comprehensive monographs that reset nomenclature and classification; 'The Distribution and Migrations of North American Birds' (1865), notable for defining biological zones and supporting organic evolution; and A History of North American Birds (1874), a three-volume study of land birds. Also directed the U.S. Fish Commission and served as secretary of the Smithsonian Institution.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of natural history at Dickinson College from 1846. Assistant to Joseph Henry at the Smithsonian Institution from 1850; became secretary of the Smithsonian in 1878. Directed the U.S. Fish Commission from 1871 until his death.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed assistant to Joseph Henry at the Smithsonian in 1850 through recommendations from politicians and scientists. Directed the U.S. Fish Commission, established by Congress in 1871.

Father_Notes: One of three children in a modest artisan family; parents made sacrifices to fund his education.

Education_Notes: Won a scholarship competition for Paris in 1886 and entered Lycée Lakanal as a boarding student, completing advanced classes in 1890 with two honorable mentions in the Concours Général de Mathématiques. Entered special mathematics section at Lycée Henri IV in 1891. Accepted to both École Polytechnique and École Normale Supérieure in 1892; chose the latter and studied there for three years. Placed first in written part of 1895 agrégation in mathematics but ranked third overall due to oral examination performance. Defended doctoral thesis on theory of functions of real variables on 24 March 1899 before Appell, Darboux, and Picard.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering work on theory of functions of real variables, particularly limit functions of continuous functions (Baire classes), semicontinuity, and discontinuous functions. Work on partial differential equations and functions of several variables. Later devoted attention to calendar reform.

Alt_Name: Avempace; Avenpace; Ibn Yaḥyā Ibn Al-ṣa'igh
Education_Notes: Self-educated in the philosophical sciences. Studied music, then astronomy, then Aristotle's Physics. No formal institutional education is recorded.

Scientific_Disciplines: Philosophy; Natural Philosophy; Physics; Astronomy; Medicine
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Established systematic study of philosophical sciences in Muslim Spain, modeling his method on al-Fārābī. Major contributions to Aristotelian physics, including dynamics, motion of projectiles, descent on inclined planes, and critique of Ptolemaic astronomy. Rejected epicycles as incompatible with Aristotelian physics. Wrote commentaries on Aristotle's Organon, Physics, De generatione et corruptione, Meteorologica, and Book of Animals. Also practiced medicine.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as vizier to an Almoravid prince. Engaged in philosophical teaching and writing, establishing systematic philosophical curriculum in Spain.
Patronage_Notes: Served as vizier to an Almoravid prince.

Father_Notes: William Baker was a Clerk in Chancery; mother Mary Pengry was a midwife of considerable practice.
Education_Notes: Apprenticed to a bookseller at age fifteen; no formal institutional education is recorded.
Religion_Notes: The entry notes his pious approach to nature and reverence for the microscope as a means to appreciate God's creation, but does not state a specific religious affiliation.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered the popularization and teaching of microscopy through two widely translated books. Conducted microscopical examinations of water creatures, fossils, and crystal morphology. Studied the freshwater polyp (Hydra viridis) with Martin Folkes. Examined and measured Antony van Leeuwenhoek's bead microscopes.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Amassed considerable fortune as a teacher of the deaf and dumb; later became honorary secretary of the Society for the Encouragement of Arts Manufactures and Commerce in 1754.
Instruments_Notes: Designed and improved microscope techniques and instruments; authored two influential books on microscope construction, adjustment, and use. Examined and documented Leeuwenhoek's bead microscopes.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Society of Antiquaries; Royal Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Fellow of the Society of Antiquaries from January 1740; fellow of the Royal Society from March 1741. Frequent contributor to Philosophical Transactions for seventeen years. Awarded the Copley Medal in 1744 for experiments on crystallization of saline bodies. Established the Bakerian Lecture through a bequest of £100 to the Royal Society.

Father_Notes: Father John Baker; family moved from Guisborough to Thirsk in 1834.
Education_Notes: Attended Friends' School at Ackworth; transferred at age twelve to Friends' School at Bootham, York, known for natural history study. Formal education ended in 1847.
Education_Locations: Ackworth, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; Bootham, York, Unknown, England, Unknown, 1846
Religion_Notes: Quaker; attended Quaker schools.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Expert on vascular cryptogams and ferns; monographic work on British roses and other plant families; substantial contributions to regional floras; pioneer investigator in plant ecology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked in drapery business in Thirsk for eighteen years (1847–1865); lectured on botany at London Hospital Medical School (1869–1881) and Chelsea Physic Garden (1882–1899); appointed first assistant in Kew Herbarium in 1866 and keeper of herbarium and library at Kew (1890–1899).
Patronage_Notes: Invited by J. D. Hooker, director of Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, to join the herbarium staff in 1866.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; Royal Horticultural Society; Linnean Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected Fellow of the Royal Society in 1878; received Victoria Medal of Honour from Royal Horticultural Society in 1897; received Linnean Medal in 1899.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Mineralogical surveyor and geology teacher. Authored the widely read Introduction to Geology (1813), which presented geological concepts to general readers through English countryside examples. Engaged with contemporary geological theories, particularly Hutton's plutonic ideas and Cuvier's catastrophism, while rejecting Wernerian geognosy and neptunism. Published articles on geological and biological subjects in the Philosophical Magazine and elsewhere.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked as a mineralogical surveyor and taught mineralogy and geology, primarily in London. Supported himself through teaching and surveying work.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Published one article through the Geological Society of London but was never admitted as a member.

Authored major geographical works including a collection of place names and a comprehensive description of routes and kingdoms across the Mediterranean, North Africa, and Europe. Also wrote on pharmacology and simple medicines.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Member of al-Muʿtasim's court at Almeria for much of his life. Also engaged in scholarly and literary pursuits as a poet and philologist.

Introduced fundamental concepts and equations in chemical kinetics, including the logarithmic dependence in the Arrhenius equation. Applied catalytic theory to petrochemical synthesis and fermentation processes.

Father_Notes: Parents were wine-growers of modest circumstances.
Education_Notes: Attended the lycée in Montpellier; trained in pharmacy from 1819 under Jacques Étienne Bérard at the École de Pharmacie in Montpellier, where he also served as préparateur in chemistry. Received a degree in pharmacy in 1826 with a thesis on cyanogen and its compounds.
Education_Locations: Montpellier, Unknown, France, 1819, 1826
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Experimental chemist with keen awareness of chemical analogies. Discovered the element bromine (ca. 1825); studied iodine in marine organisms; investigated bleaching agents and prepared hypochlorous acid and chlorine monoxide; developed techniques for extracting salts from seawater; discovered oxamic acid and named amyl alcohol. Preferred simple apparatus and homemade reagents.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as préparateur in chemistry at the École de Pharmacie in Montpellier; succeeded Joseph Anglada in 1834; assumed Louis Jacques Thénard's chair at the Sorbonne in 1842 and Théophile Jules Pelouze's chair at the Collège de France in 1851.
Patronage_Notes: Recognized by the Académie des Sciences for the discovery of bromine and awarded a medal by the Royal Society of London; elected to the Académie des Sciences in 1844.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences; Royal Society of London
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Académie des Sciences in 1844; awarded a medal by the Royal Society of London for the discovery of bromine.

Father_Notes: German-born of Italian descent; established a banking firm in Haiti.

Education_Notes: Attended law school briefly in Paris before turning to natural sciences; studied under de Blainville at the Muséum National d'Histoire Naturelle; received licencié ès sciences naturelles in 1845 and doctorate in medicine in 1854.
Education_Locations: Frankfurt am Main, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, 1840, 1845; Paris, Unknown, France, 1845, 1854
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in microscopic research and protozoology; discovered sexual reproduction in ciliata and established laws of binary fission in infusoria; performed microsurgical experiments and introduced merotomy technique; demonstrated that sexual cells derive directly from the egg and precede the individual; studied reproduction of aphids and silkworm disease (pebrine); described cytoplasmic inclusions in ovule yolks (Balbiani vesicle).
Means_of_Support_Notes: Private income from family wealth allowed him to forgo medical practice and pursue research; directed histological research at the Museum laboratory of general physiology from 1867; professor of embryogeny at the Collège de France from 13 February 1874 until his death.
Patronage_Notes: Claude Bernard, who praised him frequently, asked him to direct histological research at the Museum laboratory in 1867.
Instruments_Notes: Pioneered microscopic research techniques and microsurgical experiments; introduced the technique and term merotomy for nuclear manipulation.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Société de Micrographie; Société de Biologie
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Founded the Société de Micrographie; faithful member of the Société de Biologie; secretary of the Journal de physiologie.

Education_Notes: Classical education by private tutors at Urbino; studied mathematics with Guido Ubaldo del Monte under Federico Commandino from about 1570; enrolled at University of Padua in 1573 but returned to Urbino when the university closed due to plague. Studies at Padua centered on philology and literature; no degree obtained.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Principal contribution was a commentary on the pseudo-Aristotelian Questions of Mechanics, emphasizing centers of gravity and equilibrium in spinning tops. Translated Hero of Alexandria's Automata and Belopoieca, and Aratus's Phenomena. Compiled biographies of approximately 200 mathematicians. Worked on an extensive unpublished geography in his later years.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served Ferrante II Gonzaga from 1580; appointed abbot of Guastalla in 1585; from 1609 served the duke of Urbino as historian and biographer until his death.

Father_Notes: James Maitland Balfour; mother was Lady Blanche, daughter of the marquis of Salisbury. Came from an illustrious family; oldest brother was the prominent philosopher and statesman Arthur James Balfour.
Education_Notes: Attended preparatory school at Hoddesdon, Hertfordshire; enrolled at Harrow in 1865, where he wrote a prize-winning essay on the geology and natural history of East Lothian, judged by Thomas H. Huxley. Matriculated at Trinity College, Cambridge in 1870; took a first in Natural Science Scholarships in 1871. Worked under physiologist Michael Foster from 1872.
Education_Locations: Harrow, Unknown, England, 1865, Unknown; Cambridge, Unknown, England, 1870, 1872
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in comparative embryology following Darwin's Origin of Species. Conducted painstaking microscopic examinations of elasmobranch development, producing a monograph of nearly 300 pages. Made detailed studies of germ-layer formation, excretory system development, and the primitive streak of the chick embryo. Published a two-volume Treatise on Comparative Embryology (1880–1881), the first successful complete comparative embryology text. Investigated phylogenetic links between major taxa through studies of elasmobranchs, ganoids, amphioxus, Peripatus, and spiders.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Began lecturing on morphology and embryology at Trinity College, Cambridge in fall 1873; became director of the university's morphological laboratory. In 1882, Cambridge created a professorship of animal morphology for him to hold for life, but he died before taking full office.
Patronage_Notes: Michael Foster directed his early research and urged Cambridge to create the professorship of animal morphology for him in 1882.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Royal Society in 1878; became vice-president of the biological section of the British Association for the Advancement of Science in 1880; won the Royal Society's Royal Medal in 1881.

Father_Notes: John Hutton Balfour was professor of botany at Edinburgh University. Family ancestry included George H. Baird, principal of Edinburgh University, and geologist James Hutton.

Education_Notes: Studied at Edinburgh University, obtaining B.S. in 1873 and M.B. in 1877. Continued botanical studies, particularly morphology and physiology, at universities of Würzburg and Strasbourg. Accompanied transit of Venus expedition to Rodriguez Island in 1874 as botanist and geologist.

Education_Notes: Attended High School Edinburgh; studied at universities of Edinburgh and St. Andrews; graduated M.D. from Edinburgh in 1832; pursued further medical study in Paris before returning to Edinburgh in 1834.

Education_Notes: Entered University of Breslau as medical student in 1875; studied at Heidelberg under Robert Bunsen in 1876; returned to Berlin and worked with Carl Liebermann and A. W. Hofmann to complete his degree.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Investigated aromatic hydrocarbons and elucidated structures of retene, chrysene, pyrene, and picein. Discovered alicyclic compounds and isodiazo compounds. Extended benzene centric formula to naphthalene. Studied nitrogen compounds, hydrazones, and diazo compounds. Engaged in major controversy with Arthur Hantzsch over diazo compound formulation. Later investigated oxidation and reduction of nitrogen compounds, optical properties of anthranil derivatives, and photochemical properties of benzaldehyde derivatives.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant to Karl Rammelsberg at Technische Hochschule Berlin-Charlottenburg; assistant to Adolf von Baeyer in Munich from 1883; gave inaugural lecture in 1885; extraordinary professor of organic chemistry in Munich from 1891; professor at Eidgenössische Technische Hochschule Zurich from 1893 to 1905; continued private research with assistant after 1905.

Father_Notes: Railway official; Banach was raised by a laundress who became his foster mother.
Education_Notes: Graduated from secondary school in Krakow in 1910. Studied at the Institute of Technology in Lvov but did not graduate. Received doctorate in 1919 with an unusual exemption from complete university education.
Education_Locations: Lvov, Unknown, Poland, 1910, 1914
Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; Functional Analysis; Analysis; Topology; Set Theory
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Founded functional analysis as a comprehensive theory of normed linear spaces (Banach spaces). Made significant contributions to orthogonal series, descriptive set theory, measure and integration theory, and general topology. Proved the Hahn-Banach theorem and the Banach-Steinhaus theorem.
Means_of_Support_Notes: From age fifteen supported himself by private lessons. Appointed lecturer in mathematics at the Institute of Technology in Lvov in 1919; became associate professor and then full professor in 1927. Wrote college and secondary-school texts, including an important mechanics textbook.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Polish Academy of Sciences and Arts; Ukrainian Academy of Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected corresponding member of the Polish Academy of Sciences and Arts in 1924. Elected member of the Ukrainian Academy of Sciences. Co-founded the journal Studia mathematica with H. Steinhaus.
