Father_Notes: Arthur Banachiewicz was a landowner in the Warsaw district.
Education_Institution: Warsaw University; University of Göttingen; Pulkovo Observatory; Moscow University
Education_Notes: Received bachelor's degree in astronomy from Warsaw University in 1904, where an earlier astronomical paper won a gold medal. Continued studies under Schwarzschild at Göttingen and at Pulkovo. Received master's degree in astronomy from Moscow University in 1910.
Education_Locations: Warsaw, Unknown, Poland, Unknown, 1904; Göttingen, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Saint Petersburg, Unknown, Russia, Unknown, Unknown; Moscow, Unknown, Russia, Unknown, 1910
Scientific_Disciplines: Astronomy; Mathematics; Mechanics; Geodesy; Geophysics; Astrophysics
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Theoretical work on the three-body problem, Gyldén-Brendel perturbation theory, and parabolic orbit determination. Developed cracovian calculus, a matrix-like computational method superior to Cayley matrices for machine computation. Contributed to spherical polygonometry, heliometric observations, astrographic plate reduction, and least-squares methods. Observational work included occultations, eclipsing binaries, variable stars, and photometry. Pioneer in Poland for radio signals in time service and phototubes in photometry.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Junior assistant at Warsaw Observatory (1908–1909); assistant at Engelhardt Observatory near Kazan (1915–1915); taught at Dorpat (1915–1918); Dozent of geodesy at Warsaw Polytechnic High School (1918); professor of astronomy and director of Krakow Observatory from 1918 until his death.
Instruments_Notes: Carried out precise observations of the moon's libration using a four-inch heliometer while at Kazan. At his urging, the first Polish radio telescope was installed at Fort Skala, a branch station of the Krakow Observatory.

Education_Notes: Received B.A. from Harvard in 1888 and assisted in the chemistry department there in 1888–1889. Studied at Strasbourg, Berlin, and Leipzig under Wilhelm Ostwald, receiving the Ph.D. in 1892. Also studied under van't Hoff in Amsterdam.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of physical chemistry in the United States. Conducted research in electrochemistry, heterogeneous equilibria, colloid chemistry, emulsions, photography chemistry, dyeing theory, contact catalysis, and colloidal phenomena in anesthesia and other medical conditions.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught at Harvard from 1893 to 1895 and at Cornell from 1895 to 1937. Served in the Chemical Warfare Service during World War I with the rank of lieutenant colonel.

Father_Notes: Father was John Bannister, recorded as 'pleb.' at Banister's matriculation at Oxford in 1667.
Education_Notes: Matriculated at Magdalen College, Oxford on 21 June 1667; received B.A. in 1671 and M.A. in 1674. Served as chorister, clerk (possibly librarian), and chaplain at Oxford from 1676 to 1678. Well acquainted with American plants at Oxford and maintained a labeled herbarium with author citations.
Education_Locations: Oxford, Unknown, England, 1667, 1678
Religion_Notes: Arrived in Virginia as an Anglican minister in 1678; served as chaplain at Oxford before emigrating.
Scientific_Disciplines: Botany; Natural History; Entomology; Malacology; Anthropology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: First resident, university-educated naturalist of eastern United States. Contributed approximately 340 plant descriptions and at least eighty plant drawings cited in Ray's Historia, Morison's Historia, and Plukenet's Phytographia. Described internal anatomy of snails and explained function of balancers in Diptera. Compiled 'Collectio insectorum' of about one hundred specimens and composed significant 'Natural History of Virginia' with ethnographic material on Native Americans.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as Anglican minister in Virginia from 1678, though financially insecure and absent from Bristol Parish register by 1680. Became a planter in 1690, patenting 1,735 acres near the Appomattox River. Received encouragement and hospitality from William Byrd I and Theodorick Bland; likely received assistance from the Temple Coffee House Botany Club in London.
Patronage_Notes: Received support from William Byrd I, a trader at the falls of the James River, and Theodorick Bland of Westover. Corresponded with and sent specimens to Bishop Compton, Martin Lister, Leonard Plukenet, Samuel Doody, and John Ray, who called him 'eruditissimus.'
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Temple Coffee House Botany Club
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Likely received assistance and correspondence from the Temple Coffee House Botany Club in London, whose members included Bishop Compton, Lister, Plukenet, and Doody.

Father_Notes: William Banks of Revesby Abbey, Lincolnshire; took particular interest in the drainage of the Fenland; died in 1761.
Education_Institution: Harrow School; Eton College; Christ Church, Oxford
Education_Notes: Entered Harrow in 1752, transferred to Eton in 1756. At age fifteen developed passion for botany through self-study and instruction from women who gathered medicinal plants. Entered Christ Church, Oxford in 1760 as a gentleman commoner; studied botany under Israel Lyons, brought to Oxford at Banks's expense. Left Oxford without a degree.
Education_Locations: Harrow, Unknown, England, 1752, 1756; Eton, Unknown, England, 1756, 1760; Oxford, Unknown, England, 1760, 1764
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Principal botanizer and naturalist on Cook's first voyage (1768–1771), collecting over 800 previously unknown specimens. Established the famous Banks Herbarium. Advised King George III on Kew Gardens, transforming it into a botanical research center. Promoted the cultivation and adaptation of plants throughout the British Empire, including Chinese tea in India and breadfruit in the West Indies.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Inherited substantial estate at majority in 1764, with yearly income estimated between £6,000 and £30,000. Funded his own scientific expeditions and supported naturalists including Israel Lyons. Served as president of the Royal Society from 1778 until his death in 1820.
Patronage_Notes: Close friendship with King George III beginning in 1771, sharing interests in horticulture and agriculture. Became the king's chief adviser on Kew Gardens. Consulted by government on convict settlement at Botany Bay (1786) and authored or co-authored the 'Heads of the Plan' for New South Wales.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society of London; Linnean Society; Royal Institution; Institute of France
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1766. Elected president in 1778 at age thirty-five and served until his death in 1820, presiding over 417 of 450 council meetings. One of the founders of the Linnean Society and assisted in founding the Royal Institution. Elected to the Institute of France in 1802.

Education_Notes: Studied literary and scientific subjects in Fez and Marrakesh. Trained in geometry and Euclid's Elements by Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā al-Sharīf; introduced to fractional numbers by Abū Bakr al-Qallūsī; further mathematical training from Ibn Ḥajala and Abū 'Abd Allāh ibn Makhlūf al-Sijimāsī. Also studied medicine with al-Mirrīkh but did not pursue it deeply. The mystic al-Hazmirī directed much of his work toward the magic properties of numbers and letters.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Taught arithmetic, algebra, geometry, and astronomy at the madrasa al-ʿAṭṭārīn in Fez. Principal works include the Talkhīṣ, a summary of al-Ḥaṣṣār's lost mathematical works, containing continuing ascending fractions and approximate methods for extracting square roots; the Minhāj, a practical astronomical ephemeris with tables; and the Kitāb al-anwāʾ on acronical risings and settings. Also credited with works on the astrolabe and an early almanac. Eighty-two works attributed to him by H.P.J. Renaud.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught arithmetic, algebra, geometry, and astronomy at the madrasa al-ʿAṭṭārīn in Fez.

Father_Notes: Father was Dr. Scipione Banti, a physician.

Education_Notes: Studied medicine at the University of Pisa; graduated from the Medical School of Florence in 1877.

Religion_Notes: Described as a devout Roman Catholic with deep belief in science.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Eminent Italian pathologist of the early twentieth century. Made fundamental contributions to pathological anatomy, bacteriology, and histology. Pioneered understanding of leukemia, Banti's disease (splenomegaly with anemia and cirrhosis), hemolysis, and the spleen's role in blood cell destruction. Demonstrated the phagocytic defense mechanism and studied infectious diseases including typhoid fever and pneumonia. Contributed to knowledge of endocarditis, nephritis, and aphasia.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant at the Archihospital of Santa Maria Nuova in Florence from 1877; chief of hospital medical service from 1882; temporary professor of pathological anatomy at the Medical School of Florence from 1890; ordinary professor from 1895. Medical service at the hospital ended in 1924 after forty-seven years.

Scientific_Societies_Notes: Presented works to the Accademia Medico-Fisica Fiorentina and reported findings to the Italian Society of Pathology.

Education_Notes: Initially entered University of Toronto to study for the ministry but registered as a medical student the following year. Attracted to anatomy during medical school. Completed medical degree and clinical training at Toronto.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Initially focused on orthopedic surgery. Conducted early research on cerebellar cortex excitability under F.R. Miller. Discovered insulin through investigation of pancreatic function and diabetes, revolutionizing diabetes treatment. Later research addressed cancer, coronary thrombosis, and silicosis.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as demonstrator in anatomy and physiology at Western University medical school. Appointed professor of medical research at University of Toronto in 1923 and director of the Banting-Best Department of Medical Research. Held military commission in Canadian Army Medical Corps (1916–1918). Chaired Medical Research Committee of National Research Council and Associate Committee on Aviation Medical Research during World War II.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by J.J.R. Macleod at University of Toronto, who provided laboratory space, assistant, and dogs for initial research. Received annuity from Canadian Parliament in 1923.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society of Canada
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Became honorary member of most major scientific and medical societies worldwide. Published in Transactions of the Royal Society of Canada.

Education_Notes: Enrolled by Caliph al-Maʾmūn in the House of Wisdom, the first scientific institution in the Abbasid Empire, where they excelled in mathematics, astronomy, and mechanics.

They excelled especially in geometry and were active in astronomical observations in Baghdad. Muḥammad and al-Ḥasan focused on geometry; Aḥmad on mechanics; Muḥammad also worked in astronomy. Their most famous work was the geometrical treatise On the Measurement of Plane and Spherical Figures, which developed new proofs for measuring circles and spheres using infinitesimal methods derived from Archimedes and Eudoxus.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Supported by Caliph al-Maʾmūn and active as leading members of the House of Wisdom, where they directed scientific research and organized a school of translators.
Patronage_Notes: Recognized and enrolled in the House of Wisdom by Caliph al-Maʾmūn (813–833), who founded the institution.
Instruments_Notes: Devised a practical instrument constructed from hinged rules for solving the problem of two mean proportionals, similar to an instrument devised by Plato for the same purpose.

Scientific_Societies_Notes: Leading members and most active participants in the House of Wisdom, the first scientific institution in the Abbasid Empire.

Education_Notes: Early studies at Crevalcuore and Vercelli, continued at Novara and Milan. Took Barnabite vows on 11 March 1609 and completed religious and philosophical education. Studied Latin, Greek, Hebrew, and Chaldaic.

Religion_Notes: Member of the Barnabite religious order from 1609, taking the religious name Redento. Preached against Calvinists in Thonon, Geneva, and Béarn. His Copernican work was censured by the Church; he was required to recant and publish a corrective tract.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Published Uranoscopia seu De coelo (1617), defending the Copernican system. Engaged with experimental method against Aristotelian scholasticism. Read Patrizi and Telesio; corresponded with Tycho Brahe, Johannes Kepler, and Giovanni Magini. Francis Bacon praised him in 1622 as the first to oppose Aristotle with experimental method.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Barnabite friar from 1609. Taught philosophy at the college in Annecy (founded by Eustachio Chappuys) from 1615. Held a teaching position at the Barnabite College in Montargis from its founding until his death in 1622.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by Francis de Sales, who wrote a letter testifying to his merits when Baranzano was called to Milan by the archbishop to correct his Copernican work.

Education_Notes: Sent by the Church to Peru in 1588; no formal university education is recorded. Combined priestly duties with practical studies of mining and metallurgy in the Peruvian provinces.
Religion_Notes: Ordained priest; sent to Peru by the Church in 1588 and served in various parishes, including San Bernardo in Potosí after 1624.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in the treatment of silver ores by amalgamation using heat, copper vessels, and mechanical stirring. Developed improved processes for silver extraction that were largely responsible for provincial wealth. Advocated laboratory control of plant processes and cost computation. Described pre-Columbian smelting and early use of reverberatory furnaces.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as a priest in various Peruvian parishes from 1588 onward, including Tarabuco (1590), Tiahuanaco (1615), Yotala (1617), and San Bernardo in Potosí (after 1624). Conducted practical metallurgical research and experimentation alongside priestly duties.
Patronage_Notes: Dedicated El arte de los metales (1637) to Juan de Lizarazu, president of the Real Audiencia de la Plata of Peru, who transmitted the work to Spain with approval of the mayor and the Amalgamators Guild of Potosí.

Father_Notes: Father was a former soldier.
Education_Institution: Lycée Henri IV; École Normale Supérieure
Education_Notes: Attended Collège de St.-Omer and Lycée Henri IV in Paris; admitted to École Normale Supérieure in 1857, where he distinguished himself for mathematical and scientific ability. Passed his agrégation in 1860.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, 1857, 1860
Religion_Notes: In 1865 he attempted to enter a religious order but broke off the attempt.
Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; Geometry; Calculus; Astronomy; Physics; Chemistry; Instrumentation
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Published memoirs on spherical geometry and trigonometry, infinitesimal calculus, elementary and infinitesimal geometry, calculus of probabilities, polyhedra theory, Dupin's indicatrix, integral calculus, and number theory. Recognized as a good unspecialized mathematician of the late nineteenth century.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught mathematics at the lycée of Nice after passing his agrégation in 1860. Served as assistant astronomer at the Paris Observatory under Le Verrier. After 1880, received regular financial support from a foundation connected with the Académie des Sciences, secured by Joseph Bertrand.
Patronage_Notes: Le Verrier, director of the Paris Observatory, offered him a position as assistant astronomer. Joseph Bertrand, permanent secretary of the Académie des Sciences, encouraged his return to scientific writing and secured financial support from an Academy-connected foundation.
Instruments_Notes: Perfected a new type of thermometer; published studies on the construction of new thermometers and other instrumental techniques.

Scientific_Societies_Notes: Associated with the Académie des Sciences through Joseph Bertrand's support and published in its Comptes-rendus.

Education_Notes: Graduated A.B. from Trinity College in 1906 and M.D. from Johns Hopkins University in 1910. Spent one year as a fellow in pathology at Johns Hopkins before traveling abroad.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Primary contribution was delineation of the brain's temperature-regulating center and its mechanisms. Demonstrated that the anterior hypothalamus controls heat loss and the posterior hypothalamus controls heat generation. Became a leading authority on body temperature regulation and the effects of pyretic and antipyretic drugs.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught pharmacology at Yale University (1912–1921), McGill University (1921–1923), and University of Louisville (1923–1931). Returned to Yale in 1931 as associate professor and in 1940 as research associate in pharmacology.

Education_Notes: Studied pharmacy in Berlin, Mainz, and Vienna; traveled in Hungary and Italy. The M.D. was awarded honorarily in 1698 by the city council of Utrecht.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered the teaching of chemistry as an academic discipline at Utrecht from 1694. His chemical works systematically treated principles of chemistry, their applications to natural philosophy, medicine, metallurgy, and alchemy, and the analysis and synthesis of bodies by fire. Sought to combine chemical reactions in terms of principles or elements with a corpuscular view of matter. Made contributions to ideas on chemical affinity. His medical writings focused on the history of medicine and the importance of clinical observation and empirical therapy.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced as a physician, including briefly as physician to Francesco Morosini in 1693. From 1694 taught chemistry courses in Utrecht; granted an annual salary and the title of lector in chemistry in 1698; promoted to extraordinary professor of chemistry in 1703.
Patronage_Notes: The city council of Utrecht granted him permission to conduct chemistry courses in 1694, provided him with a laboratory in 1695, awarded him an honorary M.D. and annual salary in 1698, and promoted him to extraordinary professor in 1703.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Leading teacher of anatomy in Edinburgh in the early nineteenth century; made valuable contributions to human and comparative anatomy; assembled the Barclay Collection of Comparative Anatomy over twenty-seven years.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught anatomy at Edinburgh from 1796 onward, initially assisting John Bell before establishing his own class; lectured twice daily to accommodate up to 300 students; notably did not engage in medical practice.

Father_Notes: Henry Barcroft was active in the management of a spinning company and a tramway company, contributed mechanical inventions to both, and was also an artist interested in natural history.
Education_Institution: Leys School; University of London; King's College, Cambridge
Education_Notes: Attended Leys School, Cambridge from 1888; obtained B.Sc. from University of London while still a student at Leys; took a year off in 1892–1893 due to overstrain; entered King's College, Cambridge to study natural science and graduated in 1896.
Education_Locations: Cambridge, Unknown, England, 1888, Unknown; London, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; Cambridge, Unknown, England, 1893, 1896
Religion_Notes: Grew up a Quaker and remained active in the Society of Friends until disagreeing with its views during World War I.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in respiratory physiology and the study of oxygen dissociation curves of hemoglobin. Investigated glandular secretion, organ metabolism, high-altitude physiology, fetal respiration, and embryonic circulatory development. Authored The Respiratory Function of the Blood (1913), a landmark work in respiratory physiology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Fellow of King's College, Cambridge from 1899; lecturer from 1905; professor of physiology from 1925 until his death, holding these positions for nearly fifty years.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Fellow of the Royal Society.

Education_Notes: Attended Gymnasium in Bremen; brief engineering trainee placement at a railway maintenance depot; studied engineering at Bremen, then physics at Munich, Berlin, and Göttingen. Received doctorate from Göttingen in 1907 for dissertation on oscillation generation.
Education_Locations: Bremen, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Munich, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Berlin, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Göttingen, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1907
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Made foundational contributions to nonlinear switching elements and spontaneous oscillation theory; formulated electron-tube coefficients and their governing equations. Authored standard four-volume text on electron tubes and applications. Discovered the Barkhausen effect—acoustic detection of magnetic domain discontinuities in ferromagnetic materials. Proposed subjective loudness measurement and the phon as a unit of loudness. Developed the Barkhausen-Kurz oscillator for ultrahigh-frequency continuous-wave generation, advancing microwave tube technology and velocity modulation theory.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Research worker at Siemens & Halske laboratories in Berlin after 1907; appointed professor of communications electrical engineering at Technische Hochschule Dresden in 1911, where he remained until his death in 1956.
Instruments_Notes: Developed the Barkhausen-Kurz oscillator in 1920 with Karl Kurz, an electron tube for continuous-wave ultrahigh-frequency oscillation that became a forerunner of microwave tube technology. Contributed to electron-tube design and theory more broadly.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Institute of Radio Engineers
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Vice-president of the Institute of Radio Engineers in 1935.

Father_Notes: John Martin Barkla was secretary of the Atlas Chemical Company in Widnes.

Education_Notes: Entered University College, Liverpool in 1895 with scholarships, concentrating on mathematics and physics under Oliver Lodge. Received B.Sc. (First-Class Honours, 1898) and M.Sc. (1899). In autumn 1899 entered Trinity College, Cambridge as advanced student with 1851 Exhibition scholarship, attending lectures by George Stokes and conducting research at Cavendish Laboratory; moved to King's College after eighteen months. Returned to University of Liverpool as Oliver Lodge Fellow (1902–1905), receiving D.Sc. in 1904. Also received Cambridge B.A. from Cavendish research.
Education_Locations: Liverpool, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; Liverpool, Unknown, England, 1895, 1899; Cambridge, Unknown, England, 1899, 1901; Cambridge, Unknown, England, 1901, 1902; Liverpool, Unknown, England, 1902, 1905
Religion_Notes: Deeply religious man and faithful adherent of the Methodist Church, following his ancestors.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in X-ray physics. Discovered characteristic X-ray spectra emitted by elements and demonstrated that X rays are electromagnetic radiations through polarization and scattering experiments. Investigated secondary X radiation, its properties, homogeneity, and excitation conditions. Awarded Nobel Prize in Physics (1917) for discovery of characteristic X-ray spectra.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Demonstrator, assistant lecturer, and special lecturer at University of Liverpool (1905–1909); Wheatstone professor of physics at King's College, London (1909–1913); professor of natural philosophy at University of Edinburgh (1913–1944).
Instruments_Notes: Developed and refined ionization chamber with gold-leaf electroscope for detecting and measuring X-ray radiation. Rotated X-ray tube to study polarization of primary beam.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected Fellow of the Royal Society in 1912. Appointed Bakerian lecturer for 1916.

Education_Notes: Self-educated; competed successfully for position of assistant mathematics master at Royal Military Academy, Woolwich in 1801.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Published mathematical tables and treatises on theory of numbers. Conducted experiments on terrestrial magnetism and compass deviation caused by iron in ships, developing a method to correct ships' compasses. Investigated electromagnetism and attempted electric telegraph design. Developed achromatic telescope lens (Barlow lens). Conducted experiments on railroad design, rail shapes, gradients, and curves.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant mathematics master at Royal Military Academy, Woolwich from 1801. Worked with Thomas Telford on engineering projects including Menai Strait suspension bridge design and Thames tide calculations. Served as royal commissioner of railroads in 1830s and 1840s.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed to Royal Military Academy, Woolwich; served as royal commissioner of railroads.
Instruments_Notes: Developed a telescope lens consisting of colorless liquid between two pieces of glass; the Barlow lens, a negative achromatic combination of flint and crown glass, became a standard modification. Designed method for correcting ships' compasses using small iron plates.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; Institution of Civil Engineers

Father_Notes: Barlow inherited leisure and means from his father's estate, enabling him to pursue scientific work from his early thirties onward.
Education_Notes: Privately educated. Took a course in crystallography from H.E. Armstrong in the mid-1880s; largely self-taught in his scientific work.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in crystal structure theory based on close packing of atoms. Derived the 230 space groups independently (published 1894), contributing to the mathematical foundations of crystallography. Investigated the relation between crystal symmetry, atomic structure, and physical properties including optical and polar phenomena. Developed the valency-volume theory with W.J. Pope.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Supported by inherited wealth from his father, which afforded him leisure to pursue research from his early thirties. Collaborated extensively with academic colleagues and published in scientific journals and society proceedings.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; Mineralogical Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Royal Society in 1908. Served as president of the Mineralogical Society from 1915 to 1918.

Father_Notes: Father Reuben Barnard died before Edward's birth; family was impoverished.
Education_Notes: Only two months of formal schooling in childhood. From 1883 to 1887 attended Vanderbilt University as both student and instructor, following an irregular curriculum adapted to his lack of prior schooling and astronomical needs. Received no degree at the time but was awarded the D.Sc. six years after leaving the university in recognition of his scientific contributions and earlier studies.
Education_Locations: Nashville, Tennessee, United States, 1883, 1887
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Foremost observational astronomer of his time, ranking with Herschel. Discoveries and contributions spanned nearly all branches of astronomy: comets (seventeen discoveries), nebulae, Jupiter's fifth satellite, double stars, variable stars, novae, planetary observations, Milky Way photography, stellar parallax and proper motion, and dark nebulae. Pioneered the use of photography in astronomical observation. Discovered Barnard's star, which had the largest known proper motion until 1968.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked in portrait studio 1866–1883 while pursuing astronomy independently. From 1883 to 1887 was student and instructor at Vanderbilt University. September 1887 to 1895 at Lick Observatory; October 1895 to 1923 professor of practical astronomy at University of Chicago with complete freedom from teaching and administrative duties, based at Yerkes Observatory. Received cash prizes from H. H. Warner for comet discoveries in early career.
Patronage_Notes: Encouraged by H. H. Warner's cash prizes for comet discoveries in early career. Invited to join Lick Observatory by the distinguished group of astronomers there. Attracted to Yerkes Observatory by George Hale's group at University of Chicago.
Instruments_Notes: Purchased a five-inch telescope in 1876 for $380. Used Vanderbilt's six-inch telescope 1883–1887. At Lick Observatory used a small telescopic camera contrived from a 2.5-inch portrait lens with thirty-one-inch focal length, later the Bruce telescope. At Yerkes Observatory used the thirty-six-inch great refractor and the Bruce telescope for extensive Milky Way photography and other observations.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Astronomical Society; American Academy of Arts and Sciences; American Philosophical Society; National Academy of Sciences; Astronomical Society of the Pacific
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Foreign associate of the Royal Astronomical Society. Member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and American Philosophical Society. Director of the B. A. Gould Fund of the National Academy of Sciences. Vice-president of the American Association for the Advancement of Science in 1898.

Education_Notes: Received humanistic education with command of Greek and Latin. Studied at the University of Padua and lectured there around 1559 on Sacrobosco's Sphere.

Distinguished metamorphosis in trilobites and identified embryonic states. Studied the Silurian fauna and its geographical distribution.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Initially employed as an engineer for the construction of a horse-drawn railway in Prague. From 1840 onward, fossil collection and paleontological research became his chief occupation.

Education_Institution: Lehigh University; Lehigh University; Yale University
Education_Notes: Studied engineering at Lehigh University, graduating with high honors in 1892; earned M.S. in 1893 and M.S. in 1897 at Lehigh; received Ph.D. in geology from Yale in 1900; earned D.Sc. from Lehigh in 1916. Supported extended education through part-time teaching of mathematics, mining and metallurgy, geology, zoology, and astronomy.

Scientific_Disciplines: Geology; Structural Geology; Sedimentology; Metamorphism; Paleoclimatology; Isostasy
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Chief contributions in isostasy, sedimentology, and metamorphism. Pioneered dry-land geology and stratigraphic analysis; developed theory of magmatic stoping and concepts of lithosphere and aesthenosphere; advanced understanding of cyclic sedimentation and geological time measurement through denudation and radioactivity rates.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught mathematics, mining and metallurgy, geology, zoology, and astronomy at Lehigh in part-time positions while pursuing advanced degrees. Joined U.S. Geological Survey in Montana in 1901 to study mining districts and granite batholiths. Professor of structural geology at Yale from 1908 to 1919.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Sigma Xi Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Delivered lecture 'The Origin of the Earth' to Yale's Sigma Xi Society in 1916.

Education_Notes: Studied chemistry in Paris under Robiquet, Bussy, and Jules Pelouze; directed Pelouze's laboratory on the Rue Dauphine from 1844 to 1849.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines: Chemistry; Analytical Chemistry; Physiological Chemistry; Industrial Chemistry; Photographic Chemistry
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Early work focused on analytical chemistry, particularly separation techniques and reagents for detecting sugar (the Barreswil blue liquid, precursor to Fehling solution). Collaborated extensively with Claude Bernard on physiological chemistry, investigating digestion, gastric juices, and the role of sugar in animal metabolism. Later shifted to industrial chemistry, including dye chemistry, photographic chemistry, and sulfuric acid manufacture.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of chemistry at École Municipale Turgot and later at École Supérieure de Commerce in Paris. Also engaged in industrial chemistry research and held a position as inspector of child labor in factories of the Department of the Seine.

Father_Notes: Member of a wealthy industrial family; parents were liberals under the Restoration but became conservatives and ardent Catholics under the Second Empire.
Education_Notes: Studied with the Jesuits in Lille. Wrote a doctoral thesis on the development of living Spongiae (1876) and a thesis on Cretaceous formations of England presented in Paris in 1876 under Hébert's supervision. Studied optical petrography in the laboratory of Fouqué and Michel-Lévy at the Collège de France.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Ardent Catholic; among the militants of the Catholic party; religious convictions inhibited him from speaking freely on evolution; made a member of the Pontifical Scientific Academy by the pope in the last year of his life.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in stratigraphic paleontology and petrography; extended Hébert's paleontologic and stratigraphic zones to England; discovered that axes of deformations in English Cretaceous matched those of the Primary era, later developed as the theory of posthumous flections; mapped geological formations of Brittany, publishing twenty geological maps from 1880 to 1909; studied fossil corals, sponges, bryozoa, brachiopods, and graptolites; translated Zittel's Handbuch der Palaeontologie into French.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Named assistant at the Faculté des Sciences of Lille in 1871, where he spent his entire career; became lecturer in 1878; named professeur adjoint at the University of Lille in 1888; became director of the Institute of Geology of Lille in 1902, following Gosselet; retired from teaching in 1926.
Patronage_Notes: Jules Gosselet was his devoted mentor and lifelong influence; James Hall, the American geologist, developed a paternal affection for him and conducted him on tours of stratigraphic sequences in New York State.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences; Pontifical Scientific Academy
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected a titular member of the Académie des Sciences after several defeats; became a corresponding member of numerous academies; made a member of the Pontifical Scientific Academy in the last year of his life.

Father_Notes: Thomas Barrow was a prosperous linendraper with court connections.
Education_Notes: Attended Charterhouse as a dayboy, then Felsted School under headmaster Martin Holbeach, where he studied Greek, Latin, logic, and rhetoric. Entered Trinity College, Cambridge in 1643 as pensioner, graduating B.A. in 1648 and receiving M.A. in 1652.
Education_Locations: Felsted, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; Cambridge, Unknown, England, 1643, 1648
Religion_Notes: Took holy orders in 1660 upon the Restoration; served as royal chaplain in London from 1669; known for blunt and clear theological sermons published posthumously by Tillotson.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered the study of curves generated by combinations of moving points and lines, developing a method for finding tangents through composition of motions. Made original contributions to refraction theory and the construction of diacaustics. His geometrical lectures anticipated elements of the calculus, though their impact was limited. His optical lectures, based on mechanical corpuscular hypothesis and axiomatic principles, were rendered obsolete by Newton's work.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge (1649); college lecturer and university examiner; Regius Professor of Greek (1660); Gresham Professor of Geometry in London (1662); first Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at Cambridge (1663–1669); Master of Trinity College (1673–1677); university vice-chancellor (1675).
Patronage_Notes: Rewarded with the Regius Professorship upon the Restoration of Charles II in 1660; appointed royal chaplain in London in 1669; chosen by the king for the mastership of Trinity College in 1673.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected a fellow of the Royal Society after its incorporation in 1662, but never took an active part in its meetings.

Father_Notes: Engaged in a Nova Scotia-based mercantile concern with ships trading to North America and the West Indies.
Education_Institution: University of London; University of Paris; University of Erlangen; University of Berlin; University of Edinburgh; University of Heidelberg
Education_Notes: Studied medicine at London, Paris, Erlangen, and Berlin before receiving the M.D. from Edinburgh in 1833. After graduation specialized in anatomy and physiology under Friedrich Tiedemann at Heidelberg for about a year. Attended the Royal Infirmary at Edinburgh to further his medical knowledge.
Education_Locations: London, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; Erlangen, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Berlin, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Edinburgh, Unknown, Scotland, Unknown, 1833; Heidelberg, Unknown, Germany, 1833, 1834
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in embryological research using microscopy; made notable observations on mammalian ovum segmentation and spermatozoon penetration into the ovum. Conducted extensive histological studies on blood corpuscles and tissue formation, arguing for the unity of animal structure. Stimulated microscopic studies in Britain and promoted knowledge of German microscopic literature.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Possessed private income and never practiced medicine or held a permanent appointment. Presented physiological lectures at St. Thomas' Hospital, London in 1843. Served as house surgeon at the Royal Maternity Hospital, Edinburgh in 1844 but resigned due to ill health.
Instruments_Notes: Conducted extensive microscopical researches on embryological and histological specimens, producing numerous detailed illustrations of his observations.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; Royal Society of Edinburgh; Wernerian Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1840. Received the Royal Medal in 1839 for his embryological papers of 1838 and 1839. Active member of the Royal Society of Edinburgh and the Wernerian Society.

Education_Notes: Studied at the University of Göttingen, earning a Ph.D. in 1923. Subsequently worked closely with geomagnetician Adolph Schmidt for four years.
Education_Locations: Göttingen, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1923
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered the application of rigorous statistical methods to geomagnetism. Developed geomagnetic indices (including the Kp index) to measure solar particle influx and distinguish between wave and particle radiation from the sun. Investigated atmospheric tides and twenty-seven-day variations in geomagnetic activity, leading to the postulation of magnetically active regions (M-regions) on the sun. Co-authored the comprehensive work Geomagnetism with Sydney Chapman.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Head of the Meteorological Institute at the Fortliche Hochschule in Eberswalde (1927–1941); professor of geophysics at the University of Berlin (1941–1945); professor of geophysics and director of the Geophysical Institute at the University of Göttingen (1945 onward); director of the Max Planck Institute of Aeronomy at Lindau (from 1956).
Scientific_Societies_Membership: International Association of Geomagnetism and Aeronomy
Scientific_Societies_Notes: President of the International Association of Geomagnetism and Aeronomy from 1954 to 1957.

Father_Notes: Guillaume Barthez de Marmorières was chief engineer of Languedoc.
Education_Notes: Attended medical school at Montpellier from age sixteen, completing his degree in three years.
Education_Locations: Montpellier, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Developed vitalistic doctrines distinguishing matter, life, and soul as separate phenomena requiring distinct scientific principles. Advocated clinical teaching and inductive methods in physiology. Demonstrated limitations of mechanistic explanations for muscular control and movement.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as physician with the French army (1755–1757); employed as royal censor and editor of the Journal des savants in Paris; professor of medicine at Montpellier (ca. 1760–1781), becoming chancellor of the medical school in 1773; personal physician to Napoleon at the time of his death; honorary professor of medicine at Montpellier.
Patronage_Notes: Protégé of Falconnet, physician to Louis XV. Served as medical member of Napoleon's consular government alongside Corvisart. Appointed to the Légion d'Honneur and the Institut National.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences; Société Royale de Médecine; Institut National
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Académie des Sciences and Société Royale de Médecine; these honors were stripped during the Revolution but he was later appointed to the Institut National.

Father_Notes: Bertel Jespersen was court chaplain; mother Ane Rasmusdotter Tinckel was daughter of a clergyman from Skåne.
Education_Institution: University of Copenhagen; University of Wittenberg; University of Leiden; University of Basel; University of Padua; University of Naples
Education_Notes: Entered grammar school at age three; delivered lectures in Greek and Latin by age eleven. Matriculated at University of Copenhagen in 1603, transferred to Wittenberg in 1604 where he studied philosophy and theology, elected master of philosophy and humane arts in 1608. Studied medicine at Leiden without abandoning theology. Studied anatomy at Padua and Naples 1608–1610 under Fabricius ab Aquapendente and Casserio. Received M.D. from Basel in 1610 after defending his Paradoxa pathologica. Received D.D. in 1626.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Renowned for his anatomical manual Anatomicae institutiones corporis humani (1611), which described the olfactory nerves as the first pair of cerebral nerves and named the suprarenal glands capsulae atrabiliares. Clarified essential points in Aristotelian doctrine; wrote extensively on logic, physics, ethics, and theology. Performed dissections at Padua and Naples but not at Copenhagen.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of eloquence at University of Copenhagen from 1611; professor of medicine from 1613; professor of theology from 1624. Practiced medicine and performed anatomical studies in Italy.

Father_Notes: Father was Caspar Bartholin (1585–1629), a scholar; brother Thomas (1616–1680) was also a notable figure in medicine and natural philosophy.
Education_Institution: University of Leiden; University of Padua
Education_Notes: Matriculated at University of Leiden in 1646 and studied mathematics in Holland for several years. Traveled in France, Italy, and England. Received M.D. from University of Padua in 1654.
Education_Locations: Leiden, Unknown, Netherlands, 1646, Unknown; Padua, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, 1654
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Worked in pure mathematics, particularly the theory of equations under Cartesian influence. Observed comets of 1664–1665 and engaged in astronomical observation. Made major contributions to physics through study of double refraction in Icelandic spar, explaining the phenomenon within Cartesian theory of light. Contributed to medical knowledge through introduction of cinchona bark to Denmark.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed professor of mathematics at University of Copenhagen in 1656; transferred to extraordinary chair of medicine in 1657 and ordinary chair in 1671. Served as dean of faculty of medicine, librarian, and rector of the university. Appointed royal physician and privy councilor.
Patronage_Notes: Directed by Frederick III of Denmark to prepare Tycho Brahe's manuscript observations for publication. Appointed royal physician and privy councilor.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: In fairly close touch with French and German scientists and through the latter initially with the Royal Society. Sent copy of Experimenta crystalli Islandici to Henry Oldenburg.

Father_Notes: Father was Caspar Bartholin, who successively held professorships of anatomy and religion at the University of Copenhagen.

Education_Notes: Entered University of Copenhagen in 1634. Studied medicine at Leiden from 1637 under Sylvius and Johannes de Wale. Studied anatomy at Padua under Johan Rhode and Johann Vesling. Obtained medical degree from Basel.
Education_Locations: Copenhagen, Unknown, Denmark, 1634, Unknown; Leiden, Unknown, Netherlands, 1637, Unknown; Padua, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown; Basel, Unknown, Switzerland, Unknown, 1646
Religion_Notes: Inferred from Danish context and burial in the Vor Frue Kirke cathedral in Copenhagen.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Revised and improved his father's Institutiones anatomicae through three editions (1641, 1645, 1651). Authored the first Danish pharmacopeia and numerous medical treatises on comparative anatomy, midwifery, and medical philosophy.

Education_Notes: Entered the Society of Jesus at age fifteen; studied with the Jesuits at Piacenza and Parma; taught rhetoric at Parma; pursued theological studies at Milan and Bologna under G. B. Riccioli; took vows in 1643. No degree is named.

Sought to link speculative and experimental approaches; praised Galileo and quoted foreign writers including Harvey, Mersenne, and Gassendi, though occasionally disputed Galileo on harmonic theory.

Father_Notes: Father Pellegrino was competent in both pharmacy and surgery.

Education_Notes: Studied philosophy and medicine at Bologna and Ferrara. At Ferrara was a pupil of Antonio Cittadini and Sebastiano Dell'Aquila. Witnessed degree conferrals in 1494 and attended an anatomical dissection in 1497.
Education_Locations: Bologna, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown; Ferrara, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown

Father_Notes: Thomas Barton attended Trinity College, Dublin, came to Pennsylvania in 1750, and was ordained in the Anglican Church. He worked with Indians around Carlisle and settled on Conestoga Creek. He died in 1780 when Benjamin was fourteen.
Education_Institution: Academy; University of Edinburgh; Lisbon Academy
Education_Notes: Educated by his older brother William and at an academy in York, Pennsylvania. Commenced medical training at eighteen under Dr. William Shippen of Philadelphia. Studied medicine at the University of Edinburgh (1786–1787), where he won the Harveian Prize for his dissertation on black henbane and served as one of four annual presidents of the Royal Medical Society of Edinburgh. Received a diploma from Lisbon Academy, Portugal, though he took no pride in it. Did not receive a degree from Edinburgh or confirmed degree from Göttingen.
Education_Locations: York, Pennsylvania, Unknown, United States, Unknown, Unknown; Edinburgh, Unknown, Scotland, 1786, 1787; Lisbon, Unknown, Portugal, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines: Botany; Zoology; Natural History; Medicine; Ethnography
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Author of the first American botanical textbook, Elements of Botany (1803), which ran to six editions. Assembled the largest herbarium of native plants of his time (1,674 specimens, 1797–1807). Conducted ethnographic observations on American Indians. Worked on natural history of the Lewis and Clark expedition, though it remained unfinished. Published numerous papers on observations in medicine, natural history, and physical geography.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of natural history and botany at the University of Pennsylvania from 1789; succeeded to the professorship of materia medica in 1795 and added the professorship of the practice of physic in 1813. Served as curator of the American Philosophical Society (1790–1800) and vice-president (1802–1815). Practiced medicine.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: American Philosophical Society; Royal Medical Society of Edinburgh
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Served as one of four annual presidents of the Royal Medical Society of Edinburgh during his studies (1786–1787). Curator of the American Philosophical Society (1790–1800) and vice-president (1802–1815).

Father_Notes: William Bartram, a farmer near Darby, Pennsylvania; member of the Society of Friends.
Education_Notes: Common country schooling only; self-taught in botany and natural history from age twelve; briefly studied medicine and surgery but did not pursue formal training.
Religion_Notes: Born into the Society of Friends (Quaker); became a deist through his study of nature, expressing disbelief in the divinity of Jesus; disowned by the Friends in 1757 but continued attending meetings. Rejected ecclesiastical formalities and Quaker pacifism.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering American botanist who introduced over a hundred American plant species to Europe through systematic collecting expeditions. Also collected and described shells, insects, hummingbirds, reptiles, and other fauna. Made detailed observations of natural phenomena including geological formations.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Established himself as a farmer and plant merchant, selling seeds, plants, and shrubs to European patrons including English nobility and botanists. Received annual funding from Collinson and associates to support collecting. Named king's botanist in 1765 with an annual stipend of fifty pounds. Involved in the American Philosophical Society.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by English patrons including the dukes of Richmond, Norfolk, Argyll, and Bedford, Lord Petre, Sir Hans Sloane, and Thomas Penn. Peter Collinson served as his principal patron and correspondent, organizing funding and introducing him to European naturalists. Named king's botanist by the Crown in 1765.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: American Philosophical Society; Royal Academy of Sciences of Sweden
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Especially devoted to the American Philosophical Society, established by Franklin in 1743. Elected member of the Royal Academy of Sciences of Sweden in 1769. Awarded a gold medal in 1772 by a society of gentlemen in Edinburgh for his services to science.

Father_Notes: John Bartram, a botanist and naturalist; owned a farm and garden at Kingsessing near Philadelphia.
Education_Notes: Attended the Academy of Philadelphia from 1752 to 1756, where he studied Latin and French alongside his preferred subjects of botany and drawing. No formal degree recorded.
Education_Locations: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States, 1752, 1756
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted extensive botanical and ornithological observations during travels through the Carolinas, Georgia, and Florida (1773–1778). Made detailed natural history drawings and notes on birds, animals, fishes, and plants. Provided advice and training to naturalists including Alexander Wilson, Thomas Nuttall, and F. A. Michaux.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Supported by Dr. John Fothergill's patronage (fifty pounds annually from 1771) during his southern travels. Briefly apprenticed to a merchant (1757) and operated a failed trading store in Cape Fear, North Carolina (1761). Attempted planting rice and indigo in Florida. Worked in his brother's garden and nursery after 1778. Declined a professorship of botany at the University of Pennsylvania in 1782.
Patronage_Notes: Peter Collinson, his father's London patron, encouraged his early work and sent drawings to George Edwards. Dr. John Fothergill succeeded Collinson as patron, offering fifty pounds annually and purchasing Bartram's drawings during his 1773–1778 travels.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: American Philosophical Society; Philadelphia Society for Promoting Agriculture; Academy of Natural Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected member of the Philadelphia Society for Promoting Agriculture in 1785. Made a member of the Academy of Natural Sciences at its founding in 1812. Member of the American Philosophical Society but took no active interest and never attended meetings.

Father_Notes: Father was a musician and choirmaster; family experienced persistent financial difficulties.
Education_Institution: Columbia University School of Mines; University of Würzburg
Education_Notes: Attended Columbia University's School of Mines, then studied at Würzburg under Friedrich Kohlrausch, earning his Ph.D.
Education_Locations: New York, Unknown, United States, 1874, 1876; Würzburg, Unknown, Germany, 1876, 1879
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Developed methods for measuring high temperatures using thermocouples over a range of approximately 1,000° C, independently of Châtelier. Internationally recognized authority on pyrometry. Later investigated effects of X rays and radioactivity on water vapor condensation in fog chambers.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked for the United States Geological Survey (1880–1892), United States Weather Bureau (1892–1893), and Smithsonian Institution (1893–1894). Appointed Hazard professor of physics at Brown University in 1895, became dean of the graduate school in 1903, and taught until retirement in 1926.
Patronage_Notes: Employed by the United States Geological Survey and Weather Bureau; assisted Samuel P. Langley at the Smithsonian Institution with flying machine development.
Instruments_Notes: Designed and improved a fog chamber consisting of a wooden cylinder impregnated with resin, connected to a lower-pressure chamber via stopcock, to study condensation of water vapor under X rays and radioactivity. Later criticized by C. T. R. Wilson for design flaws including contamination from resin and inadequate shielding.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: National Academy of Sciences; American Physical Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 1892. Founder of the American Physical Society in 1899 and served as its president from 1905 to 1906.

Education_Institution: University of Padua; University of Paris; University of Vienna; University of Munich
Education_Notes: Studied geology at Padua under Giuseppe Meneghini and Giovanni Omboni, who introduced him to fossil fishes. Continued studies in Paris in 1877 under Hébert, Gaudry, and Sauvage, and in Vienna in 1878 with E. Suess and M. Neumayr. Also studied in Munich with Zittel. No degree is named in the source.
Education_Locations: Padua, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, 1877, Unknown; Vienna, Unknown, Austria, 1878, Unknown; Munich, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Primarily a student of fossil fishes, with extensive monographic work on Eocene, Cretaceous, Triassic, Miocene, and Pleistocene faunas of Italy and the Mediterranean basin. Investigated stratigraphic relations, volcanic phenomena at Vesuvius and Solfatara, marine mammals, and the contemporaneity of man and extinct animals on Capri. Became expert at discriminating shark teeth and developed concepts of fish species evolution through geologic time. Regarded as one of the leading paleoichthyologists of his day.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught natural history, geology, and mineralogy in secondary schools in Padua, Modena, and Milan from 1879 to 1887. In 1887 appointed to the chair of geology at Naples, which he occupied until his death. As director of the Geological Institute in Naples, brought about extensive improvements in laboratory facilities and collections.

Father_Notes: Father was Onorato Bassi; family owned a farm at Mairago.
Education_Notes: Studied law at University of Pavia as his parents wished, but also pursued physics, chemistry, mathematics, natural science, and some medicine. Attended lectures by Antonio Scarpa (anatomist), Alessandro Volta (physicist), Giovanni Rasori (pathology), and Lazzaro Spallanzani (natural history). Received doctorate in jurisprudence in 1798.
Education_Locations: Pavia, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, 1798
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Discovered the fungal cause of muscardine (silkworm disease) through systematic experimentation, demonstrating that a living fungus parasite caused the disease. Proposed that parasites were the cause of various human diseases including plague, smallpox, syphilis, and cholera. Conducted agricultural experiments on merino sheep breeding, potato cultivation, and winemaking.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as provincial administrator and police assessor in Lodi under French administration after 1798, and held various civil service positions. Briefly returned to public service in 1815. Managed his father's farm at Mairago and conducted agricultural experiments there. Presented research at University of Pavia.
Instruments_Notes: Used microscopic investigation to identify the fungal parasite causing muscardine and to examine the structure of the fungus spores and mycelium.

Education_Notes: Worked as technical assistant to E. O. Ulrich after high school. Withdrew from University of Cincinnati to follow Ulrich to Washington. Completed graduate work at George Washington University, earning M.S. and Ph.D.

Also studied tetra corals, Cystoidea, and conodonts. Assembled outstanding fossil collection now at Smithsonian Institution.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Employed by United States National Museum and affiliated with George Washington University for nearly four decades.
Patronage_Notes: Employed by the United States National Museum, a government institution.

Education_Notes: Studied at the Academia Mussipontana (Pont à Mousson).
Education_Locations: Pont à Mousson, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Revived atomic philosophy and pre-Socratic doctrines against Aristotelian natural philosophy. Developed a corpuscular theory of matter comprising immutable atoms of different natures and a fine corporeal ether filling the pores between atoms. Explained physical phenomena including elemental transmutation, evaporation, planetary influence, and motion of falling bodies and projectiles through atomic and ethereal mechanisms.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced as a physician.

Education_Notes: Entered University College London in 1856 and graduated M.B. seven years later (1863). Received M.D. in 1866.
Education_Locations: London, Unknown, England, 1856, 1863
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of neurology as a science; made important contributions to understanding aphasia, word blindness, and muscular sense; discovered the anterior spinocerebellar tract (1867). Devoted two periods to abiogenesis and spontaneous generation (1868–1878 and 1900–1915), becoming the last scientific opponent of Pasteur and the germ theory, though his criticisms inadvertently advanced bacteriology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant physician and lecturer on pathology at St. Mary's Hospital, London; professor of pathological anatomy at University College London from 1867; physician to University College Hospital from 1878; held chair of principles and practice of medicine from 1887 to 1898; appointment at National Hospital, Queen Square, London, from 1868 to 1902. Crown referee in cases of supposed insanity from 1884 to 1898.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society of London; Royal College of Physicians of London; Royal College of Physicians of Ireland
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society of London in 1868 at age thirty-one; served as censor of the Royal College of Physicians of London from 1897 to 1898; received honorary fellowship of the Royal College of Physicians of Ireland.

Father_Notes: Stone mason; family of modest means.

Education_Notes: Passed baccalauréat ès lettres in 1882 and baccalauréat ès sciences; earned licencié ès sciences naturelles. Doctorate in science presented 17 April 1891 with thesis on amphibian metamorphosis. Studied experimental embryology under Laurent Chabry at University of Lyons.
Education_Locations: Arbois, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; Belfort, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; Lyons, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; Lyons, Unknown, France, 1887, 1891
Religion_Notes: Refused ecclesiastical career despite scholarship to petit séminaire of Vaux-sur-Poligny.
Scientific_Disciplines: Biology; Zoology; Embryology; Anatomy; Comparative Anatomy
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in experimental embryology and artificial parthenogenesis. Discovered traumatic parthenogenesis in batrachians through mechanical pricking of unfertilized eggs. Demonstrated the dual-factor mechanism: mechanical activation and biological regulation via leukocyte inoculation. Clarified the complex phenomena of fertilization and embryonic development.

Patronage_Notes: Seconded by Pasteur early in career; appointed to state university positions throughout France.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Corresponding member from 1916; full member from 1946. Awarded the Osiris Prize of the Academy in 1951.

Father_Notes: Samuel Bateman was a druggist and commercial traveler.
Education_Institution: Manchester Grammar School; Trinity College, Cambridge; Johns Hopkins University
Education_Notes: Developed mathematical interests at Manchester Grammar School. Studied at Trinity College, Cambridge, receiving B.A. in 1903 and M.A. in 1906. Took Ph.D. at Johns Hopkins in 1913.
Education_Locations: Manchester, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; Cambridge, Unknown, England, Unknown, 1906; Baltimore, Maryland, United States, 1912, 1913
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Specialized in finding special functions to solve partial differential equations. Made significant contributions to integral equations, conformal transformations in electromagnetism, Laplace transform methods, and hydrodynamics. Developed Bateman's expansion and Bateman's function. Later work focused on collecting and systematizing special functions and integrals solving equations of mathematical physics.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught at Liverpool University and Manchester before emigrating to the United States in 1910. Taught at Bryn Mawr College for two years, held research fellowship and lectured at Johns Hopkins 1912–1917. Appointed professor of mathematics, theoretical physics, and aeronautics at Throop College (later Caltech) in Pasadena from 1917 until his death. Also worked part-time on meteorology at the Bureau of Standards.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; U.S. National Academy of Sciences; American Mathematical Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1928 and member of the U.S. National Academy of Sciences in 1930. Elected vice-president of the American Mathematical Society in 1935 and delivered the Society's Gibbs lecture in 1943.

Father_Notes: Henry Bates was a hosiery manufacturer at Leicester.
Education_Notes: Attended local schools in Leicester and Mr. H. Screaton's boarding school at Billesden until midsummer 1838. Took night classes at the local Mechanic's Institute where he excelled in Greek, Latin, French, drawing, and composition. Later taught himself German and Portuguese while in South America.
Education_Locations: Leicester, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Unitarian religious views did not hinder his acceptance of natural selection.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering entomologist specializing in Coleoptera (beetles) and Lepidoptera (butterflies). Formulated the theory of Batesian mimicry, explaining how palatable species mimic unpalatable ones for protection through natural selection. Conducted extensive systematic work on insect fauna, particularly from the Amazon region. Also contributed to understanding of geographical distribution of animals.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Apprenticed to hosiery manufacturer until 1844; worked as clerk in Burton-on-Trent. From 1848–1859 supported himself through collecting and selling specimens in South America (though profit was modest, approximately £73 per year). From 1864 served as assistant secretary of the Royal Geographical Society for twenty-eight years, editing its Journal and Proceedings. Also edited and contributed to numerous travel works and entomological publications.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed assistant secretary of the Royal Geographical Society of London in 1864, a position he held with distinction for twenty-eight years. Received the Order of the Rose from the Emperor of Brazil for his work in that country.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Entomological Society of London; Linnean Society; Zoological Society; Royal Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Entomological Society of London in 1861 and served as president in 1868, 1869, and 1878. Elected fellow of the Linnean Society in 1871, fellow of the Zoological Society in 1863, and fellow of the Royal Society in 1881. Served as secretary of the Geographical Section of the British Association but declined the office of president.

Father_Notes: William Henry Bateson was a classical scholar and master of St. John's College, Cambridge from 1857, indicating both academic standing and financial security.
Education_Institution: University of Cambridge; Johns Hopkins University
Education_Notes: Took first-class honors in the natural science tripos at Cambridge, receiving the B.A. in 1883. Student and later fellow of St. John's College, Cambridge. Studied under A. Sedgwick and W. F. R. Weldon at Cambridge; also studied with W. K. Brooks at Johns Hopkins during 1883–1884 while in Maryland and Virginia. Self-described as ill-trained in physics and chemistry with virtually no mathematics, but possessed outstanding classical abilities.
Education_Locations: Cambridge, Unknown, England, Unknown, 1883; Baltimore, Maryland, United States, 1883, 1884
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in establishing Mendelian genetics; named the discipline 'genetics' in 1905–1906. Early work focused on zoology and morphology, then shifted to heredity and variation. Demonstrated Mendelian behavior in animals as well as plants; investigated epistatic modifications, reversion, and linkage. Later work concentrated on somatic segregation and developed a vibratory theory of inheritance as alternative to chromosome theory. Ardent evolutionist who opposed natural selection and championed saltatory variation.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held Balfour Studentship at Cambridge (1887); deputy in zoology to Alfred Newton (1899); reader in zoology (1907); professor of genetics (1908)—the first such chair in Britain. From 1910 served as first director of the John Innes Horticultural Institution at Merton. Research financed with difficulty through personal funds, private gifts, and the Evolution Committee of the Royal Society.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by the Evolution Committee of the Royal Society; elected trustee of the British Museum (1922). Received Darwin Medal (1904) and Royal Medal (1920).
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; British Association for the Advancement of Science
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1894. Belonged to numerous other societies. Served as president of the British Association for the Advancement of Science (1914). Co-founded the Journal of Genetics with R. C. Punnett in 1910.

Education_Notes: Attended Winchester School; studied at New College, Oxford, earning B.A. in 1886, M.A. in 1890, and D.Sc. in 1900.
Education_Locations: Oxford, Unknown, England, Unknown, 1886
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Specialist in echinoderm morphology, particularly the Pelmatozoa and Crinoidea. Published fundamental studies on fossil echinoderms and contributed to paleoecology. His exposition of echinoderm morphology in Lankester's Treatise of Zoology (1900) remained authoritative for decades.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant geologist at the British Museum from 1887; promoted to keeper of the geology department in 1924; retired in 1928. Also held academic honors and prizes from Oxford and Cambridge.
Patronage_Notes: Employed by the British Museum, a state institution; advanced to keeper of the geology department.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Geological Society of London; Museums Association; British Association for the Advancement of Science
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Served as president of the Geological Society of London, the Museums Association, and the British Association for the Advancement of Science. Received the Rolleston Prize (1892), Wollaston Fund (1897), and Lyell Medal (1911) from the Geological Society of London.

Alt_Name: Abū 'Abd Allāh Muḥammad Ibn Jābir Ibn Sinān Al-Raqqī Al-Ḥarrānī Al-Ṣābi'; Albatenius; Albategni; Albategnius
Father_Notes: Father was Jābir ibn Sinān al-Ḥarrānī, a famous instrument maker. His proficiency in devising astronomical instruments likely derived from his father's craft.
Education_Notes: No formal institutional education is recorded. Al-Battānī's astronomical training appears to have come through family tradition and practical apprenticeship with his father, an instrument maker.
Religion_Notes: Al-Battānī was Muslim, as evidenced by his personal name Muḥammad and his kunya Abū 'Abd Allāh. His ancestors professed the Ḥarranian Ṣabian religion, which preserved ancient Mesopotamian astral theology and was tolerated by Muslim rulers until the eleventh century.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: One of the greatest Islamic astronomers. Composed the Zīj, a major astronomical treatise with tables containing his own observations of the sun and moon, corrections to Ptolemy's Almagest, and planetary motions. Developed new trigonometric methods and made precise measurements of the obliquity of the ecliptic and solar apogee. Also wrote on astrology and composed a commentary on Ptolemy's Tetrabiblos.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Spent the greater part of his life in al-Raqqa, where he carried out his famous astronomical observations. Traveled to Baghdad with the Banū al-Zayyāt, a prominent family, suggesting patronage connections. His observational work spanned from 877 to 918 A.D.
Instruments: Armillary Sphere; Mural Quadrant; Triquetrum; Sundial
Instruments_Notes: Devised a new type of armillary sphere called al-bayḍa ('the egg'). Also designed or improved a mural quadrant and a triquetrum for astronomical observations. Constructed a sundial indicating unequal hours.

Alt_Name: Muhammad ibn Abdullah; Muhammad ibn Battuta
Father_Notes: Family belonged to the legal establishment; descended from the Berber tribe of the Lawāta.
Education_Notes: Received the usual legal-religious education in Tangier. Visited and occasionally studied with famous scholars encountered during his travels, particularly during the pilgrimage journey, though formal study was not his primary purpose.
Religion_Notes: Deeply committed to Islam; made the pilgrimage to Mecca in 1325 and remained spiritually within the boundaries of the Islamic world throughout his travels. Believed in supernatural events and the miracles of saintly men.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Traveled extensively across Asia, Africa, and Europe, observing and recording geographical features, economic conditions, and natural phenomena. Provided systematic treatment of trees, fruits, and grains of South Arabia, India, and the Maldives. Documented remarkable animals, minerals, plants, and customs. Showed interest in alchemy but was skeptical of marvelous natural phenomena.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Made his living from gifts and stipends from rulers and high officials in the places he visited. Exercised judicial functions as a Mālikite judge in India and on his way from Morocco to Egypt. Undertook occasional commercial ventures and benefited from strategic marriages.
Patronage_Notes: Received support and stipends from various rulers and high officials throughout his travels. Served as a judge under Muslim political authorities.

Father_Notes: Marie Victor Baudrimont was an inspector of bridges and roads.
Education_Notes: Apprenticed to a pharmacist at age twelve. Studied pharmacy in Paris from 1823 and medicine from 1825. Received his medical degree in 1831 and first-class degree in pharmacy in 1834. Obtained his licentiate in pure science in 1839 and his doctorate in 1847.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, 1823, 1834; Bordeaux, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines: Chemistry; Organic Chemistry; Physiology; Physics; Agricultural Chemistry; Mineralogy; Geology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Active in both theoretical and experimental chemistry, with particular focus on molecular structure, chemical types, and aqua regia. Proponent of Avogadro's hypothesis. Conducted physiological research on embryonic development in chickens and amphibia with Martin Saint-Ange, winning the Académie des Sciences grand prize in 1846. Also worked in physics, testing properties of metals, and maintained lifelong interest in agricultural chemistry.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked as research assistant to E. R. A. Serres; practiced as industrial chemist in Valenciennes from 1830. Held minor positions at the Collège de France and Faculté de Médecine in Paris during the 1830s and 1840s. Practiced medicine in Valenciennes after 1831. In 1847 became assistant to Auguste Laurent at the University of Bordeaux, and was awarded the chair of chemistry in 1849, remaining there for the rest of his life.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Won the Académie des Sciences grand prize in physical sciences in 1846 for embryological research with Martin Saint-Ange.

Father_Notes: Father was a businessman.

Education_Notes: Attended lycées Condorcet and Janson de Sailly; graduated from University of Paris. Worked as first assistant to Jean Perrin at Paris; studied under Rubens and Nernst; conducted theoretical and experimental research on luminescence and blackbody radiation under Langevin, completing thesis in 1912.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Research on thermal radiation from flames and metallic vapors; Stefan constant determination; light diffusion by high-altitude atmosphere; ferromagnetic equation of state; group theory and quantum mechanics; hydrogen bonding and structure of water and ice from vibration spectra; dielectric dispersion and phase transformation; chemical kinetics. Also contributed significantly to history of science.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant to Jean Perrin at University of Paris; appointed to University of Strasbourg under Pierre Weiss in 1919; sous-directeur of Langevin's laboratory at Collège de France from 1928; professor of physical chemistry at University of Paris.
Patronage_Notes: Worked under Jean Perrin, Rubens, Nernst, and Langevin; appointed to Strasbourg by Pierre Weiss; Langevin invited him to become sous-directeur of his laboratory.

Education_Notes: Educated by Father Boccius, prior of the monastery of the Merciful Brothers in Feldsberg; worked under Nikolaus von Jacquin, professor of botany in Vienna.
Scientific_Disciplines: Natural History; Botany; Zoology; Scientific Illustration
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Master of botanical illustration whose watercolors documented plants and animals from Greece, the Levant, and Australia. Painted nearly 1,000 plant watercolors, 363 animal studies, and 131 sepia landscapes during Sibthorp's expedition (1786–1787). Over 2,000 sketches from the Australian voyage with Robert Brown, including 1,541 plant studies. His work contributed to the overthrow of Linnaean taxonomy.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Engaged by John Sibthorp as artist on his expedition to Greece and the Levant (1786–1787); worked on Flora Graeca in Oxford until 1801; joined Matthew Flinders' voyage to Australia (1801–1803); settled near Schönbrunn gardens in Hietzing from 1814.
Patronage_Notes: Patronized by John Sibthorp, Oxford professor of botany, who engaged him for the Greek expedition and Flora Graeca project; worked with botanist Robert Brown on the Australian voyage.

Patronage_Notes: Patronized by Sir Joseph Banks, who engaged him as artist at Kew and provided access to Banks's library and herbarium; collaborated with Robert Brown and other naturalists.
Instruments_Notes: Conducted microscopical observations and produced detailed microscopical paintings of botanical specimens, though his work predated modern staining and fixing techniques.

Education_Notes: Originally trained as a civil engineer. Studied at the University of Berlin from 1892 to 1895, earning the Ph.D. for a thesis on the secular variation of the earth's magnetism.
Education_Locations: Berlin, Unknown, Germany, 1892, 1895
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Founder of the Department of Terrestrial Magnetism at the Carnegie Institution of Washington. Principal work focused on terrestrial magnetism, its secular variation, and the physical nature of the earth's magnetic field. Also investigated atmospheric electricity and extraterrestrial influences on magnetism, including effects of solar eclipses. Promoted establishment of magnetic stations and developed mathematical theory and analysis of observations.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked as a computer for the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey (1887–1892, 1899–1906). Taught at the University of Chicago (1895–1896) and the University of Cincinnati (1897–1899). Appointed head of the Department of Terrestrial Magnetism at the Carnegie Institution of Washington in 1904, a position he held until his death.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed head of the Department of Terrestrial Magnetism at the Carnegie Institution of Washington in 1904 by the Institution's leadership.
Instruments_Notes: Promoted the establishment of magnetic stations worldwide for mapping the earth's magnetic field and collecting observational data on terrestrial magnetism.

Scientific_Societies_Notes: Active in various international geophysical organizations. Founded the periodical Terrestrial Magnetism (later Terrestrial Magnetism and Atmospheric Electricity) in 1896 and edited it until 1927; the journal became influential and played an important role in stimulating geophysical investigations.
