Father_Notes: Jean Bauhin, a French Protestant physician and surgeon from Amiens, settled in Basel in 1541 and became attached to the university.
Education_Institution: University of Basel; University of Padua; University of Montpellier; University of Paris; University of Tübingen
Education_Notes: Taught anatomy by his father and botany by his brother Jean from childhood. Studied at Basel under Felix Plater and Theodore Zwinger. Received Bachelor of Philosophy in 1575. Studied anatomy at Padua under Girolamo Fabrizio for eighteen months from October 1577, attended teaching at the Hospital of St. Francis, and received instruction in anatomy from Giulio Cesare Aranzio at Bologna. Attended anatomies in Paris under Sévérin Pineau in 1579. Received doctorate in medicine on 2 May 1581.
Education_Locations: Basel, Unknown, Switzerland, 1572, 1575; Padua, Unknown, Italy, 1577, 1579; Montpellier, Unknown, France, 1579, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, 1579, 1579; Tübingen, Unknown, Germany, 1580, 1580
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Reformed anatomical nomenclature, particularly of muscles, naming them by substance, shape, origin, insertion, number of heads, size, position, or function. Described the ileocecal valve (valvula Bauhini) and included description of venous valves. Authored influential anatomical textbooks including Theatrum anatomicum (1605), chosen by William Harvey as basis for his Lumleian Lectures. As a botanist, was primarily a taxonomist concerned with plant classification and nomenclature. Distinguished genus from species and introduced binomial nomenclature in Pinax (1623). Separated botany from materia medica.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of Greek from 1582; held special chair in anatomy and botany from 1589. Taught anatomy and botany throughout his career, conducting public anatomies in winter and botanical expeditions in summer. Physician to Duke Frederick of Württemberg from 1597 (with his brother Jean). Archiater to the city of Basel from 1614. Professor of the practice of medicine from 1615. Maintained private medical practice.
Patronage_Notes: Associated with Duke Frederick of Württemberg as physician from 1597.

Father_Notes: Jean Bauhin, a Protestant from Amiens, was physician to Margaret of Navarre. The family fled religious persecution under Francis I and settled in Basel in 1541.
Education_Notes: Basic education in Basel under Coelius Secundus Curione and Conrad Gesner. Attended foreign universities between 1560 and 1563, with prolonged study at Montpellier from 1561 to 1562. University records do not confirm the M.D., but he established a medical practice at Lyons in 1563.
Education_Locations: Montpellier, Unknown, France, 1561, 1562

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Primary interest was botany from youth; collaborated with Conrad Gesner on Historia plantarum and pioneered study of alpine flora. Conducted systematic explorations in Montpellier region, Provence, Languedoc, and north Italy. Published specialized botanical works on plants named after saints and on Absynthium nomenclature. Major work Historia plantarum universalis (1650–1651) described 5,226 plants. Also wrote on mineral waters, insect swarms, and fossil collections.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Established medical practice at Lyons in 1563. Appointed professor of rhetoric at Basel in 1570. Became physician to Duke Frederick of Württemberg in 1571 and was appointed archiater. Instrumental in establishing the College of Medical Practitioners in Montbéliard in 1575, which provided free medical services to the poor.
Patronage_Notes: Patronized by Duke Frederick of Württemberg, an enlightened and sympathetic patron who ruled the dual principality of Württemberg–Montbéliard. Frederick supported Bauhin's botanical gardens and archaeological collections.

Father_Notes: Guillaume Baumé ran two inns in Senlis; the family appears to have been fairly well-to-do.
Education_Institution: Not Specified; C. J. Geoffroy's dispensary
Education_Notes: Apprenticed to a pharmacist in Compiègne around 1743; by 1745 was working in C. J. Geoffroy's dispensary in Paris, where he developed his interests in theoretical chemistry and pharmacy. Became maître apothicaire in 1752.
Education_Locations: Compiègne, Unknown, France, 1743, 1745; Paris, Unknown, France, 1745, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered large-scale chemical manufacturing in France, particularly sal ammoniac production from 1767. Designed the areometer with calibrated scale (1768), a significant advance in laboratory instrumentation. Conducted experimental chemistry courses with Macquer from 1757 for sixteen years. Published extensively on chemistry and pharmacy; resisted phlogiston theory's replacement until his death.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Opened his own dispensary in Paris in 1753, which supplied drugs in bulk to pharmacies and hospitals over a wide area and manufactured chemicals at large scale. Designed and supplied laboratory and industrial apparatus. Conducted paid chemistry courses with Macquer. Elected to the Académie des Sciences in 1772 (adjoint-chimiste), becoming associé in 1778 and pensionnaire in 1785; lost his pension during the Revolution but received compensation in 1795 and obtained a place at the Institut de France in 1796.
Instruments_Notes: Designed the areometer in 1768 with a calibrated scale fixed at two points (density of distilled water and a salt solution of known concentration), enabling properly calibrated instruments to be produced. Won first prize in 1777 for an essay on furnaces, alembics, and distillation apparatus.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences; Institut de France
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected adjoint-chimiste to the Académie des Sciences on 25 December 1772; became associé in 1778 and pensionnaire in 1785. After the Revolution, obtained a place as associé non résidant at the Institut de France with minimal privileges.

Father_Notes: Father was solicitor-general at the High Court of Justice in Brussels.
Education_Notes: Attended the Latin School of Brussels; studied classical literature and natural sciences at Utrecht, graduating in classical literature (1843) and natural sciences (1844).
Education_Locations: Utrecht, Unknown, Netherlands, Unknown, 1843
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Developed quantitative methods for determining oxygen in organic substances (1853 onwards); analyzed drinking water, milk, and alcohol strength; studied meteorites and their composition; published on diamonds, marine organisms, and meteorological phenomena.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of physics and chemistry at the Royal Athenaeum in Maastricht (1845–1847); professor of chemistry at the Athenaeum Illustre in Amsterdam (1848–1865); perpetual secretary of the Dutch Society in Haarlem from 1865 until his death.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Dutch Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Perpetual secretary of the Dutch Society in Haarlem from 1865 until his death; edited the Archives néerlandaises des sciences exactes et naturelles.

Father_Notes: Father was a lithographer and merchant.
Education_Institution: University of Bonn; University of Göttingen
Education_Notes: Studied chemistry under Kekulé at Bonn, earning his degree in 1869 with a dissertation on the reduction of nitrobenzene. Pursued further study at Göttingen for one year.
Education_Locations: Bonn, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1869; Göttingen, Unknown, Germany, 1869, 1870
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Trained as a chemist but became primarily a mineralogist and crystallographer. Early work on atomic weights and periodic table arrangement; later focused on etch figures on crystal faces as a method for determining crystal symmetry, sulfosalt mineralogy, and comparative crystal morphology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held three brief teaching posts after his studies; taught chemistry at the agricultural school of Lüdinghausen, Westphalia, from 1873 to 1896; appointed first professor of mineralogy at the University of Fribourg in 1896, where he also taught inorganic chemistry for his first decade.

Education_Notes: Early education at Collège de Troyes; apprenticed to pharmacist Faciot in Rheims; studied in Paris from 1749 under P. de Chamousset and G. F. Rouelle.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted systematic analyses of French mineral waters; made quantitative observations on mercury precipitates and calcination, challenging phlogiston theory; analyzed minerals and investigated arsenic content in commercial tin.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Chief pharmacist on army expedition (1755); apothicaire-major des camps et armées du roi (1763–1793); pharmacien inspecteur to the Conseil de Santé (from 1793); member of the Institut de France (from 1795).
Patronage_Notes: Commissioned by the government in 1753 to analyze mineral waters of France; commissioned by Paris College of Pharmacy in 1781 to report on arsenic in tin.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Institut de France
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected member when the Institut de France was founded in 1795; never elected to the Academy.

Education_Notes: Enrolled at Ingolstadt University as a student of philosophy on 19 October 1592; later moved to Augsburg. No degree is recorded.
Education_Locations: Ingolstadt, Unknown, Germany, 1592, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Established the modern nomenclature of naked-eye stars by assigning Greek and Latin letters to stars within constellations. Published the Uranometria (1603), a comprehensive star catalogue with copper-plate engravings that became the standard reference for stellar identification and remains in use.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced as a lawyer; appointed legal adviser to the city council of Augsburg on 13 December 1612 at an annual salary of 500 gulden. Received an honorarium of 150 gulden from the city council in 1603 for dedicating the Uranometria.
Patronage_Notes: Dedicated the Uranometria to two leading citizens and the city council of Augsburg in 1603, which rewarded him with 150 gulden.

Father_Notes: Joshua Bayes, F.R.S., was a respected theologian of dissent and one of the first six ministers publicly ordained as Nonconformists.
Education_Notes: Privately educated; became his father's assistant at the presbytery in Holborn, London.
Religion_Notes: Member of the first secure generation of English religious Nonconformists; served as minister at the chapel in Tunbridge Wells.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Established foundations for statistical inference through his Essay on the Doctrine of Chances, introducing the converse problem of inferring probabilities of hypotheses from observed data. Also wrote a defence of Newton's calculus against Berkeley's logical critique.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as minister at Tunbridge Wells chapel; was a wealthy bachelor with independent means.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society of London
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected Fellow of the Royal Society in 1742.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Author of the Kanz al-tujjār, a mineralogical treatise on the knowledge of minerals. Possibly involved with mathematical manuscripts on clocks and timekeeping devices. First Arabic author to describe the use of the magnetic needle as a ship's compass, documenting its application in navigation.
Patronage_Notes: The Kanz al-tujjār was dedicated to either the Ayyübid ruler al-Malik al-Muẓaffar II or his son al-Malik al-Manṣūr II of Hamā, Syria, indicating court patronage.
Instruments_Notes: Documented the use of a magnetic needle floated on straw in water as a ship's compass, responding to a nearby magnet and orienting north-south when the magnet was removed. Also reported that seamen in the Indian Ocean used hollow iron fish as compasses.

Father_Notes: Sir William Maddock Bayliss, a distinguished physiologist and professor at University College, London. The family entertained generously and attracted many overseas physiologists.
Education_Institution: University College School; Trinity College, Cambridge; University of Pennsylvania
Education_Notes: Graduated from University College School, London. Entered Trinity College, Cambridge, graduating in physiology in 1922. Remained as Michael Foster Student and received Ph.D. in 1925 with thesis on tone in plain muscle. Worked under A. N. Richards at University of Pennsylvania in 1928–1929 on a Rockefeller Fellowship.
Education_Locations: London, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; Cambridge, Unknown, England, 1922, 1925; Philadelphia, Unknown, United States, 1928, 1929
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering work on blood pH using glass electrodes and electrometers; studied heart-lung preparations and kidney perfusion; investigated serotonins, water diuresis, and glomerular permeability. Major focus on blood rheology and viscosity, particularly the Fahraeus effect in capillaries. Developed pump-oxygenator perfusion techniques and various scientific instruments. Revised and expanded his father's Principles of General Physiology into two volumes.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Sharpey Scholar at University College, 1926–1929. Physiologist at Marine Biological Station, Plymouth, 1933. Lecturer in physiology at University of Edinburgh, 1934–1939. Reader in physiology at University College, 1945–1950. Joined Army Operational Research Group during World War II, directing research on antiaircraft gunnery and guided missile accuracy. Honorary research associate at University College from 1950 onward.
Instruments: Glass electrode; Electrometer; Micropipettes; Pump-oxygenator; Rotary pump; Flow recorder; Stimulation unit; Roller pump
Instruments_Notes: Developed and refined multiple instruments for physiological research, including pump-oxygenator perfusion techniques for kidneys, high-speed rotary pumps, and flow recorders. Pioneered use of glass electrodes and electrometers for blood pH measurement despite their high resistance. Designed mechanical models of the heart and circulation.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society of Edinburgh; Physiological Society; Society for Experimental Biology; Marine Biological Association
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Fellow of the Royal Society of Edinburgh. Member of the Physiological Society, Society for Experimental Biology, and Marine Biological Association.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by F. R. Winton. Books: Human Physiology (London, 1930; 3rd ed., 1948; 5th ed., 1962), written with F. R. Winton; Principles of General Physiology, 2 vols. (London, 1959–1960); Living Control Systems (London, 1966). Key papers on blood pH (1923, 1926), heart-lung metabolism (1928), water diuresis (1930), blood viscosity (1952, 1959, 1960, 1965), and rheology of blood (1952, 1962).

Father_Notes: Moses Bayliss was a manufacturer of galvanized goods and founder of the Wolverhampton firm Bayliss, Jones and Bayliss.
Education_Institution: University College London; Wadham College, University of Oxford
Education_Notes: Early education at a private school in Wolverhampton; apprenticed to a local general practitioner; studied at University College, London from 1880, gaining a B.Sc. with scholarship in zoology and physics in 1882; studied physiology and anatomy but failed anatomy at second M.B. examination and relinquished medical studies to concentrate on physiology; studied at Oxford as an undergraduate of Wadham College from 1885, taking a first-class degree in physiology in 1888.
Education_Locations: London, Unknown, England, 1880, 1882; Oxford, Unknown, England, 1885, 1888
Religion_Notes: Attended an Anglo-Catholic church but was largely tolerant in religious matters.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Devoted his life almost solely to physiology. Research spanned electrophysiology, vascular system, intestinal movements, pancreatic secretion, enzyme action, and colloids. Pioneered the discovery of hormones (secretin) and studied enzyme kinetics using physical chemistry methods. Contributed to understanding of wound shock and blood pressure regulation.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant at University College London from 1888, assistant professor from 1903, and professor of general physiology from 1912 onward. Maintained a private laboratory at his home in Hampstead. Well-off financially from family wealth.
Instruments: Thomson galvanometer; Capillary electrometer; Blood pressure apparatus
Instruments_Notes: Used Thomson galvanometer for electrophysiology studies; employed Lippmann's capillary electrometer for cardiac electrical measurements; developed a new form of optically registered blood pressure apparatus.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Physiological Society; Royal Society; Royal Danish Academy of Science; Royal Academy of Belgium; Société de Biologie of Paris
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to Physiological Society in 1890, served as secretary from 1900 to 1922 and treasurer from 1922 to 1924. Elected fellow of Royal Society in 1903, served on council from 1913 to 1915. Croonian lecturer jointly with Starling in 1904. Awarded Royal Medal in 1911 and Copley Medal in 1919. Received honorary degrees from Oxford, St. Andrews, and Aberdeen. Elected to Royal Danish Academy of Science, Royal Academy of Belgium, and Société de Biologie of Paris. Awarded Baly Medal of Royal College of Physicians in 1917. Editor of Physiological Abstracts from 1923 to 1924; joint editor of Biochemical Journal from 1913 to 1924.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Charles L. Evans. Original works include articles in Journal of Physiology, Archives des sciences biologiques, Biochemical Journal, Proceedings of the Royal Society, and British Medical Journal (1885–1920). Collaborations with J. R. Bradford, W. B. Cannon, Leonard Hill, and E. H. Starling. Books: The Nature of Enzyme Action (1908–1925); An Introduction to General Physiology (1919); Principles of General Physiology (1919–1924); The Physiology of Food and Economy in Diet (1917); Intravenous Injections in Wound Shock (1918); The Vasomotor System (1923); The Colloidal State in Its Medical and Physiological Aspects (1923); Interfacial Forces and Phenomena in Physiology (1923). Secondary: L. E. Bayliss, Perspectives in Biology and Medicine 4 (1961); C. Lovatt Evans, First Bayliss-Starling Memorial Lecture (1964); E. H. Starling, obituary in The Times (28 Aug. 1924).

Alt_Name: Abū Muḥammad ʿAbdllāh Ibn Aḥmad; Ibn al-Bayṭār al-Mālaqī
Education_Notes: Studied in Seville under Abu'l-ʿAbbās al-Nabātī, ʿAbdallāh ibn Ṣāliḥ, and Abu'l-Hajjāj, gathering herbs and studying the works of al-Ghāfiqī, al-Zahrāwī, al-Idrīsī, Dioscorides, and Galen.
Education_Locations: Seville, Unknown, Spain, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Systematized Arab pharmaceutical discoveries of the Middle Ages, adding 300–400 medicines to the ancient pharmacopoeia. Compiled the al-Jāmiʿ, an alphabetical enumeration of approximately 1,400 animal, vegetable, and mineral medicines with synonyms in Arabic, Persian, Berber, Greek, Latin, and Romance languages. Also authored al-Mughnī fi'l-adwiya al-mufrada on simple medicines for various illnesses, and a commentary on Dioscorides cataloguing 550 medicines.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Named chief herbalist by Ayyūbid Sultan al-Kāmil in Cairo, a post he retained under al-Ṣāliḥ. Traveled through Arabia, Palestine, Syria, and Iraq accompanied by disciples, conducting botanical and pharmaceutical research.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed chief herbalist by Sultan al-Kāmil and continued under Sultan al-Ṣāliḥ, to whom his work al-Mughnī was dedicated.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by J. Vernet. Original works: al-Jāmiʿ li-mufradāt al-adwiya wa'l-aghdhiya (German trans. by J. Father_Notes: Lionel John Beale (1796–1871) was a prominent London surgeon and medical author.
Education_Institution: King's College School; University of London, King's College Medical Department; University of Oxford
Education_Notes: Attended Highgate private school, then King's College School from 1840 to 1844, during which he was apprenticed to apothecary-surgeon Joseph Ross. Entered medical department of King's College, University of London in 1845; matriculated with honors in chemistry and zoology in 1847. Spent two years at Oxford as assistant to Henry Acland in the Anatomical Museum. Licensed by the Society of Apothecaries in 1849; graduated M.B. from University of London in 1851.
Education_Locations: London, Unknown, England, 1840, 1844; London, Unknown, England, 1845, 1847; Oxford, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in teaching the use of the microscope in pathological anatomy. Conducted histological studies on the structure of simple tissues and the nature of protoplasm. Developed vital staining techniques and proposed a unique terminology distinguishing 'germinal matter' (protoplasm) from 'formed matter.' Engaged in extended controversies over nerve endings and disease germs. Prolific author of practical laboratory manuals on microscopy.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as resident physician at King's College Hospital (1850–1851). Established a private laboratory in Carey Street in 1852 where he taught microscopy. Held successive professorships at King's College: professor of physiology and general and morbid anatomy (1853–1869), professor of pathological anatomy (1869–1876), and professor of the principles and practice of medicine (1876–1896). Retired in 1896 as professor emeritus and honorary consulting physician.
Instruments_Notes: Pioneered practical teaching of microscope use in pathological anatomy and authored foundational laboratory manuals on microscopy. Developed 'Beale's solution,' a carmine-in-ammonia histological stain.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; Royal College of Physicians; Microscopical Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1857 and delivered the Croonian lecture in 1865. Elected member of the Royal College of Physicians in 1856 and fellow in 1859; received the Baly Medal in 1871 and served as Lumleian lecturer in 1875. Served as president of the Microscopical Society from 1879 to 1880.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Gerald L. Geison. Father_Notes: May have been the son of Jean Beaugrand, author of calligraphy treatises, who taught calligraphy to Louis XIII.
Education_Notes: Studied under Viète. No formal degree is recorded.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Mathematician active in the 1630s; published Viète's In artem analyticam isagoge with scholia and mathematical compendium (1631); authored Géostatique (1636), proposing that weight varies with distance from center of gravity; engaged in polemical exchanges over priority and method with Desargues and Descartes; corresponded with Fermat, Mersenne, Castelli, and Cavalieri.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Mathematician to Gaston of Orléans from 1630; assumed the functions of secrétaire du roi in 1635 under Chancellor Pierre Séguier.
Patronage_Notes: Served as mathematician to Gaston of Orléans; held office under Chancellor Séguier.

Father_Notes: A farmer whose occupation Beaumont chose not to follow.
Education_Notes: Self-educated in medicine through borrowed medical books and apprenticeship. Apprenticed to Dr. Benjamin Chandler in St. Albans, Vermont, for two years; received a license to practice from the Medical Society of Vermont in June 1812. No formal degree is recorded.
Education_Locations: St. Albans, Unknown, United States, 1810, 1812
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in gastric physiology through systematic experimental investigation of digestion in the human stomach via gastric fistula. Demonstrated digestion as a chemical process, identified the role of gastric juice and free hydrochloric acid, and established foundations for practical dietetics and understanding of gastric pathology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as acting surgeon's mate in the U.S. Army (1812–1815), then as post surgeon at Fort Mackinac and other army posts (1820–1839). Practiced medicine as a general practitioner in Plattsburg (1815–1820) and in St. Louis (1839–1853).
Patronage_Notes: Commissioned as post surgeon in the U.S. Army, which provided his position and access to his experimental subject.
Instruments_Notes: Introduced a thermometer into the stomach to observe its movements and confirm that gastric contractions affected the instrument as they did food.

Father_Notes: Odoardo Beccari was a learned naturalist who explored the interior regions of Borneo.
Education_Notes: Studied in Florence; received M.D. in 1907; obtained teaching diploma in human anatomy in 1911.
Education_Locations: Florence, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, 1907
Scientific_Disciplines: Anatomy; Comparative Anatomy; Neurology; Cytology; Embryology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering work in comparative anatomy of vertebrates; major contributions to neuroanatomy, particularly the rhombencephalon and Mauthner fibers; systematic cytological studies of germ cell genesis and sex differentiation in amphibians; descriptive anatomy of the rhinencephalon in humans.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Substitute teacher of anatomy at Florence until 1915; director of the Institute of Human Anatomy at Catania University from 1921; director of the Institute of Comparative Anatomy at the University of Florence from 1925 until his seventieth year; presided over the Faculty of Natural and Physical Sciences at the University of Florence from October 1944 until his death.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Italian Society of Anatomy; Italian Society of Experimental Biology; National Academy of the Lincei
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Secretary of the Italian Society of Anatomy from 1929; associate founder of the Italian Society of Experimental Biology; member of the National Academy of the Lincei.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Pietro Franceschini. Books include Elementi di tecnica microscopica (Milan, 1915, 1927, 1940); La inversione sperimentale del sesso nei vertebrati (Pavia, 1930); Nevrologia comparata anatomo-funzionale dei vertebrati e dell'uomo (Florence, 1943); Genetica (Florence, 1945); Il problema del neurone, 2 vols. (Florence, 1945–1947); I problemi biologici del sesso (Rome, 1950); Anatomia comparata dei vertebrati, 2 vols. (Florence, 1951–1955). Bibliographical index of anatomical publications of the Institute of Human Anatomy at Florence for 1891–1921 in Archivio italiano di anatomia e di embriologia, 18 (1922), Supp. Numerous articles in Archivio italiano di anatomia e di embriologia, Monitore zoologico italiano, Lo sperimentale, Archivio di fisiologia, and Archivio zoologico italiano, 1906–1948.
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Pietro Franceschini.

Education_Notes: Entered novitiate with the Piarists in 1732; studied at Rome and Narni; began teaching career in 1737 at various locations including Narni, Urbino, Palermo, and Rome before his appointment to Turin in 1748. No university degree is named.
Education_Locations: Rome, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown; Narni, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Member of the Piarists (Clerks Regular of the Pious Schools), a Catholic teaching order; took the religious name Giambatista upon joining.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in experimental electricity and the study of atmospheric electricity; conducted systematic investigations of electrical phenomena, lightning, and thunderstorms; designed electrical apparatus including the electrical thermometer; contributed to understanding of insulators, condensers, and electrical atmospheres; work on atmospheric electricity influenced later scientists including Volta.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held the chair of physics at the University of Turin from 1748 for over twenty years; member of the Piarist teaching order.
Patronage_Notes: Marchese G. Morozzo recommended his appointment to Turin and suggested the study of electricity as a weapon against Cartesian natural philosophy; Franklin's letters of praise resulted in increased financial support for his work.
Instruments_Notes: Designed and constructed the electrical thermometer, an invention often wrongly attributed to Ebenezer Kinnersley; developed parallel plate condensers using insulators other than glass and attempted to estimate their relative powers.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by John L. Heilbron. Original works: Dell'elettricismo artificiale e naturale (Turin, 1753); Lettere al Beccari (Bologna, 1758); Electricitas vindex (Turin, 1769); Elettricismo artificiale (Turin, 1772; English version London, 1776); Dell'elettricità terrestre atmosferica a cielo sereno (Turin, 1775). Secondary: F. A. Eandi, Memorie istoriche intorno gli studi del padre Giambatista Beccaria (Turin, 1783); A. Pace, Dizionario biografico degli italiani, VII (Rome, 1965); Joseph Priestley, The History and Present State of Electricity, 3rd ed. (London, 1775); M. Gliozzi, Archeion, 17 (1933); C. W. Oseen, Johan Carl Wilcke experimental-fysiker (Uppsala, 1939); A. Pace, Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society, 97 (1952).
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by John L. Heilbron.

Father_Notes: Protestant pastor who died when Becher was eight years old.
Education_Notes: Largely self-educated; recalled only one teacher, De bus, rector of the Speyer Retscher-Gymnasium. Began Wanderjahren at age thirteen, traveling through Sweden, Holland, Germany, and Italy. Received M.D. from University of Mainz on 16 November 1661.
Education_Locations: Mainz, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1661
Religion_Notes: Converted to Roman Catholicism by 1657 while at Mainz.
Scientific_Disciplines: Chemistry; Alchemy; Iatrochemistry; Medicine; Natural Philosophy; Economics
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Earliest dated work (1654) dealt with alchemy. Published Naturkündigung der Metallen (1661) and established himself as an iatrochemist. Major work Physica subterranea (1669) presents theoretical framework combining Paracelsian and Helmontian chemistry with original theory of three earths (terra vitrescibilis, terra pinguis, terra fluida). Developed concept of terra pinguis as combustible earth, precursor to phlogiston theory. Also wrote on fermentation, metallurgical transmutation, and spontaneous generation. Influenced Georg Ernst Stahl's development of phlogiston theory.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed professor of medicine at Mainz (1663) and physician to the elector. Named Hofmedicus und Mathematicus to Ferdinand Maria, elector of Bavaria (1664). Served as imperial commercial counsellor to Emperor Leopold I in Vienna (1666). Built and organized imperial arts and crafts center including glassworks, textile facilities, and chemistry laboratory. Organized Eastern Trading Company and proposed colonial settlements.
Patronage_Notes: Served Ferdinand Maria, elector of Bavaria, as Hofmedicus und Mathematicus. Held position as imperial commercial counsellor under Emperor Leopold I.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Unsuccessfully sought membership in the Royal Society while in England; submitted a book on clock design in 1680 but was not elected.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Allen G. Debus. Original works: Naturkündigung der Metallen (Frankfurt, 1661); Oedipus chimicus (Frankfurt, 1664); Parnassus medicinalis illustratis (Ulm, 1662–1663); Politischer Discurs (Frankfurt, 1668); Physica subterranea (Frankfurt, 1669; supplements 1671, 1675, 1680); Psychosophia (Güstrow, 1673); Tripus Hermeticus fatidicus (Frankfurt, 1689); Chymischer Glückshafen (Frankfurt, 1682). Secondary: Herbert Hassinger, Johann Joachim Becher 1635–1682 (Vienna, 1951); J. R. Partington, A History of Chemistry, II (London, 1961); Hermann Kopp, Geschichte der Chemie and Die Alchemie (1869–1886); Partington and McKie, Historical Studies on the Phlogiston Theory, Annals of Science 2–4 (1937–1939).
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Allen G. Debus.

Father_Notes: Originally a bookseller in Prague; became a railway employee at Pilsen in 1866 and later at Vienna.
Education_Notes: Attended several schools before enrolling at the University of Vienna in 1874, where he studied under geologist Gustav Tschermak. Became Tschermak's assistant in 1878. No formal degree is named in the source.
Education_Locations: Vienna, Unknown, Austria, 1874, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering work on metamorphic rocks and their classification. Developed the Becke line method (1893) for determining relative refraction of light in minerals under the microscope. Introduced the Becke volume rule (1896) relating pressure to mineral formation. Classified plutonic and volcanic rocks by chemical composition (Atlantic and Pacific groups, 1903). Extensive research on crystalline schists, metamorphic facies, and regressive metamorphism. Introduced terminology for metamorphic textures (crystalloblastic, granoblastic, porphyroblastic, etc.) and developed graphic methods for rock analysis.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Associate professor (1882) and later full professor of mineralogy at the University of Czernowitz (1882–1890); professor at the University of Prague (1890–1898); professor at the University of Vienna (1898–1927). Director of the Mineralogical Institute of the University of Vienna (1906–1927). Editor of Mineralogische und petrographische Mitteilungen from 1899 onward.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Academy of Sciences (Vienna); Geological Society of London
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Appointed secretary-general of the Viennese Academy of Sciences in 1911. Received the Wollaston Medal of the Geological Society of London in 1929. Rector of the University of Vienna immediately after World War I.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Hans Baumgärtel. Original works include 'Krystalline Schiefer des niederösterreichischen Waldviertels' (1882); 'Beziehungen zwischen Dynamometamorphose und Molekularcolumen,' Neues Jahrbuch für Mineralogie, II (1896); 'Fortschritte auf dem Gebiete der Metamorphose,' Fortschritte der Mineralogie (1911, 1916); Das Wachstum und der Bau der Kristalle (1918); 'Struktur and Klüftung,' Fortschritte der Mineralogie (1924); 'Vorschläge zur Systematik und Nomenklatur der 32 Symmetrie-klassen,' Fortschritte der Mineralogie (1927). Numerous articles in Mineralogische und petrographische Mitteilungen (1883–1928). Secondary: A. Himmelbauer, obituary in Mineralogische und petrographische Mitteilungen, 42 (1932); obituary in Verhandlungen der Geologischen Bundesanstalt Wien (1931); Walther Fischer, Neue deutsche Biographie, 1 (1953).
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Hans Baumgärtel.

Education_Institution: Harvard University; University of Heidelberg; Royal Academy of Mines
Education_Notes: Studied at Harvard University; earned advanced degrees in chemistry and mathematics at the University of Heidelberg and the Royal Academy of Mines in Berlin.
Education_Locations: Cambridge, Unknown, United States, Unknown, Unknown; Heidelberg, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Berlin, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted detailed studies of mining districts and Pacific Coast ranges; published monographs on the Comstock Lode and Washoe District; developed theoretical papers on geophysical problems including Earth's rigidity and rock deformation; maintained that subsidence phenomena resulted from the Earth being solid throughout.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Instructor of mining and metallurgy at University of California, Berkeley (1874–1879); employed by the U.S. Geological Survey; director of the Carnegie Geophysical Laboratory.
Patronage_Notes: Worked for the U.S. Geological Survey under Clarence King; instrumental in establishing the Carnegie Geophysical Laboratory and served as its director.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: National Academy of Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Member of the National Academy of Sciences; biographical memoir published in the Academy's Memoirs.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Mathab. Kendall. Becker's publications include 'Reconnaissance of San Francisco, Eureka and Bodie Districts Nevada,' U.S. Geological Survey First Annual Report (1880); 'A Summary of the Geology of the Comstock Lode and Washoe District,' U.S. Geological Survey Second Annual Report (1880–1881); Geology of the Comstock Lode and Washoe District, U.S. Geological Survey Monographs III (1882); 'The Relation of Mineral Belts of the Pacific Slope to the Great Upheavals,' American Journal of Science 28 (1884); 'An Elementary Proof of the Earth's Rigidity,' American Journal of Science 39 (1890); 'The Finite Elastic Stress-Strain Function,' American Journal of Science 46 (1893); 'Finite Homogeneous Strain, Flow and Rupture of Rocks,' Bulletin of the Geological Society of America 4 (1896); 'The Witwatersrand and the Revolt of the Uitlanders,' National Geographic Magazine 7 (1896). Secondary: George P. Merrill, 'Biographical Memoir of George Ferdinand Becker,' Memoirs of the National Academy of Sciences 21 (1926).

Father_Notes: Johannes Friedrich Wilhelm Beckmann established a dye and emery works in Solingen and independently discovered Paris green in 1814.
Education_Institution: Not Specified; University of Leipzig; Technische Hochschule; University of Leipzig
Education_Notes: One year of laboratory work with Remigius Fresenius in Wiesbaden; entered University of Leipzig in 1875 and completed studies in 1878 under Hermann Kolbe and Ernest S. C. Meyer; briefly studied with Kolbe and Johannes Wislicenus at Leipzig in 1883, and with Wilhelm Ostwald after 1887. No degree is named.
Education_Locations: Wiesbaden, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Leipzig, Unknown, Germany, 1875, 1878; Brunswick, Unknown, Germany, 1878, 1883; Leipzig, Unknown, Germany, 1883, 1887
Scientific_Disciplines: Chemistry; Organic Chemistry; Physical Chemistry; Analytical Chemistry
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Developed the Beckmann transformation (1886), converting ketoximes into amides; investigated isomerism of oximes and benzoldoxime, contributing to understanding of nitrogen valence; designed the Beckmann thermometer for molecular weight determination via freezing-point depression and boiling-point elevation; identified SCI₄ and investigated furfurol properties.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant to toxicologist Robert Otto at Technische Hochschule Brunswick (1878–1883); extraordinary professor at Giessen (1891); ordinary professor at Erlangen (1892–1897); organized applied chemistry laboratory at University of Leipzig (1897–1912); director of Kaiser Wilhelm Institute of Applied and Pharmaceutical Chemistry from 1912 until his death.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed director of the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute of Applied and Pharmaceutical Chemistry, a state-founded research institution, in 1912.
Instruments_Notes: Developed a thermometer with variable mercury content in the bulb, allowing adjustment of the measurement range; used for determining molecular weight through freezing-point depression and boiling-point elevation of solutions.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Ruth Anne Gienapp. Original works include "Zur Kenntnis der Isonitrosoverbindungen," Berichte der Deutschen chemischen Gesellschaft, 19–21 (1886–1888); "Ueber die Methode der Molekulargewichtsbestimmung durch Gefrierpunktserniedrigung," Zeitschrift für physikalische Chemie, 2–3 (1888–1889); "Zur Isomerie der Oximidoverbindungen," Berichte der Deutschen chemischen Gesellschaft, 22 (1889); "Untersuchungen in der Campherreihe," Annalen der Chemie, 250 (1889); Das Laboratorium für angewandte Chemie der Universität Leipzig (Leipzig, 1908); "Ueber die Verbindung des Schwefels mit Chlor," Zeitschrift für physikalische Chemie, 55, 61 (1923, 1928). Secondary: G. Lockemann, Ernst Beckmann, Sein Leben und Werken (Berlin, 1927); O. Ostwald, "Ernst Beckmann's Anfänge als Physico-Chemiker," Zeitschrift für angewandte Chemie, 26 (1923); C. Paal, "Nachruf auf Ernest Otto Beckmann," Bericht über die Verhandlungen der Sächsischen Akademie der Wissenschaften zu Leipzig, 76 (1924); W. Schenk, "Gedächtnisrede," Sitzungsberichte der Deutschen Akademie der Wissenschaften zu Berlin, 104 (1924); Alfred Stock, "Forschungsinstitut," Zeitschrift für angewandte Chemie, 26 (1923).
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Ruth Anne Gienapp.

Father_Notes: Director of taxation and custodian of postal services; died in 1745 when Johann was six years old.
Education_Institution: Gymnasium at Stade; University of Göttingen
Education_Notes: Enrolled at Gymnasium in Stade in 1754; entered University of Göttingen in 1759 where he initially studied theology but turned to mathematics, natural sciences, public finance, administration, and philology. Studied with Linnaeus in Sweden in 1765–1766.
Education_Locations: Stade, Unknown, Germany, 1754, Unknown; Göttingen, Unknown, Germany, 1759, 1762
Religion_Notes: Mother was daughter of a Protestant parson; taught at St. Peter's Gymnasium, a Lutheran school in St. Petersburg.
Scientific_Disciplines: Natural History; Chemistry; Physics; Mathematics; Botany; Mineralogy; Geology; Engineering; Technology; Agriculture; History
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Founded agricultural science as an independent discipline with his 1769 textbook, establishing that practical agriculture required scientific foundations. Pioneered technology as a systematic science, coining the term 'techology' by 1769 and publishing the first advanced textbook in 1777. Conducted meteorological observations and became the first reliable historian of inventions with his multi-volume work beginning in 1782. Integrated natural history, chemistry, physics, and mathematics into agricultural and technological study.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught at St. Peter's Gymnasium in St. Petersburg (1763–1765). Appointed extraordinary professor of philosophy at Göttingen in 1766; ordinary professorship of economic sciences established for him in 1770, which he held until his death. Lectured on mineralogy, agriculture, technology, materials science, commerce, and public administration.
Patronage_Notes: His professorship of economic sciences was established by the university, likely with state support, to accommodate his growing focus on applied sciences and public economy. His technological textbook was addressed to governmental economic officials.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Friedrich Klemm. Original works include De historia naturali veterum libellus I (1766); Grundsätze der teutschen Landwirthschaft (1769); Anleitung zur Technologie (1777); Beyträge zur Geschichte der Erfindungen, 5 vols. (1782–1805); Lexicon botanicum (1801); Litteratur der älteren Reisebeschreibungen, 2 vols. (1808–1810). Secondary: W. Exner, Johann Beckmann, Begründer der technologischen Wissenschaft (Vienna, 1878); G. Grundke, 'Johann Beckmann als Begründer der Technologie in Deutschland,' Wissenschaftliche Zeitschrift der Karl-Marx-Universität, Leipzig (1954/1955); H. J. Herpel, Entwicklung des landwirtschaftlichen Studiums an der Universität Göttingen (1932); C. G. Heyne, 'Memoria Jo. Beckmann,' Commentationes Societatis Regiae Scientiarum Gottingensis (1808–1811).
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Friedrich Klemm.

Father_Notes: Antoine-César Becquerel, experimental physicist and professor at the Muséum d'Histoire Naturelle; devised the electrostatic balance used in his son's electrical measurements.
Education_Notes: Admitted at age eighteen to both the École Polytechnique and the École Normale Supérieure but declined both to assist his father. Received Doctor of Science degree from the University of Paris in 1840.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1840
Scientific_Disciplines: Physics; Electricity; Magnetism; Optics; Chemistry; Spectroscopy
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Measured electrical current properties and investigated their generation. Demonstrated Joule's law applied to liquids; rectified Faraday's law of electrochemical decomposition; discovered electrical current from metallic conductor displacement in liquid. Investigated diamagnetism and proposed an Archimedean law of magnetic action. Pioneered luminescence research, discovering phosphoroscope and distinguishing phosphorescence from fluorescence. Revealed Fraunhofer lines in ultraviolet spectrum photographs.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant at the University of Paris; professor of physics at Institut Agronomique de Versailles; appointed to chair of physics at Conservatoire des Arts et Métiers in December 1852; taught chemistry at Société Chimique de Paris from 1860 to 1863; served as aide-naturaliste at the Muséum d'Histoire Naturelle before succeeding his father as director in 1878.
Instruments_Notes: Used his father's electrostatic balance to measure electromotive force of voltaic piles. Constructed the actinometer to measure light intensity via photochemical electrical currents and determine temperatures of hot bodies. Invented the phosphoroscope, a rotating-disk apparatus allowing observation of phosphorescent substances in darkness and measurement of phosphorescence duration; attached a prism to examine spectra of luminescent bodies.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Académie des Sciences in 1863.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by J. B. Gough. Original works: Traité d'électricité et de magnétisme, leurs applications aux sciences physiques, aux arts et à l'industrie, 3 vols. (Paris, 1855–1856, with Antoine-César Becquerel); Recherches sur les divers effets lumineux qui resultent de l'action de la lumière sur les corps (Paris, 1859); La lumière, ses causes et ses effets, 2 vols. (Paris, 1867–1868). Secondary: Henri Becquerel, 'La chaire de physique du Muséum,' Revue scientifique 49, no. 22 (28 May 1892), 673–678; Jules Violle, 'L'oeuvre scientifique de M. Edmond Becquerel,' ibid., no. 12 (19 March 1892), 353–360; E. N. Harvey, A History of Luminescence From the Earliest Times Until 1900 (Philadelphia, 1957), 207–219, 351–360.
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by J. B. Gough.

Father_Notes: Royal lieutenant at Châtillon-sur-Loing.
Education_Notes: Entered the École Polytechnique in 1806 and graduated; no degree is named in the source.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, 1806, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in electrochemistry and the relationship between electricity, heat, light, and chemical forces. Discovered piezoelectric effect in crystals; investigated thermoelectricity and transition temperatures. Developed voltaic cells and demonstrated that electricity is generated only through chemical reaction, temperature difference, or friction. Applied electrochemistry to mineral synthesis, particularly crystallization of sulfides. Work had industrial applications in silver-ore treatment and potassium chloride extraction.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Military career in the Corps of Engineers, promoted to captain in 1812; appointed sous inspecteur of the École Polytechnique in 1813; returned to active service in 1814; after 1815 devoted himself to science; became first occupant of the chair of physics at the Muséum d'Histoire Naturelle in 1838.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed to the chair of physics at the Muséum d'Histoire Naturelle when it was founded in 1838.
Instruments_Notes: Invented an electromagnetic balance and a differential galvanometer for his electrical investigations.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences; Royal Society of London
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Académie des Sciences in 1829; awarded the Copley Medal of the Royal Society of London in 1837 for his work on mineral synthesis through electrochemistry.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by David M. Knight. Original works: papers listed in Royal Society Catalogue of Scientific Papers, I (1867), 233–239; VII (1877), 118–121; IX (1891), 164–166. Analyse succinct des travaux de M. Becquerel (Paris, 1829). Traité expérimental de l'électricité et du magnétisme, et de leur rapports avec les phénomènes naturels, 7 vols. (Paris, 1834–1840). Traité de physique considérée dans ses rapports avec la chimie et les sciences naturelles, 2 vols. (Paris, 1842–1844). Élements d'électro-chimie appliquée aux sciences naturelles et aux arts (Paris, 1843; 1864; German trans. Erfurt, 1845; 1848; 1857). Résumé de l'histoire de l'électricité et du magnétisme, et des applications de ces sciences à la chimie, aux sciences naturelles et aux arts (Paris, 1858), with Alexandre Edmond Becquerel. Secondary: Obituaries in Comptes rendus de l'Académie des sciences, 86 (1878), 125–131. Abstracts of the Philosophical Transactions, 4 (1843), 22–23. T. Cooper, ed., Men of the Time, 9th ed. (London, 1875), p. 87.
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by David M. Knight.

Father_Notes: Alexandre-Edmond Becquerel was a renowned physicist, member of the Academy of Sciences, and professor of physics at the Museum of Natural History. The family was established in the inner circles of French science.
Education_Institution: Lycée Louis-le-Grand; École Polytechnique; École des Ponts et Chaussées
Education_Notes: Educated at the Lycée Louis-le-Grand. Attended the École Polytechnique (1872–1874) and the École des Ponts et Chaussées (1874–1877), where he received engineering training. Began teaching as répétiteur at the Polytechnique in 1876 while still in school.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, 1872, 1874; Paris, Unknown, France, 1874, 1877
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Early research focused on optical phenomena: rotation of plane-polarized light by magnetic fields (1875–1882), infrared spectra (1883), and light absorption in crystals (1886–1888). Discovered radioactivity in uranium in 1896, establishing that penetrating radiation was an inherent property of uranium. Identified electrons in radium radiation (1899–1900) and published evidence of radioactive transformation (1901). Shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with Pierre and Marie Curie.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held three chairs of physics in Paris: at the Museum of Natural History, the École Polytechnique, and the Conservatoire National des Arts et Métiers. Attained high rank as an engineer in the National Administration of Bridges and Highways (Ponts et Chaussées), becoming ingénieur de première classe (1889) and ingénieur en chef (1894).
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Academy of Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Academy of Sciences in 1889 after two preparatory nominations (1884, 1886). Became vice-president on 31 December 1906, serving during 1907, and succeeded to the presidency in 1908. Elected permanent secretary on 29 June 1908.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Alfred Romer. Original works: "Recherches sur une propriété de la matière. Activité radiante spontanée ou radioactivité de la matière," Mémoires de l'Académie des sciences, Paris, 46 (1903); approximately 150 papers in various journals, with radioactivity papers listed in Comptes rendus de l'Académie des sciences, Paris, 122–133 (1896–1901). Secondary literature: Albert Ranc, Henri Becquerel et la découverte de la radioactivité (Paris, 1946); G. Darboux et al., "Discours prononcés aux funérailles de M. Henri Becquerel," Comptes rendus, 147 (1908); Les Prix Nobel en 1903 (Stockholm, 1906); O. Lodge, "Becquerel Memorial Lecture," Journal of the Chemical Society, 101 (1912); L. Badash, "'Chance Favors the Prepared Mind': Henri Becquerel and the Discovery of Radioactivity," Archives internationales d'histoire des sciences, 18 (1965).
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Alfred Romer.

Education_Notes: Received licentiate in natural sciences from the Faculty of Sciences at Paris in 1903 and doctorate in 1907. Studied under Gaston Bonnier.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1903
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Investigated the physiological nature of plant seeds, protoplasm responses to freezing and dehydration, and suspended life in seeds and microorganisms. Demonstrated that living organisms could survive exposure to liquid hydrogen and liquid helium and be revived by warming and rehydration. Studied the effects of freezing on vegetable protoplasm and the role of synaeresis in cellular freezing.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Named assistant at the Faculty of Sciences at Paris in 1907. Member of the Faculty of Sciences at Nancy after World War I. Appointed professor of general botany at the University of Poitiers in 1927, where he remained until retirement.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Alan S. Kay. Becquerel's work appeared primarily in Comptes rendus de l'Académie des sciences, Paris, including papers on liquid air effects on seeds (1905), latent life of spores at low temperatures (1910), suspended life of seeds in vacuum (1925, 1929, 1930), latent life of moss spores (1932), anhydrobiosis of plant tubers (1932), revivification of desiccated seedlings (1932), role of synaeresis in cellular freezing (1939), and effects of cold on plant cells (1949). Also published in Travaux cryptogamiques (1931) and Actes du VIème Congrès International du Froid (1932). Obituary in Comptes rendus de l'Académie des sciences, Paris, 241 (1955), 137–140.
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Alan S. Kay.

Education_Institution: University College London; University of Edinburgh
Education_Notes: Initially intended for law but studied medicine instead. Attended University College, London and University of Edinburgh, receiving M.D. from Edinburgh in 1853 with thesis on the geography of phthisis. After initial medical practice, traveled to Vienna to complete medical training and toured Austria, Hungary, Italy, and France studying medicine and physical anthropology.
Education_Locations: London, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; Edinburgh, Unknown, Scotland, Unknown, 1853
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in descriptive physical anthropology, measuring and analyzing hair color, skin color, height, cephalic index, and other physical variations throughout the British Isles and Europe. Integrated physical anthropological observations with linguistic and cultural history to explain the movements and origins of European populations.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as house physician at Royal Edinburgh Infirmary; medical staff during Crimean War at Renkioi hospital; established medical practice in Clifton, Bristol from 1857 until retirement in 1891. Elected honorary professor of anthropology at University of Bristol in 1908.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; Ethnological Society; Anthropological Society; Royal Anthropological Institute
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of Royal Society in 1873. Founding member of Ethnological Society in 1857. President of Anthropological Society 1869–1870. President of Royal Anthropological Institute 1889–1891. Gave Huxley lecture in 1905 and received Huxley Medal.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Glyndaniel. Contributions to Scottish Ethnology (Edinburgh, 1853); The Races of Britain: A Contribution to the Anthropology of Western Europe (Bristol–London, 1885); Colour and Race, Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute, 35 (1905); Memories of Eighty Years (Bristol–London, 1910); The Anthropological History of Europe, Being the Rhind Lectures for 1912 (Paisley, 1912).
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Glyndaniel.

Father_Notes: A tanner who wished his son to follow the trade; the grandfather recognized the boy's abilities and insisted on professional training.
Education_Institution: Bridgnorth Grammar School; Pembroke College, Oxford; University of Edinburgh
Education_Notes: Attended Bridgnorth Grammar School, Shropshire; read medicine at Pembroke College, Oxford, where he also studied chemistry and modern languages. Spent three years in Edinburgh (1784–1787) and visited France, meeting Lavoisier.
Education_Locations: Bridgnorth, Shropshire, England, Unknown, Unknown; Oxford, Unknown, England, 1776, Unknown; Edinburgh, Unknown, Scotland, 1784, 1787
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Translated works on chemistry by Bergman, Scheele, and Spallanzani; adhered to Lavoisier's antiphlogistic chemistry. Investigated the use of gases in treating diseases and founded the Pneumatic Institution (1798) for gas therapy. Believed medical science must have a chemical basis. Adhered to the kinetic theory of heat.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Reader in chemistry at Oxford (1788–1792), attracting large audiences. Practiced medicine and founded the Pneumatic Institution at Clifton (1798), which became a clinic for preventive medicine advice.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Lunar Society of Birmingham
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Associated with the Lunar Society during its last years.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by David M. Knight. Education_Notes: Entered monastic education at age seven under Benedict Biscop at Wearmouth-Jarrow monastery. Spent his entire life in residence at the monastery, devoted to scriptural study, learning, teaching, and writing. Benefited from the monastery's exceptional resources, including a rich library and instruction from scholars brought from Rome and the Continent.
Education_Locations: Jarrow-on-Tyne, Unknown, England, 680, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Benedictine monk; devoted to scriptural exegesis and Christian theology throughout his life.
Scientific_Disciplines: Philosophy; Natural Philosophy; Mathematics; Astronomy; Chronology; Geography; Natural History; Grammar; Music
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Excelled in scriptural exegesis and composed didactic textbooks on notae (scribal work), grammar, and computus (timekeeping). First to record a perpetual 532-year Easter cycle based on the Metonic cycle; first historian to use the Christian era as an anchor date; formulated the tidal principle of establishment of port. Wrote on natural history, cosmology, versification, figurative language, and the calculation of time. His computus texts incorporated arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, music, and practical sciences for physicians, agriculturists, and mariners.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Monk and scholar at Wearmouth-Jarrow monastery throughout his life; devoted to teaching and writing within the monastic community.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by Benedict Biscop, founding abbot of Wearmouth and Jarrow, who provided exceptional educational resources and brought scholars from Rome and the Continent. Later supported by his master and abbot Ceolfrid.

Father_Notes: Owned a factory producing candles and water conduits; Isaac entered the factory as an apprentice after completing his studies.
Education_Institution: University of Leiden; Academy of Saumur; University of Caen
Education_Notes: Studied letters, philosophy, and theology in preparation for the Reformed Church ministry. Privately studied mathematics and nautical science in Amsterdam under the Brownist scholar Ainsworth. Received M.D. from Caen in 1618 but never practiced medicine.
Education_Locations: Leiden, Unknown, Netherlands, 1607, 1610; Saumur, Unknown, France, 1612, Unknown; Caen, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1618
Religion_Notes: Reformed Church; studied for the ministry and was influenced by Brownist scholar Ainsworth.
Scientific_Disciplines: Physics; Mechanics; Mathematics; Astronomy; Engineering; Hydraulics
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in applying mathematical methods to physics and mechanics. Formulated principle of inertia (1613), law of uniformly accelerated motion of falling bodies (1618), and law of water outflow velocity (1615). Conducted experiments on air pressure and volume (1626), magnetism, and elasticity. Rejected purely rationalistic approaches in favor of mechanistic explanations verified by experiment.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as conrector (assistant headmaster) of Latin schools in Veere (1618–1619), Utrecht (1619–1620), and Rotterdam before being appointed rector of the Latin school at Dordrecht in 1627, where enrollment grew to 600 students. Also operated a candle and water-conduit factory in Zierikzee and served as unsalaried adviser to Dordrecht burgomasters on water regulation.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed rector of Dordrecht Latin school by municipal authorities; established the first European meteorological station in 1628 with help of the magistrate. Hosted visits from major French philosophers including Descartes (1628, 1629), Gassendi (1629), and Mersenne (1630).
Instruments_Notes: Established the first meteorological station in Europe at Dordrecht in 1628, recording wind velocity and direction, rainfall, temperature, and making astronomical observations.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Collegium Mechanicum
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Founded the Collegium Mechanicum in Rotterdam, a society of craftsmen and scholars focused on scientific problems with technological applications.

Religion_Notes: Member of a cultivated Jewish family; his brother was the poet Michael Beer and his half-brother was the composer Jacob Meyer Beer (Meyerbeer).
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Amateur astronomer who conducted selenographical and solar-system studies with Johann Mädler between 1830 and 1840. Their collaborative work produced the first quadrant-divided lunar map (1836) and detailed micrometric measurements of lunar craters and mountains.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Banker by profession; supported astronomical research through ownership of a private observatory equipped with a Fraunhofer refractor.
Patronage_Notes: Patron and collaborator of Johann Mädler; provided the private observatory and instrumentation that enabled their joint selenographical work.
Instruments_Notes: Owned a 9.4-centimeter Fraunhofer refractor at his private observatory, used by Mädler for the observations underlying the celebrated 1836 lunar map.

Father_Notes: Charles Beevor was a fellow of the Royal College of Surgeons.
Education_Institution: Blackheath Proprietary School; University College, London
Education_Notes: Educated at Blackheath Proprietary School, London, and University College, London. Qualified as member of Royal College of Surgeons in 1878. From 1882 to 1883 studied in Austria, Germany, and France under Carl Weigert, Julius Cohnheim, Wilhelm Heinrich Erb, and others.
Education_Locations: London, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; London, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Clinical neurologist focused on accurate diagnosis of nervous system diseases. Conducted landmark research on cerebral cortical function and motor representation through electrical stimulation experiments with Victor Horsley (1883–1887). Studied muscle movements and their central representation. Investigated cerebral arterial distribution through injection experiments, publishing important findings on the five main cerebral arteries.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant physician to the National Hospital, Queen Square, London (1883) and to the Great Northern Central Hospital (1885), becoming full physician at each. Practiced clinical neurology and internal medicine.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal College of Surgeons; Royal College of Physicians of London
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Qualified as member of Royal College of Surgeons in 1878. Elected member of Royal College of Physicians in 1882 and fellow in 1888. Delivered Croonian Lectures before Royal College of Physicians in 1903.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Edwin Clarke. Education_Notes: Studied at the École Normale Supérieure from 1894 to 1897; placed first in the mathematics agrégation in 1897. No university degree is named.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, 1894, 1897
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Specialist in rational mechanics, nonholonomic systems, and percussion problems. Extended Carnot's theorem and Painlevé's paradox. Developed theory of gyrostatic compass and servomechanisms, with applications to automatic piloting of ships and aircraft. Studied elastic impact, friction effects, and vibration elimination.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught mechanics at the lycée in Brest (1899–1908) and at the École Navale (1908–1921). Held chair of mechanics at Montpellier (1921–1924) and Lille (1924–1929). Lectured in fluid mechanics at Paris (1929–1932) and was professor of physical and experimental mechanics and director of the mechanics laboratory. Also taught at the École des Beaux-Arts (1924–1930), École Supérieure d'Aéronautique (1930–1939), and École Polytechnique (from 1936). Organized training of radio electricians during World War I.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Académie des Sciences on 25 February 1946.

Education_Notes: Received a good classical education; possibly studied at Sedan before arriving in Paris.
Religion_Notes: Acknowledged the authority and censorship of the Paris Faculty of Medicine; omitted a Paracelsian quotation in the 1615 edition, possibly due to religious or institutional pressure.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of chemical medicine and public chemical instruction in Paris. Defined chemistry as the art of separating and recombining natural mixed bodies to produce medicines. Synthesized Galenic and Paracelsian approaches; credited with the first mention of acetone (called 'the burning spirit of Saturn'). Believed in transmutation and cited hermetic authorities.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Gave public lectures on chemical medicaments in Paris; earned 700 crowns by his skill as of 1613; served as almoner to Henry IV.
Patronage_Notes: Almoner to Henry IV (documented in the dedication signature of the 1608 edition). Benefited from the influence of royal physician Jean Ribit and Turquet de Mayerne, who enabled him to set up his laboratory and give public lectures.

Father_Notes: Grandson of René-Louis-Maurice Béguyer de Chancourtois, a noted artist and architect.
Education_Notes: Entered École Polytechnique in 1838 and École des Mines in 1840. At age twenty-three left to travel through Armenia, Turkestan, the Banat, and Hungary studying mountainous regions. Returned to École des Mines in 1848.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, 1838, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, 1840, 1843
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Specialized in descriptive geometry, subsurface topology, and stratigraphic geology. Developed the telluric screw, a precursor to the periodic table, classifying chemical elements based on their distribution in the Earth's crust and their equivalent weights. Studied mineral associations and geological distribution of mineral deposits. Advocated for improved cartographic methods and geological collections.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of descriptive geometry and subsurface topology at École des Mines from 1848 until his death; became professeur suppléant to Élie de Beaumont in 1852 and succeeded him as professor of geology in 1875. Named assistant director of the French Geological Survey by Élie de Beaumont. Appointed director general of mines in France in 1875.
Patronage_Notes: Protégé of Élie de Beaumont, head of the French Geological Survey. Invited by Prince Napoleon to participate in the voyage of the Reine Hortense to polar regions in 1856. Served as secretary of Prince Napoleon's Imperial Commission for the 1867 Universal Exposition and as chef de cabinet during Prince Napoleon's administration of Algeria and the African colonies.

Father_Notes: Family engaged in mercantile trade extending from Venice to Flanders; Behaim began in the textile business as a youth.
Education_Notes: Likely learned astronomical instrument use from Regiomontanus; influenced by Regiomontanus's Ephemerides (1475–1506). No formal degree recorded.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Participated in African coastal expedition (1485–1486) under Diogo Cão; possibly conducted latitude observations of the North Star using a quadrant. Member of King John II's Council of Mathematicians in Portugal. Designed and constructed the famous Nuremberg globe (1491–1493), a 51-cm sphere with 111 miniatures, 48 banners, and 15 coats of arms, depicting geography of 1,100 localities and representing an adaptation of nautical charts onto a sphere.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Engaged in textile business in Flanders and Lisbon from 1480; member of the Council of Mathematicians under King John II; entrusted with official missions for the Portuguese crown.
Patronage_Notes: Served King John II of Portugal as a member of the Council of Mathematicians and undertook official missions on behalf of the crown.
Instruments_Notes: Used a quadrant to measure latitude of the North Star during the 1485–1486 African expedition. Designed and constructed the celebrated Nuremberg globe (1491–1493) with the painter Glockenthon, a sphere covered with parchment and adorned with miniatures, banners, and coats of arms, representing world geography with equator and tropics marked.

Father_Notes: August Georg Behring, a teacher; family lived in simple circumstances; intended Emil for teaching or ministry, traditional family professions.
Education_Institution: Gymnasium of Hohenstein; Friedrich Wilhelms Institute
Education_Notes: Attended Gymnasium of Hohenstein in East Prussia from 1866. Received free medical education at Friedrich Wilhelms Institute in Berlin (1874–1878) in return for ten years of military service; received M.D. in 1878 and passed state board examinations in 1880.
Education_Locations: Hohenstein, Unknown, Germany, 1866, Unknown; Berlin, Unknown, Germany, 1874, 1878
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in serum therapy and antitoxin theory; discovered that immune blood serum contained substances that neutralized bacterial toxins; developed passive and active preventive vaccinations against diphtheria and tetanus; investigated disinfectants and their mechanisms; attempted tuberculosis vaccination research.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Military surgeon in Prussian Army (1880–1889); assistant at Charité Hospital Berlin (1880); cavalry regiment surgeon in Posen and Wohlau (1881–1883); assistant at Pharmacological Institute Bonn (1887–1888); assistant at Institute for Hygiene University of Berlin under Robert Koch (1889–1894); associate professor of hygiene at Halle (1894–1895); professor of hygiene at Marburg (1895–1917); also practiced as physician.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by Friedrich Althoff, powerful figure in Prussian Ministry for Education, who secured his Marburg professorship against faculty opposition. Backed financially from 1892 by Farbwerke Meister, Lucius and Brüning, a dye works in Höchst. Received Prussian title of Geheimrat (privy councillor) in 1895 and elevation to hereditary nobility in 1901.

Father_Notes: Friedrich Beilstein was a salesman and tailor from Lichtenberg near Darmstadt, related to Justus Liebig. He died during Konrad's career, prompting family difficulties that led Konrad to relocate to St. Petersburg.
Education_Institution: University of Heidelberg; University of Munich; University of Göttingen; University of Paris; University of Breslau
Education_Notes: Sent to Germany at age fifteen by his uncle Johannes Conrad Rutsch. Studied under leading chemists including Bunsen and Kekulé at Heidelberg, Liebig at Munich, and Wöhler at Göttingen. Received doctorate from Göttingen in 1858. Continued postdoctoral studies with Wurtz and Charles Friedel in Paris, and with Löwig in Breslau.
Education_Locations: Heidelberg, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Munich, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Göttingen, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1858; Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; Breslau, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Focused on organic chemistry, particularly structural formulas and the arrangement of atoms in compounds. Investigated isomerism, aromatic compounds, chlorination of benzene derivatives, and petroleum chemistry. Best known for the Handbuch der organischen Chemie, a comprehensive reference work that systematized organic chemistry.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Began teaching at Göttingen in 1860 and was appointed extraordinary professor in 1865. Moved to the Technical Institute of St. Petersburg in 1866, where he remained for the rest of his life.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Deutsche Chemische Gesellschaft; St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Member of the Deutsche Chemische Gesellschaft. Elected to the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences in 1881. Co-edited the Zeitschrift für Chemie with Hübner and Fitting from 1865 to 1871.

Education_Notes: Graduated from Kazan University in 1849. Completed master's thesis in 1853 and doctoral dissertation in 1865, both at Kharkov University.

Later focused on physical and inorganic chemistry, studying metal reduction by hydrogen and other metals, establishing an activity series of metals. Discovered alumino-thermal reduction of metals from oxides. Conducted extensive thermochemical research on heats of formation and hydration of metal oxides and halides.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Junior scientific assistant at Kharkov University from 1855; professor of chemistry from 1859 to 1886. Worked in Zinin's laboratory at the Academy of Medicine and Surgery in St. Petersburg early in career.

Education_Notes: Graduated from Vyatskaya Gymnasium before enrolling at the Medical and Surgical Academy of St. Petersburg in 1873. Graduated in 1878 and prepared for a teaching career in the clinic of I.P. Merzheevsky. Defended his M.D. dissertation in 1881 on the relation between body temperature and mental illness. Subsequently worked with leading European neurologists including Flechsig, Meinert, Charcot, Du Bois-Reymond, and Wundt.
Education_Locations: Sorali, Vyatskaya oblast, Russia, Unknown, Unknown; St. Petersburg, Unknown, Russia, 1873, 1878
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in neuroanatomy and neurophysiology of the central nervous system. Defined the pathways of posterior spinal rootlets, described Bekhterev cells and lateral column bundles, studied the reticular formation (1885), and established the taste center location in the brain cortex (1900). In nervous diseases, isolated diagnostic reflexes and symptoms, and described numerous conditions including Bekhterev's disease (numbness of the spine), apoplectic hemitonia, syphilitic dissipating sclerosis, and various forms of tic and ataxia. In his final years devoted himself to reflexology (objective psychology) and broader psychological research.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of psychiatry at Kazan University from 1885, where he organized the first laboratory for nervous system research. From 1893 to 1913 headed the department of nervous and psychic diseases at the Military Medical Academy in St. Petersburg.
Patronage_Notes: Held salaried academic positions at state institutions: Kazan University and the Military Medical Academy of St. Petersburg.

Father_Notes: Father was General T. M. Beliaev.
Education_Notes: Studied military engineering at the Mikhailovskoi Artilleriiskoi Akademii (St. Petersburg) from 1902 to 1905. Remained at the academy as tutor and later professor, but no degree is named.
Education_Locations: St. Petersburg, Unknown, Russia, 1902, 1905
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Specialized in metallurgical chemistry and the crystallographic structure of steel. Conducted foundational research on the Widmanstätten structure in steel and the history and metallurgy of Damascus steel, demonstrating how Oriental forging methods unknowingly produced iron-carbide coalescence.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of metallurgical chemistry at the Mikhailovskoi Artilleriiskoi Akademii from 1909 to 1914. After World War I, worked as an industrial consultant in England and later in Paris.
Patronage_Notes: Sent to England in 1915 by the Russian government in connection with munitions supply during World War I.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by C. S. Smith. Father_Notes: Jean-Baptiste Forest de Bélidor, a French officer of dragoons on duty in Spain at the time of Bernard's birth; died within five months of Bernard's birth.
Education_Notes: Received practical mathematical training through fieldwork on the meridian survey under Jacques Cassini and Philippe de La Hire (completed 1718). Appointed professor of mathematics at the artillery school at La Fère in the 1720s, where he authored textbooks and technical manuals.
Religion_Notes: The Duc d'Orléans discouraged him from taking holy orders, suggesting a Catholic upbringing; received the Order of Saint Louis.
Scientific_Disciplines: Mechanics; Engineering; Military Engineering; Ballistics; Hydraulics; Architecture
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in engineering mechanics and the application of mathematical principles to practical construction. Authored foundational treatises on fortifications, hydraulic engineering, and ballistics. His works systematized engineering practice and influenced generations of engineers including Carnot, Coulomb, Meusnier, Coriolis, Navier, and Poncelet.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of mathematics at the artillery school at La Fère; active military duty in Bavaria, Italy, and Belgium during the War of the Austrian Succession; held rank of brigadier in Paris.
Patronage_Notes: The Duc d'Orléans (regent) arranged his appointment as professor at La Fère and discouraged him from taking holy orders.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Academy of Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected associé libre of the Academy of Sciences in 1756; published two memoirs in the Mémoires de l'Académie Royale des Sciences (1756).
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Charles C. Gillispie. Original works: Nouveau cours de mathématique à l'usage de l'artillerie et du génie (Paris, 1725); La science des ingénieurs dans la conduite des travaux de fortification et d'architecture civile (Paris, 1729, ed. Navier 1813); Le bombardier françois (Paris, 1731); Architecture hydraulique (Paris, 1737–1739, ed. Navier 1819); two memoirs in Mémoires de l'Académie Royale des Sciences (1756).
