Father_Notes: Alexander Melville Bell was a teacher of elocution and inventor of Visible Speech, a written code for phonetic representation.
Education_Notes: No formal degree recorded. Early education in Scotland; family moved to Canada in 1870. Bell conducted experimental work in Boston and Washington.
Scientific_Disciplines: Technology; Instrumentation; Physics; Medicine; Natural History; Aeronautics
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Inventor of the telephone (patented 1876). Conducted experiments on hereditary deafness and longevity; developed a selective breeding program for sheep with increased nipples. Made suggestions on medical uses of electricity. Experimented with kites and organized the Aerial Experimental Association (1907), which investigated flight.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Wealth derived from telephone patent and licensing. Used fortune to support scientific research, establish the Volta Bureau, subsidize the journal Science, and finance the National Geographic Society.
Patronage_Notes: Provided financial support to S.P. Langley's research at the Smithsonian Institution and flight experiments. Subsidized the journal Science with his father-in-law G.G. Hubbard. Financed the Aerial Experimental Association through his wife.
Instruments_Notes: Invented the telephone, patented in 1876. Experimented extensively with kites in connection with aeronautical research.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: National Academy of Sciences; Smithsonian Institution; National Geographic Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 1883. Appointed regent of the Smithsonian Institution in 1898. Helped organize and finance the National Geographic Society, serving as its president from 1898 to 1903.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Bernard S. Finn. Original works: complete list in Osborne's article (see below); notebooks, letters, and documentary material at National Geographic Society, with microfilm copies at Library of Congress and Bell Telephone Company of Canada; court testimony in The Bell Telephone (Boston, 1908); apparatus at Smithsonian Institution. Father_Notes: Minister of the Church of England; died when Charles was five years old.
Education_Notes: Received basic education from his mother; tutored in art; attended Edinburgh High School for three years. Learned medicine from his older brother John Bell's private anatomy classes and from lectures at Edinburgh University. Admitted to the Royal College of Surgeons in 1799.
Education_Locations: Edinburgh, Unknown, Scotland, Unknown, Unknown; Edinburgh, Unknown, Scotland, Unknown, 1799
Religion_Notes: Son of a Church of England minister.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered experimental methods for determining functional anatomy of the nervous system by cutting and stimulating nerve divisions and observing behavioral changes in experimental animals. Demonstrated differing functions of spinal nerve roots. His techniques and observations influenced Johannes Müller's generalizations on sensory nervous function and the principle of specific nerve energies. Also published on the anatomical and physiological basis of facial expression.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Opened his own school of anatomy in London in 1804 and built up a surgical practice. Co-owner and principal lecturer at the Great Windmill Street School of Anatomy from 1812 to 1825. Instrumental in founding the Middlesex Hospital Medical School in 1828. Returned to Edinburgh University as professor of surgery in 1836.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal College of Surgeons; Royal Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Admitted to the Royal College of Surgeons in 1799. Published papers in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Peter Amacher. Essays on the Anatomy of Expression in Painting (London, 1806); Idea of a New Anatomy of the Brain (London, 1811); An exposition of the natural System of Nerves of the Human Body (London, 1824); The Nervous System of the Human Body (London, 1830); The Hand, Its Mechanism and Vital Endowments, as Evincing Design (London, 1833). Secondary: Gordon-Taylor and E. W. Walls, Sir Charles Bell, His Life and Times (London, 1958); J. M. D. Olmsted, François Magendie (New York, 1944).

Father_Notes: James Bell of a London commercial family.
Education_Institution: Stanford University; University of Washington; Columbia University
Education_Notes: Tutored before Bedford Modern School, where E. M. Langley inspired his interest in elliptic functions and number theory. Graduated Phi Beta Kappa from Stanford in two years. M.A. from University of Washington in 1908; Ph.D. from Columbia in 1912. Between degrees worked as ranch hand, mule skinner, surveyor, schoolteacher, and telephone company partner.
Education_Locations: Stanford, California, United States, Unknown, 1902; Seattle, Washington, United States, Unknown, 1908; New York, New York, United States, 1908, 1912
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Significant contributions to numerical functions, analytic number theory, multiply periodic functions, and Diophantine analysis. Arithmetical Paraphrases won the Bôcher Prize in 1921. Authored approximately 250 research papers and four learned mathematical books. Also wrote widely read popularizations including Men of Mathematics and The Development of Mathematics, which influenced professional mathematicians despite historical inaccuracies.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught at University of Washington from 1912, lectured at Chicago and Harvard, and held position at California Institute of Technology from 1926 until emeritus status in 1953. Prolific author of research papers, mathematical books, popularizations, and science fiction novels under the pseudonym John Taine.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Mathematical Association of America
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Active in organizations of research mathematicians, teachers, and authors. Served as president of the Mathematical Association of America from 1931 to 1933.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Kenneth O. May. Original works: An Arithmetical Theory of Certain Numerical Functions (University of Washington Publication no. 1, 1915); Arithmetical Paraphrases (Transactions of the American Mathematical Society, 1921); Algebraic Arithmetic (American Mathematical Society Colloquium Publication no. 7, 1927); Before the Dawn (Baltimore, 1934); Men of Mathematics (New York, 1937); The Development of Mathematics (New York, 1940; 2nd ed., 1945); Mathematics, Queen and Servant of Science (New York, 1951); The Last Problem (New York, 1961). Father_Notes: Father was Reverend Andrew Bell.
Education_Notes: Began work with the Canadian Geological Survey at age fifteen while in high school and college. Received civil engineering degree from McGill University in 1861 and won the Governor General's Gold Medal. Spent a year at Edinburgh. Obtained M.D., C.M. degree in 1878. Received honorary D.Sc. degrees from Queen's and Cambridge universities.
Education_Locations: Montreal, Quebec, Canada, Unknown, 1861; Edinburgh, Unknown, Scotland, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted thirty years of reconnaissance mapping and exploration from Lake Superior northward to the Arctic and from Saskatchewan to Hudson Bay's east shore. Mapped both shores of Hudson Bay and parts of the Nottaway, Churchill, and Nelson rivers. First to survey Great Slave, Nipigon, and Amadjuak lakes. Produced over thirty reports on geology of surveyed areas and more than 200 titles on geography, zoology, botany, resources, and Indian lore.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed professor of chemistry and natural history at Queen's University in 1863; resigned in 1867 to devote full time to the Canadian Geological Survey. Served as chief geologist and acting director of the Survey from 1901 until retirement in 1906. Also served as medical officer on government ships visiting Hudson Bay.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed to the Canadian Geological Survey as junior assistant at age fifteen and continued throughout his career, eventually serving as chief geologist and acting director.
Instruments: Compass; Sextant; Boat Log; Rochon Micrometer
Instruments_Notes: Used these instruments during his extensive canoe-based exploration and mapping work across northern Canada.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Geological Society of London; Royal Society of Canada; Geological Society of America; Royal Society of London; Royal Astronomical Society (Canada)
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Fellow of the Geological Society of London (1862), Royal Society of Canada (1882), Geological Society of America (1889), and Royal Society of London (1897). Also member of the Royal Astronomical Society (Canada). Received the Imperial Science Order (1903), King's Gold Medal from the Royal Geographic Society (1906), and Cullum Gold Medal from the American Geographic Society (1906).

Education_Institution: Merate dei Somaschi; School of Monza; Seminary of Milan
Education_Notes: Educated in religious institutions. Studied rhetoric at the Merate dei Somaschi school; philosophy at the school of Monza, run by former Jesuits; and theology at the seminary of Milan, where he was ordained a priest.
Education_Locations: Merate, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown; Monza, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown; Milan, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Ordained a priest; appointed honorary canon of the basilica of Monza.
Scientific_Disciplines: Physics; Chemistry; Meteorology; Natural History; Agriculture
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered thermometer design and construction, including the thermometergraph with double scale for automatic temperature registration. Investigated combustion, liquefaction and ebullition of phosphorus, and distinguished catalytic function of platinum sponge with hydrogen. In meteorology, constructed improved hygrometers and atmidometers; formulated theory of hail formation and critiqued Volta's ideas on the subject. Later work included natural history and agricultural studies, particularly silkworm cultivation and plant physiology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Member of the Istituto Lombardo Accademia di Scienze e Lettere and Società Italiana delle Scienze di Verona. Established and operated a thermometer manufacturing factory in Milan from 1808, which flourished commercially.
Instruments_Notes: Designed the thermometergraph with double scale for automatic registration of maximum and minimum temperatures, which inspired the English physicist Six. Constructed a hygrometer from fish bladder (1836) and perfected Landriani's atmidometer. Developed a phosphorus eudiometer to overcome limitations of Giobert's design used by Spallanzani.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Istituto Lombardo Accademia di Scienze e Lettere; Società Italiana delle Scienze di Verona
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Active member of both academies; participated in congresses of Italian scientists.

Education_Notes: Studied law at family's wishes; self-taught in natural sciences through field collecting and research.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Primary focus on Cenozoic Mollusca of Piedmont and Liguria; published monographs on fossil gastropods, cancellaries, pleurotomes, columbelles, and mitres. Conducted entomological research on Piedmont diptera between 1854 and 1874. Early Italian discussion of phylloxera and viticulture. Later work demonstrated evolutionary relationships among molluscan forms.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught natural history for thirty years at Liceo Gioberti; served as curator of the paleontological collection of the Royal Geological Museum of Turin. Received royal commission to teach natural sciences to the sons of King Victor Emmanuel II.
Patronage_Notes: King Victor Emmanuel II requested Bellardi to teach natural sciences to his sons.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected honorary member of many academies and scientific societies; specific names not provided in entry.

Father_Notes: Vincenzo Bellarmino; mother was Cynthia Cervini, half-sister of Pope Marcellus II, indicating a prominent and well-connected family.
Education_Notes: Joined the Jesuit order in 1560. Earned master's degree in philosophy at the Roman College in 1563, where natural philosophy was studied in the Aristotelian tradition. Completed theological studies in Louvain and was ordained priest in 1570.
Education_Locations: Rome, Unknown, Italy, 1560, 1563; Louvain, Unknown, Belgium, 1563, 1570
Religion_Notes: Jesuit priest; became the leading Catholic theologian in the Protestant-Catholic controversy over scriptural interpretation.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Primary work was theological polemic and scriptural scholarship. His relevance to the history of science derives from his role in the Galileo affair and his epistemological views on astronomy. He engaged with questions of cosmology, the interpretation of Scripture in light of astronomical evidence, and the distinction between mathematical and physical astronomy.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Rector of the Roman College from 1592; cardinal from 1599; archbishop of Capua from 1602. In his last years served as the pope's major theological adviser at the Vatican.
Patronage_Notes: Successive popes employed him in increasingly prominent ecclesiastical roles and relied on his theological expertise.

Father_Notes: Ernesto Bellavitis was an accountant with the municipal government of Bassano. The family belonged to the nobility but was in modest circumstances.
Education_Notes: Did not pursue regular studies but was tutored by his father, who directed his interest toward mathematics. He surpassed his tutor and pursued studies independently.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Developed the method of equipollencies, a form of geometric calculus enabling operations on geometric entities analogous to algebraic operations on numbers. Contributed to algebraic geometry, classification of curves, descriptive geometry, infinitesimal analysis, and the theory of complex numbers. Also explored physics, optics, electrology, and chemistry.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked for the municipal government of Bassano from 1822 to 1843 without pay for the first ten years. Appointed professor of mathematics and mechanics at the liceo of Vicenza in 1843, then full professor of descriptive geometry at the University of Padua in 1845, transferring in 1867 to the professorship of complementary algebra and analytic geometry.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Istituto Veneto; Società Italiana dei Quaranta; Accademia dei Lincei
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Istituto Veneto on 26 September 1840. Became fellow of the Società Italiana dei Quaranta on 15 March 1850. Elected member of the Accademia dei Lincei in 1879.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Ettore Carruccio. Original works: Bibliographies in A. Education_Institution: University of Montpellier; University of Avignon
Education_Notes: Studied medicine at Montpellier from October 1584; received physician's degree from Avignon in June 1587; received doctorate from Montpellier in July 1595.
Education_Locations: Montpellier, Unknown, France, 1584, 1595; Avignon, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1587
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Held the chair of anatomy and botanical studies at Montpellier from 1593. Founded and devoted his career to the botanical garden at Montpellier, which comprised three sections: the King's Garden (medicinal plants), the Queen's Garden (mountain plants from foreign countries), and the King's Square (plants of botanical interest). Planned a comprehensive herbarium of Languedoc with binary nomenclature, illustrated with numerous plates, at the time of his death.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held the chair of anatomy and botanical studies at the medical college of Montpellier from 1593. Practiced medicine in Avignon and Pézenas before his appointment.
Patronage_Notes: Henri de Montmorency, governor of Languedoc, became his lifelong protector after they met in Pézenas. Henri IV created the chair of anatomy and botanical studies for him at Montpellier.

Father_Notes: Born to a family of small businessmen.
Education_Notes: Studied philosophy and mathematics at the University of Pisa under leading scientists including Giovanni Alfonso Borelli. No degree is named in the source.
Education_Locations: Pisa, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines: Medicine; Physiology; Anatomy; Medical Theory; Physics
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in applying mechanical philosophy to human physiology and medical theory. Made important anatomical discoveries of renal structure and function, rejecting Galenic theory. Developed hydraulic iatromechanism as a mathematical and mechanical approach to disease and medical phenomena, treating the body as a system of fluids and mechanical forces.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed professor of theoretical medicine at Pisa at age twenty; acquired chair of anatomy five years later. Resigned around age fifty to become first physician to Duke Cosimo III of Tuscany.
Patronage_Notes: Benefited from patronage of Duke Ferdinand II of Tuscany from early youth, which enabled his university attendance and early academic appointments. Later served as first physician to Duke Cosimo III.

Education_Notes: Began naval career as a cadet in Kronstadt in 1789. Participated in the first Russian round-the-world voyage (1803–1806) under Kruzenstern, gaining knowledge of physics, astronomy, hydrography, and cartography.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Led the Russian Antarctic expedition (1819–1821), discovering the Antarctic continent and conducting the first systematic oceanographic observations of Antarctic waters. Determined the position of the South Magnetic Pole with precision, classified Antarctic ice types, explained coral island formation, and made important observations on equatorial and tropical Pacific temperatures and trade winds.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Naval officer commanding various ships on the Baltic and Black seas (1806–1819); headed the Antarctic expedition (1819–1821); commanded naval units in the Mediterranean, Black, and Baltic seas thereafter; served as military governor of Kronstadt from 1839 until his death.
Patronage_Notes: Designated commander of the Antarctic expedition by the Russian government based on his scientific knowledge and naval experience. Corresponded with Gauss regarding magnetic observations.
Instruments_Notes: Used a bathometer with an internal thermometer to measure water temperature and specific weight at depths up to 402 meters, conducting early oceanographic depth measurements.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Russian Geographic Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: One of the founders of the Russian Geographic Society in 1845.

Education_Institution: University of Wittenberg; University of Paris
Education_Notes: Apprenticed as a boy to an apothecary at Foulletourte. About 1535 became apothecary to Guillaume Duprat, bishop of Clermont. Studied under botanist Valerius Cordus at the University of Wittenberg. In 1560 obtained the licentiate in medicine from the Paris Faculty of Medicine.
Education_Locations: Wittenberg, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1560
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of comparative anatomy, comparing human and bird skeletons. First to classify fish systematically and to distinguish bird types (raptorial, diurnal, web-footed, river, field). Depicted porpoise embryo and set forth early notions of embryology. Botanist who recorded observations of Near Eastern plants with woodcuts and advocated acclimatization of exotic plants in France. Studied medicinal substances including bitumen.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as apothecary to Guillaume Duprat, bishop of Clermont, and to François Cardinal de Tournon. Held licentiate in medicine from Paris Faculty of Medicine (1560). Received pension and residence at Château de Madrid from Charles IX.
Patronage_Notes: Protégé of René du Bellay, bishop of Le Mans, who enabled his study at Wittenberg. Served as apothecary to Cardinal de Tournon. Charles IX installed him at Château de Madrid and granted him a pension.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by M. Wong. Father_Notes: Apollon Grigorievich, a gymnasium teacher who did not complete his medical degree at Moscow University due to lack of funds.
Education_Notes: Graduated from gymnasium in 1873; studied at Moscow University, graduating from the Faculty of Physics and Mathematics in 1877. Master's thesis on solar spots (1886). Doctoral dissertation on the spectrum of δ Cephei defended in 1896.
Education_Locations: Moscow, Unknown, Russia, 1873, 1877
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in astrophysical spectroscopy and radial velocity determination. Conducted photographic studies of the sun, planets, and stars. Investigated spectroscopic binary stars, Cepheid variables, and novae. Verified the Doppler principle experimentally. Studied solar rotation, sunspot temperatures, and Saturn's rings.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Supernumerary assistant at Moscow Observatory from 1879; junior assistant in astronomy at Pulkovo Observatory from 1888; staff astrophysicist from 1891; vice-director of Pulkovo from 1908 to 1916; director from 1917 to 1919; honorary director from 1933.
Patronage_Notes: Worked within the Russian Imperial Academy of Sciences system; elected extraordinary academician in 1903 and ordinary academician in 1906.
Instruments: Spectrograph; Refractor; Meridional Circle; Transit Instrument
Instruments_Notes: Built and improved spectrographs at Pulkovo; pioneered use of dry photographic plates instead of colloidal plates. Constructed an original device with rotating water-wheel mirrors to verify the Doppler principle. Used 30-inch refractor and other powerful refractors at Pulkovo Observatory.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: International Union for Cooperation in Solar Research
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Joined the International Union for Cooperation in Solar Research in 1904, organized by G. E. Hale. Participated in the Commission for the Investigation of the Sun in Russia.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by P. G. Kulikovsky. Original works: "Pyatna na solntse i ikh dvizhenie" (1886); "Issledovanie spektra peremennoy zvezdy δ Cephei" (1895); "Astrospektroskopia" (Petrograd, 1921); and numerous papers in Izvestiya Imperatorskoi akademii nauk and other journals. Zhukov, Byulleten' Komissii po issledovaniya solntsa (1934).

Father_Notes: Father Eugenio painted miniatures; grandfather Giovanni was an engraver of precious stones and cameos. Family was artistic but faced financial difficulties.
Education_Notes: Studied mathematics at the University of Pavia from 1853 to 1856 under Francesco Brioschi. Financial difficulties interrupted formal education; continued mathematical studies independently while working as a railroad engineer's secretary.
Education_Locations: Pavia, Unknown, Italy, 1853, 1856
Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; Geometry; Differential Geometry; Applied Mathematics; Physics
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Early work focused on differential geometry of curves and surfaces, influenced by Gauss, Lamé, and Riemann. Major contribution was the interpretation of non-Euclidean geometry through surfaces of constant curvature, demonstrating its consistency within Euclidean geometry. Later work encompassed elasticity, fluid mechanics, potential theory, wave theory, thermodynamics, optics, and Maxwell's electromagnetic theory.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held successive chairs of mathematics at Bologna (1862–1864), Pisa (1864–1866), Bologna again (1866–1873), Rome (1873–1876), Pavia (1876–1891), and Rome again (1891–1900). Also worked as secretary to a railroad engineer in Verona and Milan before his academic career.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Accademia dei Lincei
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Became president of the Accademia dei Lincei in 1898.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by D. J. Struik. Beltrami's works collected in Opere matematiche, 4 vols. (Milan, 1902–1920). Key papers: 'Saggio di interpretazione della geometria non-euclidea,' Giornale di matematiche 6 (1868); 'Richerche di analisi applicata alla geometria,' Giornale di matematiche 2–3 (1864–1865); 'Teoria fondamentale degli spazi di curvatura costante,' Annali di matematica ser. 2 (1868–1869); 'Richerche sulle cinematica dei fluidi,' Opere II (1871–1874). Alt_Name: Edouard Van Beneden; Edward Van Beneden
Father_Notes: P.J. Van Beneden was a zoologist and professor at the Catholic University in Louvain; he organized a modest laboratory on the Belgian seacoast at Ostend where Edouard studied fauna.
Education_Notes: No formal degree is named in the entry. Edouard studied under his father's direction and at the laboratory at Ostend; appointed professor at Liège in 1870.
Religion_Notes: His father was professor at the Catholic University in Louvain; no explicit statement of Edouard's own faith.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Studied protozoa, hydraria, cestodes, nematodes, tunicates, dicyemida, and vertebrates, particularly mammals. Made major contributions to understanding egg maturation and fertilization in Ascaris, demonstrating the union of male and female pronuclei and the individuality of chromosomes. Pioneered cell lineage studies and tunicate embryology. Proposed the phylum Mesozoa as a transition between unicellular and multicellular forms.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed professor (chargé de cours) at the University of Liège in 1870, promoted to ordinarius in 1874, and held this position until his death.

Education_Notes: Apprenticed to pharmacist Louis Stoffels, a natural history collector whose house inspired his scientific vocation. Studied humanities, then medicine at the University of Louvain, where he obtained the M.D. Subsequently studied zoology in Paris.
Education_Locations: Louvain, Unknown, Belgium, Unknown, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Appointed professor at the Catholic University of Louvain in 1835.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Naturalist whose work spanned most animal phyla, with emphasis on embryology in systematic classification. Principal contribution was elucidating the life cycle of cestodes (tapeworms), demonstrating the relationship between cysticerci and taenias (1849). Later devoted himself to cetacean studies, both living and fossil, and determined that a fossil skeleton from Bernissart belonged to Iguanodon. Extensive work on parasites including trematodes, nematodes, and acanthocephalans.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of zoology at the Catholic University of Louvain from 10 April 1835 until his death.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie royale de Belgique
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Member of the Belgian Royal Academy; received an important prize from the Institut de France in 1853 for a paper on the development and transmission of intestinal worms.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Marcel Florkin. Original works: complete list in Notices biographiques et bibliographiques de l'Académie royale de Belgique (1886, 1896). Father_Notes: Father was Lorenzo Benedetti; maternal uncle was also a physician, indicating a medical family.
Education_Notes: Received excellent education in letters and medicine. Studied at Padua, where he also taught. Giorgio Merula, a historian and humanist, was among his teachers.
Education_Locations: Padua, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Principal contributions to anatomy through dissection demonstrations and his treatise Historia corporis humani sive anatomice, which described the human body systematically and encouraged empirical observation over reliance on written authorities. Also compiled a thirty-book codification of diseases and worked on the text of Pliny's Natural History.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught at Padua; practiced medicine in Venice; served as a physician in the war against Charles VIII of France in 1495; served Venice abroad in Greece, Crete, Melos, and the Dalmatian coast.
Patronage_Notes: Served the Venetian state in military and diplomatic capacities; maintained friendships with families high in Venetian nobility and government.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Dorothy M. Schullian. Alt_Name: Jean Baptiste Benedetti; John Baptist Benedetti
Father_Notes: Described by Luca Guarico as a Spaniard, philosopher, and physician (or student of nature); provided most of Benedetti's education, making him a philosopher, musician, and mathematician by age eighteen.
Education_Notes: No formal education beyond age seven except study of the first four books of Euclid's Elements under Niccolò Tartaglia, probably around 1546–1548. Relations with Tartaglia were poor; Tartaglia never acknowledged him as a pupil.
Education_Locations: Venice, Unknown, Italy, 1546, 1548
Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; Physics; Mechanics; Astronomy; Astrology; Music
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in mathematical physics and mechanics, particularly the theory of falling bodies and impetus. Made contributions to hydrostatics, perspective, geometry, and the mechanics of musical consonance. Admirer of Copernicus; astronomical interests were largely astrological. Explained the ruddy color of the moon during total eclipse through atmospheric refraction.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Court mathematician to Duke Ottavio Farnese at Parma (1558–c.1566); taught mathematics and science at the court of Duke Emanuele Filiberto of Savoy at Turin (1567–1590). Served as astrologer and adviser on engineering and university affairs. Had considerable private means.
Patronage_Notes: Patronized by Duke Ottavio Farnese of Parma and Duke Emanuele Filiberto of Savoy. Granted a patent of nobility in 1570 by the Duke of Savoy.
Instruments_Notes: Designed and constructed sundials at Parma and Turin; published the most comprehensive treatise on sundial theory and construction to that time (De gnomonum, 1573), covering dials at various inclinations and on cylindrical and conical surfaces.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Stillman Drake. Father_Notes: Father Edvard Otto Benedicks and mother Sofia Elisabeth Tholander came from families long involved in the Swedish steel industry.
Education_Notes: Concentrated on natural sciences at Uppsala; received Ph.D. in 1904 with dissertation on physical and physicochemical research on carbon steel.
Education_Locations: Uppsala, Unknown, Sweden, Unknown, 1904
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in metal microscopy and metallography; investigated cooling power of liquids, quenching velocities, and steel constituents; studied thermoelectrical phenomena and physical properties of steel; researched non-metallic inclusions in iron and steel and superconductivity mechanisms.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed professor of physics at University of Stockholm in 1910; director of the Swedish Institute of Metallography from 1920 for fifteen years; continued research at his private Laboratorium Benedicks for twenty years thereafter.
Patronage_Notes: Swedish Institute of Metallography established 1920 with sponsorship from iron and steel industry and government; Benedicks served as director.
Instruments_Notes: Pioneered metal microscopy; personally designed and constructed much of his experimental apparatus in collaboration with assistants.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Iron & Steel Institute
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Awarded the Iron & Steel Institute's gold medal in 1908 for investigations on cooling power of liquids and steel constituents.

Father_Notes: Washington Gano Benedict was a businessman of middle-class background with secondary-school education.
Education_Institution: Massachusetts College of Pharmacy; Harvard University; University of Heidelberg
Education_Notes: One year of chemistry study at Massachusetts College of Pharmacy (1888–1889); continued at Harvard, receiving B.A. (1893) and M.A. (1894) in chemistry; additional year at Heidelberg under Victor Meyer, earning Ph.D. magna cum laude.
Education_Locations: Boston, Massachusetts, United States, 1888, 1889; Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States, 1889, 1894; Heidelberg, Unknown, Germany, 1894, 1895
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Transformed from chemist into world expert on animal calorimetry and respiratory gas analysis. Invented apparatus to measure oxygen consumption, expired air, and heat simultaneously (1924). Established basal metabolic-rate standards for humans (1919) and investigated lipogenesis, insensible perspiration, and metabolic rates in various physiological conditions including diabetes.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Lecturer in chemistry at Wesleyan University (1905), professor (1907); director of Boston Nutrition Laboratory (1907–1937). Supplemented income through research as chemist at Storrs Agricultural Experimental Station (1896–1900) and as physiological chemist for U.S. Department of Agriculture (1895–1907).
Patronage_Notes: Carnegie Foundation trustees established the Boston Nutrition Laboratory under Benedict's direction, following endorsement by William Welch and John Shaw Billings.
Instruments_Notes: Designed and improved apparatus for animal calorimetry and respiratory gas analysis. His respirator (1924) measured oxygen consumption, expired air, and heat simultaneously and provided the foundation for the basal metabolic-rate test.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: National Academy of Sciences; American Philosophical Society; American Academy of Arts and Sciences; Society of American Magicians
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to National Academy of Sciences (1914), American Philosophical Society (1910), American Academy of Arts and Sciences (1930), and Society of American Magicians (1930). Honorary member of medical and scientific societies across Europe.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Charles A. Culotta. Original works: Experiments on the Metabolism of Matter and Energy in the Human Body, bull. no. 69, U.S.D.A. Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Charles A. Culotta.

Father_Notes: Paolo Benivieni was a nobleman and notary.
Education_Notes: Studied medicine at the University of Pisa.
Education_Locations: Pisa, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Buried in the chapel of St. Michael in the Church of the SS. Annunziata, Florence. Well regarded by both Ficino and Savonarola.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of pathological anatomy; authored De abditis nonnullis ac mirandis morborum et sanationum causis, an early systematic study of disease causes based on autopsy observations. Performed at least twenty autopsies and observed gallstones, urinary calculi, scirrhous cancer of the stomach, fibrous tumor of the heart, peritonitis, and fetal transmission of syphilis. Also practiced as a competent surgeon.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced as a physician in Florence, treating prominent families including the Medici, Strozzi, Pazzi, Guicciardini, Brunelleschi, and Bardi. Associated with the University of Pisa through colleagues Bernardo Torni and Lorenzo Lorenzi, who were teachers there.
Patronage_Notes: Physician to Lorenzo the Magnificent and the Medici family; dedicated De pestilentia ad Laurentium Medicem to Lorenzo de' Medici.

Father_Notes: Justin Benoit was a distinguished surgeon and dean of the faculty at the medical school of Montpellier.
Education_Institution: University of Montpellier; École des Hautes Études
Education_Notes: Studied medicine at Montpellier at his father's insistence, receiving his medical doctorate in 1869. Subsequently turned to physics and entered the laboratory of the École des Hautes Études, where he conducted experiments on temperature dependence of electrical resistance in metals and received his doctoral ès sciences in 1873.
Education_Locations: Montpellier, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1869; Paris, Unknown, France, 1869, 1873
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted experimental research on electrical resistance in metals and its temperature dependence. As director of the Bureau International des Poids et Mesures, standardized units of length, temperature, and electrical resistance. Investigated thermal expansion, thermometer design, and the relationship between the standard meter and wavelengths of light. Determined the standard ohm and worked on standardization of surveying wires.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked four years in the electrical industry after receiving his doctorate. Served as assistant director and then director (1889–1915) of the Bureau International des Poids et Mesures. Held honorary position of president of the Société Française de Physique.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed assistant director and subsequently director of the Bureau International des Poids et Mesures, a government standards institution.
Instruments_Notes: Studied and compared various thermometer designs for standardization purposes. Associated with standardization of twenty-four-meter Jaderin surveying wires.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Société Française de Physique; Académie des Sciences; Physical Society of London
Scientific_Societies_Notes: President of the Société Française de Physique; correspondent of the Académie des Sciences; honorary fellow of the Physical Society of London.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Eugene Frankel. Father_Notes: Robert Daniel Bensley was a prosperous farmer.
Education_Institution: Collegiate Institute; University College of the University of Toronto; University of Toronto
Education_Notes: Graduated from Collegiate Institute in Hamilton in 1883. Entered University College of the University of Toronto in 1884; received Governor General's Medal in both arts and sciences upon graduation. Entered medical department of University of Toronto in 1889 and received M.B. in 1892.
Education_Locations: Hamilton, Ontario, Canada, Unknown, 1883; Toronto, Ontario, Canada, 1884, Unknown; Toronto, Ontario, Canada, 1889, 1892
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in the study of cell organelles and histological technique. Demonstrated the replenishment of gastric mucosa cells, differentially stained the islets of Langerhans (1906), confirmed the Golgi apparatus in cells (1910), and with B.C.H. Harvey demonstrated the mechanism of gastric hydrochloric acid secretion (1912). Modified the freezing-drying technique with I. Gersh (1934) to isolate and analyze mitochondria.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant demonstrator in biology at University of Toronto after 1892. Joined anatomy department of University of Chicago in 1901, became acting head in 1901 and director in 1907, serving for twenty-six years.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by P. G. Roofe. Father_Notes: Samuel Bentham, inspector-general of naval works, ennobled in 1809. George inherited adequate wealth from his father and uncle Jeremy Bentham.
Education_Institution: Faculty of Theology at Montauban; Lincoln's Inn
Education_Notes: Early education sporadic and largely by private tutors. Attended faculty of theology at Montauban, where he studied French and Latin literature, natural philosophy, mathematics, and Hebrew. Later studied law at Lincoln's Inn and was called to the bar in November 1831, but abandoned law for botany in 1833. Self-taught in botany and acquired reading proficiency in fourteen languages.
Education_Locations: Montauban, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; London, Unknown, England, Unknown, 1831
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering systematic botanist whose principal work was the classification and description of plant families and genera. First became interested in botany at age seventeen during travels in France. Made major contributions to the taxonomy of Labiatae and other plant families. Collaborated with Joseph D. Hooker on Genera plantarum (1862–1883), a comprehensive synthesis of plant classification based on the Kew Herbarium.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Inherited wealth from father and uncle Jeremy Bentham allowed him to abandon law in 1833 and pursue botany full-time. Held honorary position as secretary of the Royal Horticultural Society from 1829 to 1840. Worked at Kew Gardens after 1854 with special research facilities provided by the Hookers.
Patronage_Notes: Collaborated closely with Joseph D. Hooker and the Hooker family at Kew Gardens, who provided research facilities and support after 1854.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Linnean Society; Royal Society; Royal Horticultural Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Admitted fellow of the Linnean Society in 1828 and served as its president from 1861. Elected F.R.S. in 1863 and awarded the Royal Medal in 1859. Honorary secretary of the Royal Horticultural Society from 1829 to 1840.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by George Taylor. Original works: Catalogue des plantes indigènes des Pyrénées et du bas Languedoc (Paris, 1826); Outlines of a New System of Logic (London, 1827); Labiatarum genera et species (London, 1832–1836); Handbook of the British Flora (London, 1858); Flora Hongkongensis (London, 1861); Genera plantarum (London, 1862–1883); Flora Australiensis (London, 1863–1878); On the Recent Progress and Present State of Systematic Botany, Report of the British Association for the Advancement of Science (1875). Secondary: Leonard Huxley, Life and letters of Sir Joseph Dalton Hooker (London, 1918); B. Daydon Jackson, George Bentham (London, 1906).

Father_Notes: Heinrich Benzenberg was a Protestant clergyman and theological writer.
Education_Institution: University of Herborn; University of Marburg; University of Göttingen; University of Duisburg
Education_Notes: Studied theology at Herborn and Marburg; later turned to natural sciences at Göttingen; received doctorate from University of Duisburg in 1800 with thesis on determining longitude by transiting stars. Encouraged by physicists A. G. Kästner and Georg Lichtenberg.
Education_Locations: Herborn, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Marburg, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Göttingen, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Duisburg, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1800
Religion_Notes: Son of a Protestant clergyman; initially studied theology.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted pioneering simultaneous observations of meteors with H. W. Brandes (1798 onward), determining their height and velocity for the first time and supporting Chladni's cosmic origin theory. Performed original experiments on falling bodies demonstrating Earth's rotation through eastward displacement of falling spheres (1802, 1804), predating Foucault by fifty years. Later work included ballistic experiments and geodetical surveys. Built private observatory in Bilk two years before death.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of mathematics at the Lyceum in Düsseldorf from 1805; directed land survey and registry of the duchy of Berg (1805–1810); after leaving government service, devoted himself to science as a private citizen while writing on politics and constitutional law.
Patronage_Notes: Directed the land survey and registry of the duchy of Berg under government appointment.
Instruments_Notes: Built a small private observatory on his property in Bilk two years before his death; bequeathed it to the city of Düsseldorf with an endowment for an resident astronomer. Johann Schmidt, F. Brünnow, and R. Luther subsequently made important astronomical observations there, particularly of minor planets.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Bernhard Sticker. Original works: Versuche die Entfernung, die Geschwindigkeit und die Bahnen der Sternschnuppen zu Bestimmen (Hamburg, 1800, with H. W. Father_Notes: Étienne Bérard was a chemical manufacturer and associate of Chaptal; recommended his son to Berthollet.
Education_Institution: University of Paris; University of Montpellier
Education_Notes: Studied at the newly reestablished University of Paris around 1807–1811, earning bachelier-ès-lettres (1811) and licencié-ès-sciences. Received M.D. from Montpellier on 9 July 1817. Also trained as laboratory assistant to Berthollet at Arcueil.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, 1807, 1811; Montpellier, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1817
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Early work on salt analysis and solubilities; collaborated with Malus on polarization of infrared and ultraviolet radiation; best known for specific heats of gases research with Delaroche (prize 1811); pioneered scientific study of fruit ripening and oxygen consumption in stored fruit.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught in the faculty of medicine at Montpellier after 1813; also practiced as a physician (M.D.).
Patronage_Notes: Recommended to Berthollet by his father's associate Chaptal; lived in Berthollet's house at Arcueil and became member of the Society of Arcueil; elected correspondent in chemistry section of Paris Académie des Sciences on 20 December 1819.
Instruments_Notes: Designed and used a copper calorimeter filled with water to measure specific heats of gases by passing them through a spiral tube and observing temperature rise.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Society of Arcueil; Paris Académie des Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Member of the Society of Arcueil from ca. 1807; elected correspondent in the chemistry section of the Paris Académie des Sciences on 20 December 1819.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by M.P. Crosland. Original works: 'Sur les élémens de quelques combinaisons' (Annales de chimie, 1809); 'Mémoire sur la détermination de la chaleur spécifique des différens gaz' with François Delaroche (Annales de chimie, 1813); 'Mémoire sur les propriétés physiques et chimiques des divers rayons qui composent la lumière solaire' (Mémoires de la Société d'Arcueil, 1817); 'Mémoire sur la maturation des fruits' (Annales de chimie et de physique, 1821); 'Lettre à M. Gay-Lussac sur les usines de gaz inflammable de la houille' (Annales de chimie et de physique, 1825). Secondary: Maurice Crosland, The Society of Arcueil (Cambridge, 1965); Dana G. Dalrymple, The Development of Controlled Atmosphere Storage of Fruit (Washington, D.C., 1967).

Education_Notes: Earned M.D. from Montpellier with thesis on natural medicine (1811). Later worked in Paris on the Dictionnaire des sciences médicales before returning to Montpellier.
Education_Locations: Montpellier, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1811
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Physician and medical theorist; contributed articles on cranioscopy, trance states, and muscle physiology to the Dictionnaire des sciences médicales. Wrote extensively on the doctrines of the Montpellier medical school and comparative medical philosophy across European schools. Advocated for empirical observation and analytical method over synthetic theorizing.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Successful private teacher of medicine in Montpellier; collaborated on the Dictionnaire des sciences médicales in Paris; appointed professor of public health at the Faculté de Médecine of Montpellier in 1823, taking the chair in 1826.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Pierre Huard. Original works incl. (Paris, 1824). Secondary: E. Beaugrand, Dictionnaire Dechambre, IX (1868); R. de Saussure, Bulletin of the History of Medicine, supp. 3 (1944).

Father_Notes: Faustino Barigazzi was a surgeon of Carpi; Giacomo received rudimentary training in anatomy and surgery from him.
Education_Notes: Received rudimentary training from his father and possibly classical education from Aldus Manutius. Studied more systematically, perhaps in Ferrara or Bologna, before entering the medical school of the University of Bologna, where he studied under Girolamo Manfredi, Lionello dei Vittori, Gabriele Zerbi, and Alessandro Achillini, receiving his degree on 4 August 1489.
Education_Locations: Bologna, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, 1489
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in anatomical investigation based on personal dissection and observation. Authored the Commentaria, the first major work since Galen to present extensive anatomical information from direct investigation. Recognized numerous anatomical structures including the vermiform appendix, arytenoid cartilages, thymus, sphenoidal sinus, and corrected traditional Galenic errors regarding the rete mirabile and cardiac anatomy. Also wrote an important neurosurgical treatise on skull fractures.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Lecturer in surgery at the University of Bologna from 1502, becoming responsible for anatomy instruction as well. Practiced surgery independently, possibly as a military surgeon during Italian wars. Served as medical consultant to prominent figures including the Medici family and various nobles.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by the Medici family, particularly Pope Leo X and Cardinal Giulio de' Medici (later Pope Clement VII), who enabled his leave of absence and commissioned works. Called to Rome for medical consultation during the pontificate of Julius II. Served as physician to Alessandro Soderini and other Medici-connected patients. Commanded by Pope Clement VII to assist Giovanni dalle Bande Nere in 1525.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by C. D. O'Malley. Berengario's works: Anothomia Mundini noviter impressa ac per Carpum castigata (Bologna, 1514; Venice, 1529, ca. 1530, 1538, ca. 1575); Tractatus de fractura calvae sive cranei (Bologna, 1518; Venice, 1535; Leiden, 1629, 1651, 1715, 1728); Commentaria cum amplissimis additionibus super anatomia Mundini (Bologna, 1521); Habes in hoc volumine...libros tres de crisi (Bologna, 1522); Isagogae breves (Bologna, 1522, 1523; Strasbourg, 1530; Venice, 1535); Libri anatomici (Bologna, 1529). Father_Notes: Simon Gregor'evich Berg, a notary.
Education_Notes: Graduated from Second Kishinev Gymnasium in 1894 with gold medal. Enrolled in natural science section of Faculty of Physics and Mathematics at Moscow University, receiving gold medal and first-degree diploma in zoology in 1898 for dissertation on pike embryology. Received degree of doctor of geography in 1909 for dissertation on the Aral Sea. Awarded degree of doctor of zoology in 1934.
Education_Locations: Kishinev, Unknown, Russia, Unknown, 1894; Moscow, Unknown, Russia, 1894, 1898
Scientific_Disciplines: Geography; Ichthyology; Limnology; Zoology; Paleontology; Geology; Climatology; Biogeography
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of limnology in Russia; conducted foundational studies of lakes in Kazakhstan examining salinity, temperature, fauna, and origin. Major contributions to ichthyology including anatomy, embryology, systematics, and geographical distribution of Soviet fishes; studied fish migration and spawning. Developed system of geographical zones based on climatic, soil, and biological factors. Conducted paleoclimatic and paleogeographic reconstructions; studied loess formation and soil development. Analyzed zoogeographical distribution to determine timing of glacial epochs. Addressed origin of life and species development.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Inspector of fisheries in Aral Sea and Syr-Dar'ya River (1898–1902). Zoologist and director of ichthyology section at Zoological Museum of Academy of Sciences, St. Petersburg (1904–1914). Professor of ichthyology at Moscow Agricultural Institute (1913–1917). Professor of geography at Petrograd University (1917–1950). Head of applied ichthyology section at State Institute of Experimental Agronomy / Institute of Fish Industry (1922–1934). Head of fossil fish section at Zoological Institute of Academy of Sciences (1934–1950). Taught at Pedagogical Institute and Geographical Institute.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Russian Geographical Society; All-Union Geographical Society; Academy of Sciences of the U.S.S.R.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Awarded P.P. Semenov Gold Medal by Russian Geographical Society in 1909. Elected associate member of Academy of Sciences in 1928 and academician in 1946. President of All-Union Geographical Society from 1940 to 1950. Awarded Konstantinovsky Medal of Russian Geographical Society (1915) and Medal of Asiatic Society of India (1936). Honored Scientist of R.S.F.S.R. (1934) and Laureate of the State, first degree (1951).
